World.title: US threatens EU over its green reporting rules
World.content:
The dispute centers on two pillars of the EU’s corporate sustainability rulebook: the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, which requires large companies to address human rights and environmental harms linked to their operations and supply chains, and the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, which requires companies to disclose sustainability-related information.

Brussels has scaled back both laws in its drive to cut red tape, but has stopped short of Washington’s demand to shield U.S. companies from their reach.

Last week, Puzder similarly attacked the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism as a tariff on U.S. exporters. On Thursday, the White House also accused the EU and more than 40 countries of enabling Chinese goods to skirt U.S. tariffs by rerouting them through their markets.

A European Commission spokesperson told POLITICO that Brussels had made “considerable efforts” to explain its rules and highlight "its willingness to cooperate with the US to increase trade where possible," but drew a line at changing its regulatory regime in response to U.S. pressure.

“We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation,” said the spokesperson.

This story has been updated.

Koen Verhelst contributed reporting.

World.title: Le Conseil constitutionnel censure la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs
World.content:
“L’interdiction instituée par la loi est susceptible de s’appliquer à des services de communication en ligne dont les risques pour la santé et la sécurité des mineurs ne sont pas établis”, estime encore le Conseil constitutionnel, insistant sur l’imprécision autour du champ d’application de l’article.

Le risque avait été soulevé au moment de l’examen du texte au Sénat, certains élus de la Chambre haute ayant tenté d’imposer l’établissement d’une “liste noire” qui définirait plus précisément les plateformes concernées par cette limitation d’accès aux mois de 15 ans – et éviterait ainsi le risque de censure par le Conseil constitutionnel.

Un élément du texte retiré au moment de son examen en Commission mixte paritaire pour assurer sa conformité avec le droit européen.

Le Conseil constitutionnel estime par ailleurs que le texte ne définit pas les garanties légales propres à assurer le droit au respect de la vie privée des utilisateurs qui seront contraints de faire vérifier leur âge par les plateformes pour prouver leur majorité.

“Le gouvernement n’a pas assez écouté le Sénat et le risque d’inconstitutionnalité que nous pointions depuis des mois. Désormais, le risque, c’est que le texte soit vidé de sa substance”, a réagi, sur ce point, la rapporteure du texte au Sénat, Catherine Morin-Desailly, auprès de POLITICO.

Un constat partagé par le député socialiste Arthur Delaporte, à l’origine de l’une des saisines du Conseil constitutionnel. L'autre émanait du groupe de la France Insoumise (LFI).

World.title: French court blocks social media ban for under 15s
World.content:
The French president has also pushed restrictions to the top of the EU agenda, with an expected announcement of bloc-wide measures by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September.

In a statement late Friday, the French presidential office said the government would not be giving up on the bill. It has set a new target date for spring 2027, which coincides with when Macron will leave office.

The statement said Macron “has instructed the Prime Minister to work, as quickly as possible, on a legally sound draft that takes into account” the court's decision. The ruling hinted at what would make the age restriction align with fundamental rights: giving parents more flexibility.

Peter Craddock, a senior Brussels-based attorney advising social media firms, said the French court decision could have far-reaching implications.

"What they're basically saying here is: 'Listen, government, if you want to get this to succeed, you can't just work on the basis of a general ban. There have to be limitations," said Craddock, a partner at Keller & Heckman. "There have to be ways for people to say, 'well, actually, in my case, my son, my daughter is of a certain degree of maturity and is able to use this properly.'"

The government bill had passed through the French legislative procedure after a lengthy back-and-forth earlier this summer. It was set to bring forward Europe's first social media age restrictions, with Greece and Denmark planning to follow suit.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Latvia's military warned that similar incidents may happen again in the future. "While the Russian aggression in Ukraine is ongoing, the recurrence of such cases when a foreign unmanned aircraft enters or approaches Latvian airspace is possible," it said.

An air raid alert was declared in four eastern Latvian municipalities at around 4 a.m. local time. The military urged people to stay indoors and away from exterior walls.

After the drone was downed, Sandra Kapteine, head of the Rugāji village administration, told the Latvian Information Agency that the incident “caused no casualties,” as the drone wreckage fell in a “wooded area.”

There has been an uptick in similar incidents over recent months in countries close to the war-zone. A week ago, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said a Ukrainian-made drone crossed Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded near the village of Kardam.

World.title: Spain and Morocco reinforce border amid fears of fresh Ceuta migrant surge
World.content:
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska traveled to Ceuta on Thursday to inspect border infrastructure and a new sea barrier designed to keep people from swimming into the city. The exclave’s security personnel has also been reinforced with an additional 300 police officers and 2,000 soldiers.

“We do this to dissuade anyone who aspires to enter Ceuta and Melilla irregularly,” said Grande-Marlaska. “None of them will remain in Ceuta, none of them will make it to the Iberian Peninsula, none of them will be given legal status.”

The rumored mass crossing has been cited by critics of Spain’s migration policies.

Austria’s conservative Europe, Integration and Family Minister Claudia Bauer, last week mentioned the rumored Aug. 15 surge in a written statement, demanding Madrid “immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold.”

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government also cited the possibility of a mid-August mass arrival last week while justifying its decision to maintain border checks on travelers from Spain.

World.title: NATO fighter jets shoot down drone over Romania near Moldova border
World.content:
Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets, which were already on alert as a precaution, received authorisation to intervene at 04:44 on Sunday morning. The drone was sighted 24 kilometres north of the town of Galati.

 

The drone, whose origin has not been confirmed by the Romanian authorities, was intercepted and destroyed between the towns of Baleni and Cudalbi, in the south-east of the country, in an area close to the border with Moldova.

The defence minister congratulated both the Spanish pilots and the Romanian military personnel in charge of the command centre. In his message, Miruta stressed that Romania "is defending its airspace" and that it has the backing of its allies, which he described as a tangible security guarantee based on vigilance, rapid response and solidarity among the countries of the Alliance.

The minister emphasised that Romania is on the front line of the European Union's defence, a position he attributes to the roughly 614 kilometres of land border the country shares with Ukraine.

The incident also comes after another night of exchanges of attacks between Russia and Ukraine. Russian bombardments triggered large fires in Kyiv, with at least two people injured, while Moscow claimed it had been targeted by more than 600 drones launched by Kyiv, leaving three people wounded on Russian territory.

A string of incidents on the eastern flank

This latest incident adds to a long list of incursions recorded in recent weeks in Romanian airspace.

Last Thursday, two Spanish F-18s had already taken off from the Mihail Kogălniceanu base after an airborne object was detected near the river border with Ukraine, a drone that spent around 12 minutes in Romanian territory before returning to Ukraine, forcing the authorities to send an SMS alert to residents of Tulcea county.

A day later, while a drone crashed in Romania after crossing the country's airspace undetected by radar because it was flying at very low altitude, tensions were also mounting in the Baltic, where allied fighter jets shot down another drone over Latvian territory.

At the start of the month, another unidentified device exploded in Bulgarian airspace, near the border with Romania, after entering from Romanian territory.

The most serious precedent dates back to 29 May, when a Russian drone struck a residential block in Galati, sparked a fire and injured two people, in what the Atlantic Alliance at the time described as an irresponsible escalation by Russia.

The NATO secretary-general, Mark Rutte, reiterated at the time that the organisation is ready to defend every inch of allied territory against this type of threat.

World.title: UK police apologise for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims
World.content:
London's Metropolitan Police has apologised after accidentally exposing the email addresses of people who came forward to report sexual abuse by Mohamed Al Fayed.

 

The force blamed “human error”, saying officers sent a monthly email update to victims in which the email addresses of 143 people were visible to other recipients instead of being hidden. A number of additional recipients also received the email.

A group representing victims described the incident as "appalling".

In a statement, the Metropolitan police said "The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken," adding that those affected had all been contacted.

The force has apologised and added that "The incident is being investigated as a matter of priority, and we are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar breach from happening again."

The Met police has referred itself to the UK information watchdog, the Information Commissioner's Office.

Who was Mohamed Al Fayed?

Born in Egypt, Mohamed Al Fayed was best known as the billionaire owner of the Ritz Hotel in Paris, Fulham Football Club and the famous London department store, Harrods. He was also the father of Dodi Al Fayed, who died in a 1997 car crash alongside Princess Diana.

Following his death in 2023 at age 94, hundreds of women accused Al Fayed of rape, sexual assault and trafficking. Many of the alleged crimes relate to his time as owner of Harrods.

Al Fayed (right) outside Harrods in 2005 Copyright 2005 AP. All rights reserved.

Though some complaints were made against him before his death, he never faced any charges.

Earlier this month, at least five women who say they were victims of Al Fayed were formally recognised by the UK's Home Office as victims of modern slavery.

The Metropolitan Police is continuing to investigate allegations against Al Fayed, as well as people who may have facilitated or enabled his offending. So far six people have been questioned, but no arrests have been made.

World.title: Morocco prevents new attempts to cross into Ceuta, army says
World.content:
Moroccan security forces on Saturday say they have prevented hundreds of people from crossing into Ceuta. Reports say the group, mostly originating from sub-Saharan Africa, had been hiding on the outskirts of Fnideq, known in Spanish as Castillejos.

 

Moroccan media says 294 people were arrested, 46 of them Moroccan and the rest from sub-Saharan Africa.

According to Moroccan security sources cited by the EFE news agency (source in Spanish), the incident took place in a mountainous area to the south-west of Ceuta, where officers moved in to disperse the group.

The same reports said the migrants remain in the area and that, for the moment, there has been no fresh attempt to approach the border fence.

Chams Edine Yakoub, 25, a Sudanese migrant hoping to cross into Ceuta, told AFP that he had been looking for opportunity. "In Ceuta, in Europe, people are better cared for," he said. "There's no work here. There's no money. There's no housing. There is absolutely nothing, I swear."

This latest attempt comes just two weeks after a mass crossing of around 72,000 mostly Moroccan men crossed into Ceuta, a Spanish territory. The vast majority of them have now been returned to Morocco.

Police deployment and checks on access roads

Fnideq's town centre woke up to a calm Saturday morning, albeit under a heavy police presence. The authorities say they have been maintaining checkpoints on the main roads into the town, particularly on the routes coming from Tetouan and Tangier.

During the early hours, surveillance was stepped up on land and at sea around the border with Ceuta, with fast boats from the Moroccan Royal Navy and surveillance drones taking part.

Despite the operation, a 17-year-old young woman managed to reach Castillejos during the night and told EFE she had travelled from Tetouan on a bus that was stopped at three checkpoints along the roughly 35 kilometres between the two towns, underlining the extent of Morocco's screening in the area.

Saturday's operation forms part of a wider deployment organised by Rabat to prevent a mass crossing into Ceuta that had been called for on social media.

The call came just a few weeks after the tragedy of 30 and 31 July, when tens of thousands of people crossed on foot and by swimming to the Spanish enclave. According to humanitarian organisations, that episode left at least 141 people dead, one of the highest death tolls ever recorded on the border between Morocco and Spain.

World.title: At least 12 people killed in a Polish tourist bus crash in Hungary
World.content:
In the early hours of Sunday, a coach overturned on a motorway in north east Hungary between Mezőkeresztes and Mezőnagymihály, Hungarian authorities reported. Units already at the scene entered the coach through its windows and have been rescuing passengers trapped inside, it added.

 

At 3 a.m. on Sunday, the disaster management service reported that firefighters had so far rescued thirty-five people from the coach, while several passengers had been trapped beneath the vehicle.

Meanwhile, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar published on his social media about the coach crash, reporting the deaths of a dozen passengers.

Statement from the prime minister Facebook

"12 people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured during the night, when a Polish coach overturned into a ditch on the M3 motorway," the prime minister said.

Péter Magyar offered his condolences to the families of the victims and wished the injured a swift recovery. He also thanked those taking part in the rescue operation for their work.

The Polish foreign minister has also confirmed the disaster, saying that they are in constant contact with the Hungarian authorities, but the details still need to be confirmed.

While, Polish President Karol Nawrocki sent his thoughts to the families of the victims, Nawrocki said, "I join in prayer and extend my deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims".

According to information provided by Hungarian Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai 47 people were travelling on the coach, several of whom were seriously injured, adding that "The driver of the vehicle involved in the accident has been taken into custody".

World.title: Großpörthen's pillory lime: 900-year-old tree with dark history
World.content:
In the small village of Großpörthen, around five kilometres south-east of Zeitz in Saxony-Anhalt, stands a tree that has witnessed history over the centuries. The mighty winter lime tree beside the village church is estimated to be between 700 and 900 years old. Its trunk has a circumference of around 9.85 metres and it is about twelve metres tall. This probably makes it the thickest known winter lime tree in Germany.

 

Related This cave village in France offers a natural escape from extreme heat

But it is not just its age that makes the lime tree special. It owes its name to its presumed role as a "court" and pillory tree. A rusty iron collar can still be seen on its trunk today. It is a reminder of a time when public punishments were part of everyday legal practice.

The iron collar on the tree is rusty but otherwise well preserved. Prof. Dr. Andreas Roloff, nationalerbe-baeume.de

Middle Ages: punishment by chaining offenders with iron collars

An iron collar was a metal ring that was placed around the neck of a convicted person and locked. Public pillory punishments involving iron collars are documented in the German-speaking world from at least the 14th century.

This form of so-called shame or honour punishment was particularly widespread in the late Middle Ages and the early modern period. However, it remained in use for several centuries and is documented in German legal sources well into the 18th century. The punishment was aimed above all at public humiliation and thus the destruction of the offender's reputation and, depending on the place and the judgement, was combined with corporal punishment.

In some cases, the offenders were given signs to wear stating their offence.

The pillory was historically used for a very wide range of offences. Sources mention, among other things, minor theft, insults, slander, disturbing the peace, violations of moral norms or cheating on measures and weights.

Court lime tree almost 1,000 years old

The exact age of the lime tree cannot be determined. For trees of this age, precise dating is difficult, partly because the trunk changes over the centuries. The unusual position of the winter lime on a slope has led to severe thickening and overgrowth in the trunk and root area. Experts from the German Dendrological Society estimate its age at between 700 and 900 years.

The tree has also survived serious damage. A larger part of the trunk is said to have broken off around the mid-20th century. Nevertheless, the lime tree has recovered and is considered to be in good health.

Germany's now second-oldest tree stands in Upstedt in Lower Saxony. It recently lost the top spot to a yew about 1,100 years old on an alpine pasture in the Allgäu. The Upstedt tree is also a lime tree, more precisely a summer lime, which is regarded as less robust. The historic square in the centre of the village where it stands was already used as a meeting place in the early second millennium; in the 13th century the lime tree became a court tree.

There is, however, no evidence that this tree, like the winter lime in Großpörthen, was also used as a pillory.

World.title: Lima Grand Prix 2026: Breakthrough victories on Day Two
World.content:
Welcome back to Lima for day two of the Judo Grand Prix as more World class judoka take to the tatami in the Peruvian capital.

 

In the -63kg category, Seiko WATANABE faced Laura VAZQUEZ FERNANDEZ. In a well matched contest, WATANABE scored a yuko in the final minute to win her first World Judo Tour gold medal.

International Judo Federation Gender Equality & Development Commission Member Mrs Katiuska SANTAELLA awarded the medals.

At -73kg, Vlad MITRU faced Jack YONEZUKA. It was MITRU’s first World Tour final and he struck gold with a cleverly worked ippon. A breakthrough performance from the Moldovan on the international stage with the biggest victory of his career so far.

International Judo Federation International Relations Commission Director Mr Oscar CASSINERIO awarded the medals.

Lima is a beautiful city with beautiful people. The atmosphere is very nice and see you next time in Lima. Vlad MITRU (MDA)

In the -70kg category, Dena POHL faced Nauana SILVA. The German judoka was determined to take the top spot on the podium and with a waza-ari score earned herself a first World Judo Tour gold medal. A landmark victory for POHL in Lima.

International Judo Federation Head Referee Director Mr Armen BAGDASAROV awarded the medals.

I didn’t think I was winning today, to be honest, because we did some hard training before but I think in the end we kind of managed to do it, the training, and I’m like, I don’t know what to say… Amazing. Dena POHL (GER)

At -81kg, David LIMA faced Francois GAUTHIER DRAPEAU.

LIMA scored a yuko early into the contest and managed to keep the advantage for the Grand Prix gold medal.

Peruvian Olympic Committee Director Mrs Leyla CHIHUAN awarded the medals.

The action continues tomorrow with the heavyweights here in beautiful Peru!

World.title: ‘Excellent profit’: Meet the Bavarian hop farmer securing his harvest and income with solar 'hats'
World.content:
A wave of farm closures is washing over Germany’s lush hop-growing regions as climate change, falling prices and declining demand for beer leave desolation in their wake.

 

As of 2026, there are just over 900 agricultural businesses in Germany specialising in hops – a dramatic drop of 40 per cent since two decades ago, with many farmers either switching to other crops or giving up altogether.

The phenomenon is so acute, it has even earned its own name: ‘höfesterben’ describes the creeping structural decline and closing of small and family-owned farms.

Increasingly, even traditional Bavarian farmers now speak openly of climate change as rising temperatures, water shortages and dry soils squeeze their yields.

Beer is integral to their region’s cultural identity, with school summer holidays timed to coincide with hop harvests replete with ‘hop queens’. Bavaria produces 86 per cent of German hops and roughly one third of global output.

The Hallertau, in the heart of the southeast German region, is the largest continuous hop-growing area in the world. Dating back to at least 860 AD, it is home to 722 of the country’s remaining hop farms.

“The years are getting hotter and drier,” says hop grower Josef Wimmer from Neuhub near Osseltshausen. Hans von der Brelie

One of them is run by fourth-generation hop grower Josef Wimmer. “The years are getting hotter and drier,” he tells Euronews Earth.

To secure the future of his farmstead in the small hamlet of Neuhub near Osseltshausen, drastic action was a necessity.

Could solar 'hats' save German hop farms?

Seven metres above the ground on Wimmer’s farm, solar panels glint, forming a sea of pale blue.

“We wanted to shade the hops because hops are a shade-loving plant,” the farmer explains. Heat slows the production of alpha acids, the compound that gives beer its pleasantly aromatic bitterness. Heat-related drought and the ensuing decline in soil health can also spark dramatic drops in yield.

Of course, the photovoltaic modules come with another key benefit: providing renewable energy for the farm. “In the first step we covered five hectares of hops with PV,” says Wimmer. “That gives us an output of two megawatts at its peak.”

Hops are a shade-loving crop. The plants climb up seven-metre-high poles. Hans von der Brelie

He first came up with the idea 10 years ago, after seeing the benefits of rooftop solar he installed in 2009. His neighbours were awash with skepticism: “There were voices saying ‘Wimmer’s lost it now, that’ll never work!’,” he recalls.

“When we started building, we became the hot spot of the Hallertau. Everyone came by to have a look. And after every big storm… everyone wanted to know whether the installation was still standing or had been blown away,” Wimmer laughs. “But everything is still standing, even after the storms.”

After the curious neighbours came the hop farmers from more distant villages to inspect the system. They were followed by local councillors and district officials, right up to ministers from the Bavarian state capital Munich.

Now Wimmer plans to expand his successful project over 20 hectares and add a one-megawatt battery storage system.

How red tape is slowing farm solar installations

He got there with the help of Bernhard Gruber, a former Airbus engineer turned solar innovator who ran with Willmer’s unconventional idea.

After two years of planning and permitting negotiations, a five kilometre power cable is being installed to connect the panels to a substation capable of sending excess energy to the grid.

“Long approval procedures are a problem. They put some farmers off going for agri-PV on a larger scale, because the bureaucratic effort is simply too great for many of them,” Gruber tells Euronews Earth.

“Especially for hop growing, but also for other agricultural specialty crops, the decisions and approvals could be made much more easily. Why things aren’t moving faster is honestly a mystery to me,” he adds.

Engineer Bernhard Gruber talking to hop farmer Josef Wimmer. Hans von der Brelie

Agri-PV keeps soil moist – and hops like that

“We’ve found that the soil has become wetter since the agri-PV modules were installed,” Wimmer says, pointing to a moisture sensor tucked among the trellises, which takes measurements both at the surface and deeper down.

“Evaporation is lower, we can keep the water from rainfall in the soil for longer – and that is good for the hops, especially in June, July and August. That’s when the hops need water.”

Balancing the right amount of shade with a solar panel angle conducive to energy production from the sun is no easy feat.

Gruber puzzled over daily and seasonal movements of the sun, hourly fluctuations in power prices, and the outcomes for the crops.

Too much shade resulted in the hop plants producing bushy shoots in the shaded upper zone – but fewer cones. Overall yields fell and less hop extract was produced.

After two years of tweaks, he achieved a happy medium, settling on a 45-degree angle for the panels instead of the original 20 degrees. This means the panels receive slightly less direct sunlight, but the hops produce more cones.

Innovation among the hops: agrivoltaics is being further developed in the Hallertau. Hans von der Brelie

Less energy but higher income

Despite producing less energy, the steeper panels actually earn Willmer more money.

If the modules are almost flat (as in the first prototype), the PV system generates most power around midday, precisely at the time when there is already surplus power in the grid and producer prices are accordingly low.

Positioned at a steeper angle, the solar system starts working efficiently from the early morning, as soon as the sun rises, or, depending on orientation, in the late afternoon and early evening – the times when electricity prices are high.

The 45-degree solution also boosts energy production in the winter, when the sun sits low on the horizon for longer periods.

“And in winter in particular you need every kilowatt hour,” says Gruber.

“At the moment we’re looking at a payback period of around 14 years, and the PV system will last at least 30 years,” the engineer calculates. “So you can imagine how much you can earn.”

Josef Wimmer’s hop farm is known throughout the region: the state-of-the-art agri-PV installation attracts visitors from all over Bavaria. Hans von der Brelie

Cutting-edge research in the hop garden

Wimmer and Gruber are not alone out in the fields. Their pilot project is the subject of several research programmes. Their cooperation and funding partners include the University of Applied Sciences Weihenstephan–Triesdorf, the internationally renowned Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Freiburg, and the Federal Office for Agriculture and Food.

The Technical University of Munich, with its agricultural research station at Dürnast, and the Hop Research Centre in Hüll are also providing scientific support for the agri-PV project. Last but not least, the Agriculture Ministry is funding the three-year trial phase with €1.4 million in research money.

Analysis by Weihenstephan–Triesdorf university reveals that Wimmer’s agri-PV installation has resulted in a 10 to 20 per cent reduction in hop yields. But the farmer says these losses are more than made up for: “The profit from electricity generation is excellent, really very good. The strong power yield offsets the lower hop yield… It’s worth it.”

Agri-PV pioneers Bernhard Gruber and Josef Wimmer on a site visit in the hop garden. Hans von der Brelie

And with only two grams of hop extract needed to brew one litre of beer, one kilo of hops can be turned into 500 litres.

“In the end this is a win-win situation,” agrees Gruber. “You’re not only earning money from electricity, you’re also earning secure money from the hop harvest.”

“Even in the part of the year when no hops are growing, the soil is still partially shaded by the PV modules,” he adds. “This keeps the soil’s moisture profile more uniform overall – and that means the land is better prepared for the next planting season.”

Researchers are now testing whether the significant improvements in soil health beneath 20-degree panels are retained under a 45-degree shade.

Soil moisture is also measured precisely. Hans von der Brelie

Could agri-PV slow the decline of farming in Europe’s south?

As human-caused global warming continues to shift Europe’s climate, traditional growing areas, developed over centuries, may have to be abandoned for cooler climes.

It’s a pattern already troubling winemakers, and bringing new opportunities for vineyards in places like Scandinavia and the UK.

Bavaria’s hop farmers jokingly quip among themselves that in 30 years’ time the hops for good Bavarian beer may have to be imported from Norway. Sooner or later, some hop farmers in the Hallertau fear it could turn into bitter reality.

Agri-PV makes it possible to do both at once: grow hops and generate solar power. Hans von der Brelie

Farmers are desperately searching for solutions but not everyone can afford to install costly irrigation systems, which are also politically controversial due to their high water use.

Some hop growers are experimenting with cover crops between the hop rows to reduce evaporation, while researchers are breeding varieties that can cope better with drought.

Others have been forced to bid a reluctant farewell to the hop business – in some cases carpeting their former farmland with solar panels instead.

Wimmer has thought about this too: “I could have said, fine, I’ll rip out my hops and install ground-mounted solar instead of hop gardens everywhere. But then I’d no longer be a farmer, just a PV entrepreneur,” he says.

Related A Japanese inventor is turning soil into a source of electricity

The first documented reference to hop growing anywhere in the world is found in Bavaria. Hans von der Brelie

‘Energy must never compete with food production’

“For me it’s about preserving hop-growing on my land,” says Wimmer. “I want to hand the farm on to the next generation in a way that gives it security and a future – but with additional income from photovoltaics.”

On a broader scale, adds Gruber, “Energy must never compete with food production” – and agri-PV could be an important way to ensure both thrive in harmony.

Agri-PV makes hop growing in the Hallertau more resilient to climate change and global warming. Hans von der Brelie

Already, agri-PV trials have cropped up over vineyards, berry patches, apple orchards and asparagus fields in Germany.

“What we’re doing could become a model for the whole of Europe,” says Gruber, as French hop farmers battle sandy, drifting soils and drought, while Czech, Slovenian, Slovakian, Polish and Austrian hop growers face similar challenges.

With extreme dry spells worsening in Europe – Germany’s ‘drought monitor’ at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research shows extreme droughts in 1976, 2003 and then almost continuously since 2018 – solutions like Wimmer’s could be a lifeline.

World.title: Exploring Andorra: The best things to do in the microstate aside from skiing and shopping
World.content:
When I told my hairdresser I’d just come back from a trip to Andorra, their immediate response was, “I couldn’t point to it on a map”.

 

Given how little the country hits the headlines, that’s hardly surprising.

Located in the east Pyrenees between France and Spain, some 85,000 people call Andorra home, with around 8 million tourists descending on the country each year. To put that into context, France, the world’s most-visited country, has 102 million tourists a year, with Spain also potentially hitting 100 million visitors in 2026.

Spanning some 468 square kilometres, it’s technically the largest of the six European microstates (the others being Vatican City, Monaco, Malta, Liechtenstein and San Marino), but it’s not exactly on the typical tourist route – unless you’re a skier, that is.

Ahead of my trip in July this year, its ski resorts were the only thing I associated with the country. And, given I have zero experience in the winter sports department, it’s not exactly been on the top of my to-visit list.

Still, with more and more of us opting for lesser-known destinations as tourist hotspots grapple with overtourism, I thought it was high time – quite literally, as Andorra la Vella is the highest capital city in Europe – for me to see what’s on offer outside of the slopes.

Things to do in Andorra la Vella

You'll find Salvador Dalí’s La Noblesse du Temps statue in the centre of Andorra La Vella Dianne Apen-Sadler

Snap a photo with Salvador Dalí’s La Noblesse du Temps

In tourist destinations across the globe, there are certain “shots” that are a must-capture when visiting. In Santorini, it’s the blue domes of Oia; in Dubai, it’s the Burj Khalifa as seen from near the fountains.

In Andorra, the frame centres on Salvador Dalí’s La Noblesse du Temps statue with the Puente de Paris in the background, helpfully decorated with a large “Andorra la Vella” sign, in case it wasn’t clear where you were.

Thankfully, you won’t have to battle crowds to get a good shot of the sculpture, which was installed in its current spot in 2010 having been gifted to the Andorra government by Enric Sabater, a close friend of the artist, in 1999.

The bronze work, which weighs around 1,400 kilos, features a melting clockface set on a tree trunk. The crown above the clock “represents the dominion of time over humanity”, according to the Andorra La Vella tourism board.

After completing the Rec del Solà, you can head into the old quarter Dianne Apen-Sadler

Walk the Rec del Solà

For another spectacular view of Andorra La Vella, consider walking the Rec del Solà.

The short route runs along an irrigation channel in the hills near the capital, offering views of the city from above, and you can find exact details for the trail on the Visit Andorra website.

The website advises it takes up to three hours, but I completed it in less than an hour. From the end of the trail, you can reach the pretty old quarter in just 15 minutes.

Casa de la Vall played served as the seat of the General Council of Andorra until 2011 Dianne Apen-Sadler

Learn about the country’s history at Casa de la Vall

Speaking of the Barri Antic, aka the old quarter, if you only visit one museum or gallery during your trip, make it Casa de la Vall.

The historic home dates back to 1580, and served as the seat of the General Council of Andorra until 2011.

Here, you can learn about the origins of the co-principality, with the current heads of state being the Bishop of Urgell and the President of France, as well as the history of the flag and coat of arms. You’ll also be able to see the cabinet of the seven keys, which has locks for each of the parishes of Andorra.

Next door, you can see the new parliament, and you can also visit Església de Sant Esteve, one of the country’s most historic churches.

7 Poets by Jaume Plensa was installed in 2014 Dianne Apen-Sadler

See the 7 Poets

In the plaza below the new parliament, you’ll be able to see another of Andorra’s most recognisable artworks: 7 Poets by Jaume Plensa.

Installed in 2014, the seven fibreglass figures have been placed on pedestals and are lit up at night.

According to the artist, “Poets are an integral part of society. They are condemned to failure, because they know they won’t even sell three books, but they are a source of fertility, like a light drizzle that penetrates the earth. In my opinion, this long process, akin to that of a farmer, is highly courageous.”

Splash the cash on the Shopping Mile

With some of the lowest rates of VAT in Europe, Andorra is known for its shopping.

Plenty cross the border to do their weekly food shop, but the main Shopping Mile is also home to many well-known international clothing brands, if that’s your cup of tea.

The Caldes Project explores the history of the natural hot springs and their use in the textile and hotel industries Dianne Apen-Sadler

Explore the country’s spa heritage through the Caldes Project

The final ‘S’ associated with Andorra after skiing and shopping is spas.

The natural hot water springs found in Escaldes were originally used for the country’s textile industry until the first thermal hotels were opened here in the mid-19th century.

Today, you can explore that history with a walk alongside Javier Balmaseda’s Water and Form, which features a series of pipes, fountains and washhouses next to the river between the Engordany Bridge and the Tosca Bridge.

If you care less about the history and more about experiencing the springs for yourself, book a visit to Caldea, the largest thermal spa in southern Europe.

You can catch the light and water show just after sunset in the summer months Dianne Apen-Sadler

See the fountain show in front of Puente de Paris

As night falls, the Passeig de les Fonts de la Rotonda promenade in front of Puente de Paris plays host to a water and light fountain show.

The time differs depending on the season (more information can be found on the Andorra La Vella website), as does the choice of music, but no matter which songs play, it’s a nice way to end a day of exploration.

Where to eat and drink in Andorra

Andorra is known for its bordes, aka farmhouse restaurants, which are typically found outside of the city centre.

If you’re looking for a quick energy boost via carbs that won’t cost an arm and a leg, swing by Laganum, which serves freshly made pasta.

Next time I’ll visit Andorra for…

As picturesque as Andorra is in the summer, I imagine a fresh sprinkling of snow makes the scenery even prettier.

Just don’t expect to see me on the slopes. Unless it’s for après-ski drinks…

How to get to Andorra

The nearest major international airports to Andorra are Toulouse–Blagnac and Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat.

On the way to Andorra, I took a bus from Lleida, which took around two and a half hours. For the return journey, I went to Barcelona, which took around three hours. I booked both buses through Andbus.

World.title: In Turkey, one of the world's longest conflicts reaches a turning point
World.content:
Turkey stands on the threshold of closing a conflict spanning almost 50 years, after the Turkish parliament this week passed a law allowing exiled Kurdish militants to return home and rejoin society. The legislation aims to end the war with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has battled the Turkish state for independence since 1984.

Advertising

On Monday, legislators voted 468-88 in favour of a law detailing how the PKK will lay down arms, disband and guide most members back into civilian life.

Many see this legislation as a turning point after decades of bloodshed.

“This law in question is going to make a giant contribution,” predicts sociologist Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

“If the PKK militants are convinced that they can be safe in Turkey, it's estimated that some 15,000 people in Europe, in Syria, in Iraq and in the prisons in Turkey are going to be either released or are going to be able to come back home.”

The PKK leadership, based primarily in Iraq, is not covered by the legislation. Nor is the group's founder and leader Abdullah Ocalan, imprisoned since 1999 in a Turkish jail.

He initiated the peace process and last year called for the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK.

People hold a photograph of Abdullah Ocalan, the jailed leader of the militant Kurdish group PKK, in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Hope, caution

Istanbul, now the city's with the world’s largest Kurdish population, became a sanctuary in the 1990s as hundreds of thousands fled the violence raging in Turkey's southeast. At the conflict’s peak, the Turkish army destroyed villages in relentless scorched-earth campaigns.

In Istanbul's Bagcilar district, home to a vibrant Kurdish community, conversations reveal a fragile mix of hope and caution.

“This law seems good for the honour of the Kurds and to stop bloodshed,” said 31-year-old Ahmet, who only wanted to be identified by his first name. “Mothers should not shed tears anymore.”

But others were more wary. “The state has been delaying our rights for decades; I do not believe this process will be different,” said Kava, who also preferred not to give his full name. “I do not trust an arrangement in which Kurds do not have legal status.”

Kurds make up around a fifth of Turkey’s population, but are not legally recognised as a minority.

Emotions appear equally divided among Turks. “If they’re agreeing to live under the Turkish flag and love our country, that’s fine – let them,” said 51-year-old Mehmet Tas.

But 40-year-old Ertugral Zengin is unconvinced. “They committed a crime – and now they are to be pardoned? Do I want something like that? No, I won’t accept it.”

PKK ends 40-year fight but doubts remain about the next steps

Political momentum

The decades-long conflict has claimed 40,000 lives and forced more than 3 million people from their homes.

While major political parties support the peace process, hardline nationalist groups remain staunchly opposed, insisting it rewards a PKK they see as already defeated.

The process hinges on the laborious task of disarming the PKK and verifying its weapons are gone.

Maintaining the current political momentum is vital, warns Asli Aydintasbas, a Turkey expert at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington DC.

“If this drags on, political support for the legislation and for the return of former PKK members, seen by many Turks as terrorists, would become politically problematic for the government. Timing and moving fast is very important to achieve reconciliation,” she says.

The government is expected to face growing pressure to address Kurdish rights, including Kurdish-language education in schools and local autonomy, along with broader democratic reforms.

Social media buzzes with questions: how can PKK members walk free while critics of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan remain behind bars?

Kurdish demonstrators in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Peace or politics? Turkey’s fragile path to ending a decades-long conflict

Yegen warns that since the new legislation fails to address Kurdish rights and democratisation reforms, the government needs to move swiftly.

“The fact that these two issues are not touched upon by the law has created many doubts on both Kurdish and Turkish sides about whether disarmament will be the government's only agenda,” he says.

For Erdogan, steering the peace process to success could secure the vital Kurdish vote in the 2028 elections. Yet extending Kurdish cultural rights risks alienating Turkish nationalists, and relaxing pressure on the opposition brings its own perils as their electoral strength grows.

For now, the negotiations present a rare window for reconciliation and lasting peace.

World.title: Moscow says 600 drones targeted region overnight
World.content:
Moscow says hundreds of drones targeted the Russian capital overnight, while NATO jets were again called into action farther south. The incidents underline the growing reach of drone warfare well beyond Ukraine itself.

Hundreds of drones have targeted the Moscow region in a sustained overnight assault that wounded three people, according to the Russian capital's mayor, as Ukraine steps up long-range attacks deep inside Russia.

Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 600 drones had been flying toward the Moscow region between Saturday evening and 6:30 a.m. local time (0330 UTC) on Sunday, adding that 201 were destroyed over the region.

What happened in the Moscow drone attack?

Sobyanin said three people were wounded in the area inside Moscow's MKAD ring road and were receiving medical treatment.

Ukraine has intensified long-range strikes inside Russia in recent weeks, targeting military and industrial facilities as well as warehouses far from the front line.

Ukraine's Kyiv Independent newspaper reported that Ukrainian forces had targeted a warehouse belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries as well as industrial facilities in several cities across the Moscow region.

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There was no immediate independent confirmation of the scale of the attack.

Spanish fighter jet shoots down drone over Romania

The attack came as NATO countries on Ukraine's borders faced fresh drone incursions of their own.

Romania's Defense Ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone early Sunday after it entered Romanian airspace from Moldova near the border with Ukraine.

The aircraft was operating on NATO duties and intercepted the drone at 5:01 a.m. local time (0201 UTC).

Debris fell in an unpopulated area of Galati county, close to the Ukrainian border.

Romanian authorities did not immediately identify the drone's origin or say who launched it.

Romania has repeatedly reported drone debris on its territory since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube.

On Friday, an Italian Eurofighter operating under NATO command also shot down a foreign drone that entered Latvian airspace.

World.title: Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
World.content:
Intelligence agencies report that North Korea is preparing to send up to 50,000 troops to Russia. But military experts doubt that this will make a fundamental difference in the course of Russia's war with Ukraine.

In late 2024, North Korea sent troops to help defend the Kursk region of Russia from Ukraine. International officials estimate that 14,000-15,000 North Korean troops were initially deployed to assist Russia in its war in Ukraine..

Now, Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect that North Korea is planning to send an additional 30,000-50,000 troops to Russia. Ukrainian officials have also stated that North Korean ballistic missiles are being fired from Russia.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has raised concerns that North Korea's improved combat and weapons experience could pose a security threat to Ukraine, as well as the Asia-Pacific region.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Defense in Russia

Observers have had mixed responses to Zelenskyy's remarks. Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military and political expert at the Ukrainian Center for Security Studies, told DW that new troops from North Korea would likely be used to secure Russia's border territories. Aside from remaining in Kursk, North Korean soldiers could also help secure southwestern Vornezh.

"These forces could free up Russian occupational forces," Kovalenko said. "Russia would then be able to deploy around 15,000 troops to battles along front lines in Vovchansk, Kharkiv, Sumy or even Chernihiv."

Kovalenko does not expect North Korean troops to fight on Ukrainian territory.

The Russian military analyst Ruslan Leviev agrees. "It's one thing to recapture Russian territory," he told DW, "and an entirely different thing to be present on internationally recognized Ukrainian territory, taking part in a war of aggression."

"Diplomatically speaking," he said, "those are two entirely different concepts."

Russia has spread terror in Ukraine with rocket attacks on civilian targets Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

Russia not outgunned

Leviev said he had not seen concrete evidence of a noteworthy North Korean presence in Russia. He said Moscow had enough troops available without having to draw foreign soldiers into the fight.

"If you look at the front line, you can see that Russia's forces have been fairly active since mid-July," Leviev said. "That's a clear sign they still have enough forces."

Estimates by the economist Janis Kluge, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), back this up. "While Russia's recruitment campaign has shown signs of strain this year, regional spending figures indicate that Russia is still recruiting around 1,000 contract soldiers each day," he recently wrote in a report .

Intelligence on North Korea's short- and medium-range ballistic systems, the KN-23 and KN-24, is far less speculative. Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) states that North Korea has delivered 148 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles since 2025.

In July, Zelenskyy said one such missile had struck a home near Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih, killing two parents and three children.

The HUR recently reported that a North Korean missile unit was deploying to Russia's Voronezh region, where it could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has taken this as indication that Russia's strategic reserve is depleted.

Kovalenko has come to a different conclusion. Instead of having run out of reserves, he said, he believes that Russia is looking to launch a higher number of missiles "to spread more terror."

'Instruments of terror'

Ukrainian military sources say North Korean missiles are similar to Russia's Iskander missiles, but with a greater payload, longer range and lower accuracy.

The military expert Yuri Fyodorov calls North Korea's missiles "instruments of terror." He told DW that "it is very difficult to hit a small target with North Korean weapons." He said he believed that Russia had deliberately targeted residential areas with these missiles.

Like the Russian Iskander 9M723, KN-23 and KN-24 missiles can only be stopped by US-made Patriot air-defense systems, which Ukraine has run critically low on.

Leviev said ballistic missiles would play a key role in this phase of the war. As Ukraine's stockpiles run low, he said, it will become a growing priority to Russia to keep a steady supply.

This summer, Leviev said, he has seen Russia launch far more ballistic missiles than in previous years. Should Russia's missile supply run low by winter, he said, "there will still be North Korea reserves, to make sure Ukraine cannot catch its breath."

No turning point

None of the experts DW spoke with believes that North Korea's involvement will bring about a turning point in Russia's war with Ukraine.

Jenny Town, of the US-based Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the time had passed for North Korea's involvement to make a significant difference. Instead, she said, Russia and North Korea have established a mutually beneficial partnership that is only likely to deepen through the course of the war with Ukraine.

Kovalenko also doesn't expect Russia to make substantial territorial gains along the front lines, but he is concerned about the upcoming winter. "October, November and December could become very trying for Ukraine," he said.

Russian forces could benefit from a possible new military call up, from freeing up fighters it replaces with North Korean troops and from a further stream of ballistic missiles. "That would be no good for the course of the war, and for Ukraine's war interests," Fyodorov said.

This article was originally written in Russian.

World.title: US: Hurricane Lala brings Hawaii heavy rain, strong winds
World.content:
The Category 1 storm passed over Hawaii's Big Island without making landfall and is expected to weaken gradually. However, the hurricane caused roads to flood and turned rivers into raging torrents.

Hurricane Lala passed over Hawaii's Big Island on Saturday without making landfall and is expected to weaken gradually after bringing strong winds and heavy rain to the region.

The hurricane had earlier strengthened to Category 1 as its eye approached the southern part of Big Island.

It was expected be the Big Island's first possible direct hit from a hurricane in 155 years but that was not to be as the storm passed the island's southern tip.

National Weather Service meteorologist Joseph Clark said landfall is not expected at this point.

However, hurricane-force winds are expected to last through the night, with the strongest gusts likely in areas with higher elevation, the National Hurricane Center said.

Experts warn of flooding, mudslides

Earlier, Lala had maximum sustained winds of 75 miles per hour (120 kilometers per hour), with its center forecast to move over or near the southern end of the Big Island.

The National Hurricane Center warned the island could receive 10 to 20 inches (25 to 50 cm) of rain, with up to 25 inches possible in some areas.

"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the US National Hurricane Center said.

The Big Island, also known as the island of Hawaii, is the archipelago's largest island by landmass — and with some 200,000 inhabitants, the second-most populous.

A hurricane warning was in effect for the Big Island, while tropical storm warnings covered Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau Image: NOAA/AP Photo/picture alliance

Hawaii declares state of emergency

More than 40,000 utility customers across Hawaii were without power, including over 31,000 on the Big Island, according to outage data.

The tropical storm covering Oahu — home to the state capital, Honolulu, and around 70% of the state's inhabitants— as well as the other major islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Kauai and Niihau is still in place.

The hurricane damaged an electrical utility pole near Ocean View on the Big Island Image: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/AP Photo/picture alliance

A storm surge of one to three feet is expected to be accompanied by "large and dangerous waves," according to officials.

Hawaii Governor Josh Green had declared a state of emergency and urged residents to shelter in place. "It's a serious storm," Green said.

Authorities also announced the closure of Hilo International Airport, adding that Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport would also be shut down.

Risk of wildfires rise

Authorities opened shelters and advised residents to clear drains and gutters, move valuables off the ground and prepare for possible extended power outages.

Lala was expected to dump 10 to 20 inches (25 to 50 centimeters) of rain on the Big Island Image: Taylor Cozloff/Civil Beat/dpa/picture alliance

Vanessa Almanza, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Honolulu, said dry and breezy conditions outside the storm would raise risk of wildfires.

In 2023, the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds as a hurricane passed far to the south.

Meteorologists said Lala's arrival coincides with a powerful El Nino event, which can increase hurricane activity in the Pacific.

Hawaii has not experienced a major hurricane landfall since Hurricane Iniki struck Kauai in 1992, causing six deaths and billions of dollars in damage.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Africa's low-key high-stakes Strait of Hormuz diplomacy
World.content:
African governments have kept a low profile on the international stage during the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz. But that doesn't mean they haven't been engaging with the issue behind the scenes.

One of the principal arteries of world trade has been chronically blocked for almost six months. Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has been reduced to a bare minimum since the first US-Israeli airstrikes on Iran at the end of February. Cargo ships have at times been fired on by Iranian forces; at others, threats from Tehran or Washington have been enough to bring shipping to a standstill.

So far, various rounds of talks, a joint memorandum and third-party deliberations about the creation of a maritime mission have not succeeded in stabilizing the situation. It remains to be seen whether a deal between Iran and Oman on establishing a shipping route through the strait will do so.

The war has prompted fossil fuel prices to soar all over the world, with inflation rising as a result. Despite its relative proximity to the Gulf region, some parts of Africa have experienced serious shortages because of the bottlenecks, with long lines of cars at gas stations that have run out of fuel. As many fertilizers are also sourced from the Gulf region, this year's harvests also threaten to be bad. African governments therefore have every reason to engage diplomatically in finding a permanent solution.

Cautious diplomacy

"I believe their long-term plan is still based on the assumption that the crisis in the Middle East may continue for some time," says Liesl Louw-Vaudran from the International Crisis Group , an NGO that works to prevent conflicts.

The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but Louw-Vaudran, an expert advisor working with the African Union, comments: "We don't see any evidence that there was some kind of optimism or revising of any economic planning after the MOU. I think everyone literally is just waiting to see how this is going to pan out in the next couple of months."

The Strait of Hormuz, viewed from Oman: There's hope that a recent deal between Oman and Iran can secure passage for shipping Image: REUTERS

It's certainly the case that a low-key approach has dominated African diplomacy with regard to Hormuz in recent months. There have been numerous calls for negotiated solutions, praise for diplomatic initiatives and an emphasis on the rules-based order. Some African governments have also shown solidarity with the Arab Gulf states, which, as US allies, have come under fire from Iran.

The current African members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Somalia and Liberia — also backed a UN resolution adopted in March that strongly condemned Iranian attacks on the Gulf states.

The elephant in the room: Donald Trump

However, it is apparent from their communications that African governments are trying to avoid apportioning blame — especially to the US president, who, together with Israeli president Benjamin Netanyahu, was the one who started the war.

"Every rational human being in the world knows that this crisis has been occasioned by Mr. Donald Trump," says Dismas Mokua, a political risk analyst with the Kenyan advisory firm Tricarta. "But the majority of African leaders, and indeed across the world, fear to call him out because of the consequences. And I've seen European leaders tiptoeing around this issue, I've seen leaders from Asia — leaders all over the world. I've not seen a single leader who has come out to call Mr. Trump, because I guess they fear the consequences of their speech."

African countries have been careful to avoid blaming anyone for the crisis, especially Donald Trump Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What if the whole of Africa were to speak with one voice — perhaps through the African Union? Louw-Vaudran from the International Crisis Group thinks a recent negative experience is still too fresh.

"The African Union Commission in Addis Ababa burned its fingers in the early days of the Ukraine war, in 2022, when the previous chairperson criticized Russia. And heads of state then immediately silenced him, and said that the commission doesn't have the mandate to speak on foreign affairs issues on behalf of the continent," Louw-Vaudran says.

She points out that the AU, with 55 member states, is "very much divided," and says that, since then, "when it comes to political statements in this big, rapidly changing geopolitical situation, the commission has been hesitant."

Ease the symptoms, don't create new problems

The crisis also requires governments to take action rather than just make statements.

"For most countries, or even companies, to be successful wherever there is a disruption in this global supply, you have to reevaluate your supply chains and find out which fits your interest," Mokua says. "And in my view, Kenya has managed to do that with a lot of success."

He comments that he hasn't seen anyone — and, in particular, commercial farmers — complaining about deliveries.

"And even for the supply of oil and gas products, people anticipated that there were going to be shortages. But there were no shortages. The suppliers have been constant and reliable, despite the increase in cost."

In Ethiopia, gas stations have had to close at times after running out of fuel Image: Marco Simoncelli/AFP

But the experience of neighboring Ethiopia has been very different. Delivery bottlenecks forced the government to temporarily prioritize security agencies, public transport and agriculture when distributing fuel. Private individuals were stuck waiting at empty gas stations.

Before the war, Ethiopia was one of Iran's most important African trading partners. That connection is now also at risk, since Ethiopia also relies on maintaining good relations with the United Arab Emirates and increasingly with Saudi Arabia, too.

Countries like Ethiopia and Kenya may also be about to feel another, delayed effect of the Iran war. If the rich Gulf states' economies falter, East African migrant workers there will transfer less money back home.

Opportunity for African countries to work together

But there are also some African countries for whom the uncertain situation in the Gulf might actually be helpful. Nigeria's huge new Dangote refinery came online at just the right time. Intended to ease fuel shortages in the oil-rich country, it's now a mainstay of the world market. In April, the refinery became the world's largest exporter of aviation fuel.

Responding to the Hormuz crisis, Nigeria has offered itself as a partner for African clients. The Dangote corporation is already planning another refinery in Kenya. And the government is standing with the Gulf states: On the oil market, countries seek to be partners, not competitors.

"Nigeria has been very smart, at least in terms of that economic positioning, having the crude itself," says Liesl Louw-Vaudran. "But obviously Nigeria has got huge governance and security issues that are very difficult to overcome."

Perhaps the least visible issue in the short term but one that is likely to have the most lasting impact: The crisis provides another argument for pressing ahead with the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

"There are a number of countries that do not understand the meaning of dismantling these artificial borders. They fear that they are going to lose political control," says the analyst Dismas Mokua.

But he added that he believes many African countries will eventually embrace the dismantling of arbitrary borders drawn up by European colonizers at the infamous Berlin Conference in 1885. "If you want to immunize yourself from the vagaries associated with the global disruption, then you must learn to trade within Africa," he says.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: How Germany supports recovery of Berlin Pride attack victims
World.content:
After a terrorist attack, public attention tends to focus primarily on the perpetrator. But what about the victims? What support can they expect? And what lies ahead for them?

On the evening of July 25, according to German authorities, Abdul Ballout, drove a white van into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate, where thousands were celebrating Berlin Pride. He then got out of the vehicle and began attacking people at random with a large knife. He killed a 65-year-old woman from Poland and injured her daughter, along with 30 other people, some of them seriously.

Many details have emerged about the perpetrator, his links to extremists, his criminal record and his family. Two days after the incident, he was shot dead by police officers while trying to flee during an arrest attempt.

The identities of the victims, and how they are coping after the attack on the event celebrating LGBTQ+ rights, are not publicly known. Still, many are likely to live with its consequences for months, if not years, to come. The only details disclosed by Berlin's governing mayor concern the age and nationality of the woman who was killed. Otherwise, Germany's strict data protection laws protect victims' privacy.

Victims can approach the media themselves at any time if they choose to make their stories public, Roland Weber, the German federal government's commissioner for victims of terrorism and extremist violence , told DW.

Calls for political consequences after Berlin Pride attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Support for the victims

In Germany, people affected by such attacks are often reluctant to come forward publicly or identify themselves as victims, says Julia Kühne. She should know: Kühne is the spokesperson for the Association for Victims of Terrorism (VoT Germany ), which is part of an international federation of terrorism victims.

"The perpetrator needs to disappear from the media, now that he has been caught and killed. Those affected should naturally be brought much more to the forefront," Kühne told DW.

How are those who were injured in the attack doing today? Weber has visited some of them in hospital.

"What I saw there was distressing. But thanks to modern medicine, and because the doctors are optimistic, there is reason for hope that everyone will recover as fully as possible," he said. "In some cases, however, that remains uncertain. Only time will tell. Some of the injured have already been discharged from hospital and are now receiving outpatient treatment. Others will begin various forms of therapy and rehabilitation."

How are the victims being supported?

The Federal Commissioner for Victims and "Weisser Ring" , a victim support organization, arrange trauma treatment, provide immediate financial assistance, and advise victims on long-term care and victims' pensions.

Weisser Ring is a volunteer-run organization that works closely with the police to provide advice and support to victims of crime in Germany.

"In cases of terrorist attacks, there is also a special provision: victims can apply for hardship payments," says Weber. "These are funds made available by the Bundestag. Hardly anyone knows about them, and making people aware of them is part of our job. We provide guidance and help ensure that applications are submitted as quickly as possible."

Weber is also responsible for supporting the relatives of the Polish woman who was killed and her daughter, who was injured in the attack. Nationality is not a factor in this regard. He assists victims with follow-up costs and compensation whenever an act of terrorism or extremist violence has been committed on German soil.

Number of traumatized victims still unclear

The victims of the attack are not only those who sustained physical injuries. According to VoT Germany's Kühne, even people who witnessed the attack from several hundred meters away may be considered victims.

"There are people who do not develop problems until years later," she said. "They may suddenly begin to suffer from sleep disturbances, experience nightmares, develop panic attacks or struggle with social phobia. In some cases, these symptoms do not emerge until years afterward because those affected were initially either still in shock or had returned to their everyday lives and were therefore able, at least to some extent, to suppress what they had experienced."

Kühne also notes that survivors of previous terrorist attacks may be retraumatized by media coverage of the current attack in Berlin and find themselves in need of support once again. She knows this from personal experience: she herself survived the 2016 attack on Berlin's Christmas market, which ultimately claimed 13 lives and left more than 70 injured.

In the shadow of RAF terror: The children left behind To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Victim support: Problems in practice

Weisser Ring, which supports victims of crime across Germany, believes that adequate compensation schemes and pension entitlements for victims of terrorism are now in place. However, not everything runs smoothly in practice, says Rolf Schmachtenberg, the organization's state chairman in Berlin.

"In cases where people have suffered permanent harm, the assessment procedures are often quite lengthy. We also continue to encounter administrative bottlenecks, with some authorities still relying on paper files and fax communications. They then have to wait for information from other agencies, which can significantly delay the application process. In my view, the main problem is one of implementation."

Over the past decade, Germany has experienced 13 terrorist attacks motivated by Islamist or political extremist ideologies, leaving 39 people dead and 475 injured. The support provided by the federal government's commissioner for victims has no time limit. Roland Weber continues to assist people affected by attacks dating back to the 1980s.

Commemoration continues of the nine people killed in 2020 in a racially motivated terrorist attack in the city of Hanau Image: Kadir Ilboga/Anadolu/picture alliance

Victims seek answers

For many victims, coming to terms with the horror and suffering also means finding answers to the question of why the perpetrator acted and why they, in particular, were targeted, says Weber. In some court proceedings, perpetrators have remained silent. In the case of the Berlin Pride attack, however, the perpetrator was killed, meaning there will never be complete clarity about his motives.

In Germany, investigations are discontinued once a suspect has died. No court will ever determine whether Abdul Ballout selected his victims for one particular reason or another.

"As a result, some questions will remain unanswered,"Weber told DW. "The search for answers is something most victims have in common, but it cannot always lead to certainty."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Belgium battles record wildfire at German border
World.content:
A rapidly spreading wildfire in the High Fens nature reserve near Belgium's border with Germany has scorched around 2,700 hectares. The German town of Monschau has also warned residents of possible evacuation orders.

Belgium is battling its largest wildfire on record which has burned around 2,700 hectares in the eastern High Fens nature reserve near the German border.

The fire has approached to within some 3 kilometers (almost 2 miles) of the German border, causing authorities in Germany to warn of smoke danger.

On Saturday, the European Union deployed three helicopters and two water bombers as Belgium deployed additional firefighters in a bid to bring the massive blaze under control.

Authorities ordered around 600 residents in parts of Waimes, Sourbrodt and Buetgenbach to evacuate as shifting winds and heavy smoke raised concerns that the fire could reach homes. Tourists were also advised to leave the area.

Reinforcements were pulled from across the country to fight the blaze Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

"You can't see a thing anymore, there's smoke everywhere," David Rodolfs, a restaurant owner in Waimes, told the AFP news agency.

A gymnasium in a neighboring municipality was opened up to offer shelter.

How have firefighting efforts fared?

The blaze, which broke out on Friday, has spread rapidly across peatlands and pine forests. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told AFP he was "shocked" at the fire's speed and extent of the destruction.

Residents in parts of the nearby villages were ordered to evacuate on Saturday afternoon as a precautionary measure Image: Dimitri Korczak/AFP

"There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said.

Difficult terrain has hampered firefighting efforts, with operations relying heavily on aerial resources and forcing firefighters to allow difficult-to-access areas to burn, according to Yernaux.

Meanwhile, Belgium activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, bringing in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands.

Local farmers have headed to the fire zone to support emergency crews Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

Firefighters from Germany and Luxembourg have also joined the response, while farmers have helped emergency crews by wetting down the area.

Residents in Germany's Monschau warned of possible evacuation

Authorities in the German town of Monschau in the Eifel region, which is located just 2 kilometers from the border, have warned residents to prepare for possible evacuation.

They also warned of health dangers from smoke and have advised people living in three districts of the town to temporarily seek accommodation elsewhere if possible.

However, the local fire brigade has said it does not expect the fire to enter German territory any time soon.

"We are continuing to monitor the situation," Philipp Krüger, the operations manager of the Monschau fire brigade, told the DPA news agency.

Monschau, a major tourist attraction in the Eifel region, has some 12,000 residents. It is particularly known for its picturesque Old Town with its half-timbered houses.

It is located just some 23 km from the site of another major blaze in Germany's Eifel region that forced some 2,000 people from their homes on Thursday.

Climate change making wildfires spread faster

Belgium has experienced another spell of extreme heat this week, with temperatures reaching 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country.

Scientists say human-caused climate change is increasing the likelihood of hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer.

European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib called the blaze the latest sign of the "climate upheaval" affecting the continent.

"Never before has the wildfire season started so early in the year and reached such northern latitudes," she said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton, Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Iran war: Qatar denies holding missing Iranian fighter pilots
World.content:
Tehran said the three pilots "were captured alive" by Qatari forces after their fighter jets were shot down in the early days of the US-Israel war with Iran. Qatar has denied Iran's claims.

Qatar on Saturday denied that it was detaining Iranian pilots who went missing early in the US-Israeli war with Iran after their aircraft were downed.

"We categorically deny the claims circulating regarding the detention of Iranian pilots and are surprised by these misleading statements," Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari said on X.

He added that the remains of one of ​the pilots were found and that Qatar contacted Iran to coordinate ​a handover.

However, Tehran had not responded to the invitation, the spokesperson said.

Iran calls on Qatar to release downed pilots

Qatar's response comes after Iranian media published a statement by the head of the Committee for Missing Persons at the General Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces.

"Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian, and Omran Behraveshian have been held by Qatari forces for six months,” General Mohammad Bagherzadeh said in a letter.

Bagherzadeh also said that three Iranian pilots had ‌been ​"captured alive" after their fighter jets crashed during a mission targeting a military base in Qatar shortly after the start of the Iran war.

In the letter, the general alleged that Qatar had not allowed the pilots to contact or meet with families or Iranian officials handling their cases.

The official also asked the International Committee of the Red Cross for help to follow up on the fate of the pilots.

Gulf nations caught between Iran, US as war escalates To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Qatar shot down Iranian jets in early March

Tehran responded to the ⁠US-Israeli attacks ​in late February with a series of strikes across the region, including US military facilities in the Gulf.

On March 2 — the third day of the war — Qatar's Defense Ministry said it had downed two Iranian Sukhoi Su-24 bombers. However, it was unclear if those jets were flown by the pilots Iran claims are being held in Qatar.

Qatar had condemned Iran for its "reckless and irresponsible" targeting of its territory .

Iran launches retaliatory strikes across Gulf region To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
