World.title: Albania Ruling Party Documents Highlight Country’s Ageing Demographic
World.content:
Documents produced by governing Socialist Party experts for a reform of the country’s municipal set-up, seen by BIRN, reveal an ageing population that could have adverse economic consequences for Albania.

The “Administrative-Territorial Reform 2.0” documents, prepared by experts on a special parliamentary committee, also show how emigration and internal migration have emptied out small towns and rural areas while concentrating the population in a few urban centres.

At one end are several urban centres where both population and economic activity are increasingly concentrated. At the other end are peripheral areas, particularly in the northeast, southeast and mountainous regions, which are caught in a vicious cycle of population decline and subsistence economies, with few formal jobs.

In these areas, municipal budgets survive largely on central government transfers, with funds often used mainly to cover the salaries of local administration staff.

The Urban Mass Index, UMI, one of three analytical documents underpinning the proposed new map of 46 municipalities – which would merge 15 local government units with larger municipalities – documents the territorial transformation of Albania since the 1990s, with a few centres continuing to grow as an increasing number of municipalities lose residents.

The “dependency ratio” in the index, which measures the burden that children and elderly people place on the working-age population, shows that in 51 municipalities out of 61 in total, this burden is higher than the national average. In many of them, the number of elderly residents exceeds the number of children.

The data highlights an Albania divided into three distinct realities: a small group of municipalities that continue to attract population and economic activity; a group of municipalities with intermediate potential; and a majority of the country’s territory, which is losing the critical mass of population needed to sustain local economies and public services.

The analysis is based on data from the 2023 census and, as part of the technical report accompanying the reform proposal, suggests that Albania is experiencing a growing concentration of its population in an ever-smaller number of urban centres, while the rest of the country is losing residents, functions and development capacity.

The index results show that only 13 municipalities are classified as having a high level of urban mass and are home to 62.5 per cent of the population.

By contrast, 30 municipalities – covering almost half of the country’s administrative map – are classified as having a low level of urban mass and account for just 14.2 per cent of the population.

Another 18 municipalities fall into the intermediate or medium category.

According to the data, the country’s population is concentrated in the capital, which is home to more than half a million people, followed at a considerable

distance by the municipalities of Durres, Vlora, Elbasan, Shkoder, Fieri, Kamza and Berat.

At the other end of the scale, municipalities such as Pustec, Libohova, Himara, Kelcyra, Memaliaj, Selenica, Dropull, Finiq, Delvina and Kolonja have the smallest populations.

The ruling-party experts did not build the index solely on population size. It also combines other indicators, including population density, the spatial distribution of residents, the demographic dependency ratio and the level of urbanisation.

This means that a municipality may cover a large area, but if its population is concentrated in a small town while the rest of its territory is largely empty, it is considered structurally weak.

One of the most significant findings is that, on average, 57 per cent of Albania’s territory is uninhabited.

The analytical document notes that the country no longer has the same population distribution it had in 2014, when the current administrative-territorial division was introduced with the aim of creating larger and more efficient municipalities.

“Some areas have grown, while others have lost a significant share of their population,” the report says, arguing that some municipalities are struggling to secure sustainable finances, qualified staff and adequate administrative capacity.

The Socialists have submitted a bill to parliament proposing a new administrative-territorial map that would merge several smaller municipalities with larger neighbouring ones – without explaining how the proposed map would address these underlying problems.

The proposal has faced opposition from residents in the affected areas. Some fear mergers will leave them with even more limited access to public services.

World.title: Kosovo Detains Man Suspected of Spying for Serbian Intelligence
World.content:
Fehim Sali, second left, at a court hearing in Pristina on August 14, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Pristina Basic Court on Friday ordered 30 days of detention for a dual Kosovo and Serbia citizen, Fehim Sali, who is suspected of spying for Serbia’s intelligence agency, the BIA.

It is alleged that he passed the BIA information about Kosovo officials, politicians and Islamist radicals, including potential recruitment targets, and received money in return.

Sali, a resident of Kosovo’s southern Dragash/Dragas municipality, was arrested on Thursday at the Merdare border crossing point while entering from Serbia. He appeared before the Basic Court in Pristina on Friday.

“The court’s assessment took into account the circumstances relating to the risk of absconding, the risk of influencing witnesses and evidence, and the risk of repetition or continuation of the criminal offence,” the court said in a statement.

According to the prosecution file, Sali is suspected of “maintaining contact with BIA officers using four different mobile phones”, which were found during raids at his house on Thursday, alongside around 40,000 euros in cash.

The prosecution file alleges that Sali “worked as a recruited agent for Serbia’s Security Information Agency, BIA, in exchange for material benefits”. The file alleges that he acted on the instructions of a senior BIA officer identified as Zelimir Matovic, nicknamed Zeljko.

It alleges that Sali provided the BIA with information about Kosovo’s political situation and helped it identify officials of Kosovo’s own intelligence agency, the AKI. According to the case file, he photographed some of its officials to facilitate their identification.

Sali is also accused of providing information about members of the radical Islamist Wahhabi movement as well as other people whom he allegedly proposed to the BIA officer as potential targets for contact and recruitment.

According to prosecutors, Sali also “mediated matters and documents connected to Serbian state institutions and maintained contacts with people with political and social influence in Serbia and Kosovo, particularly members of non-majority communities”.

The prosecution stated that he provided some of these people with “guidance on political activity, with the aim of gathering and transmitting information of interest to the BIA”.

Prosecutors argue that these activities were carried out against the state interests of Kosovo and endangered its constitutional order and national security.

The prosecution also alleges that the 40,000 euros found and seized during a search of Sali’s home came from his alleged activities on behalf of the BIA.

According to the case file, the evidence against Sali includes his own statement.

Prosecutors claim he described in detail his alleged activities, including how and where he communicated with BIA officials, exchanged information and provided assistance to the Serbian intelligence service.

Prosecutor Bekim Kodraliu told media that Sali admitted having been recruited and maintained regular contact with BIA officials.

“The suspect himself stated that he had been recruited and had ongoing contacts with BIA officials,” Kodraliu said.

The case comes two months after another Kosovo espionage conviction involving Serbia’s intelligence service.

In June, the Pristina Basic Court sentenced a Kosovo Albanian man, Hysri Selimi, a former Islamic State member, to six years in prison for espionage.

Prosecutors said Selimi had provided the BIA with information about religious radicalisation in Kosovo, former members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, and people who had joined Islamic State.

World.title: Week in Review: Between the Absurd and the Unexpected
World.content:
Kosovo’s governance drama is beginning to border on the absurd. Weeks after the June election results were certified, two months after the elections were held, MPs have yet to elect a parliamentary speaker and deputies and, in doing so, constitute the new parliament.

The winning party, Vetevendosje, has the votes to elect a new speaker, and indeed a new government. But it has conditioned the election of a speaker on reaching a wider agreement with the opposition on the election of a new president. With deadlines imposed by the Constitutional Court passing, is Kosovo heading to a fourth parliamentary election in two years?

World.title: Thousands Flee, 14 Hospitalised as Wildfire Menaces Croatian Coastal Town
World.content:
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said on Friday that 14 people have been hospitalised, with ten in intensive care, after a wildfire that reportedly forced some 2,000 people to evacuate homes around the Dalmatian coastal town of Omis overnight.

“The government and all relevant services are coordinating to protect people and rectify the consequences of the large fire in Omis,” Plenkovic wrote on X.

The fire swept through forested areas to destroy property and vehicles. Chief national fire officer Slavko Tucakovic told media that he had “never experienced anything like this in my career”.

“Unfortunately, many houses were damaged or burned down. A large number of vehicles were also burned up,” he said.

The Croatian coast has seen record high temperatures this summer. The heatwave left dry vegetation as fuel for the fire, and the flames were spread by high winds, Tucakovic explained.

World.title: Kosovo’s LDK Drops Demand to Choose President in Bid to Resolve Crisis
World.content:
LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku addresses media on August 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN .

The opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, said on Thursday it had withdrawn its demands to name the country’s new president in an attempt to end the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June.

Lumir Abdixhiku, the LDK leader, said that while talks with the poll-winning Vetevendosje party’s leader Albin Kurti over a government partnership had not yet produced results, he was offering new talks about the election of a new president – which is crucial to avoid new parliamentary polls.

“From this moment, no one has any reason, alibi or the right to delay the inauguration of parliament, the formation of the government and starting negotiations on a new president. We are late and should not waste any more time,” Abdixhiku said in a video message after a meeting with the party’s parliamentary group.

“The constitutional uncertainty is a reality we cannot ignore … The crisis does not seem to have an end and it’s getting worse and worse,” he added.

“We are ready to discuss the election of a president who defends our republic’s interests and its constitution, represents people’s unity and exercises the constitutional responsibilities. We are not asking for any posts or any political compensation in return,” he continued.

In the June elections, Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, well ahead of the Kosovo Democratic Party, PDK, which won 22. The LDK won 18 seats and has until now insisted on having the president’s post, which Vetevendosje has deemed a “disproportionate” demand.

Kurti will likely obtain a simple majority in the Assembly to form a new government, by again relying on the support of MPs from various ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk, Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

However, the wider crisis that led to the June 7 elections has not been solved; the parties still need to agree on the election of a new president within two months of the inauguration of the new parliament, or it will trigger another election.

Speaking on Friday, Kurti did not specifically say if he will accept the LDK offer, but welcomed Abdixhiku’s willingness to include other parties in negotiations over the presidency.

“We are open to further discussions in order to come to a name or names [for the presidency], someone who is out of the current political scene, out of daily party polemics, and who is a unifying figure,” Kurti said.

“We want to agree in advance in order to avoid new elections. The election of a parliament speaker and a cabinet is not a challenge, so we have to agree on the election of a president,” he added.

Meanwhile a group PDK MPs protested on Friday for the second day in a row in front of acting premier Kurti’s office, demanding the resumption of parliament’s inaugural session. This was interrupted last Saturday when Kurti asked for “more time” to discuss the issue of a new president with other parties.

So far, Abdixhiku and Kurti have met twice but have not found a common ground on new institutions. In his video address, Abdixhiku disclosed that the LDK was offered three ministries in Kurti’s next cabinet – “a disproportion we could not afford”.

World.title: Democracy Digest: US Charges Mexican Cartel Members over Czech Weapons Deal
World.content:
Russia on the radar; Slovakia picks a fight with Brussels over same-sex marriage

Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has been forced into an embarrassing retreat over speed cameras with suspected Russian links, a week after dismissing opposition warnings about their origin. The National Security Authority (NBU) confirmed on Tuesday that the two devices in question contain Russian components. The finding vindicates concerns raised by Progressive Slovakia (PS), the country’s strongest opposition party, which had warned that the cameras could pose a security risk. There were red flags from the start. Journalists found that the cameras closely resembled equipment made by the St Petersburg-based company Simicon. More strikingly, the measurement software listed in the Slovak certification had the same digital fingerprint as software used in a Russian CORDON speed camera. The ministry’s story has shifted ever since. It first insisted the cameras were not Russian, then conceded it could not prove their origin, before ordering IT supplier Soitron to remove the test devices. It now says two ministry employees will lose their jobs and cooperation with Soitron will end. Interior Minister Matus Sutaj Estok, of the governing Hlas party, has resisted calls to take political responsibility. “We were lied to,” he said on Thursday, blaming the Slovak Institute of Metrology, which certified the cameras. The institute says checking cybersecurity risks, supply chains or the origin of components is not its job. Soitron also denies misleading the state. Soitron obtained the devices from a Slovak distributor whose CEO had worked in Russia for many years and had previously imported similar equipment to Slovakia through another company. The ministry will not publish the NBU analysis, and it is unclear why the country’s security services failed to spot the potential problem before opposition politicians and journalists did. The General Prosecutor’s Office has now said it will examine the case.

There was another controversy this week involving the Interior Ministry, and Interior Minister Sutaj Estok in particular. His ministry has refused to register same-sex marriages legally concluded abroad. Several Slovak same-sex couples applied in December to have their foreign marriage certificates entered into Slovakia’s special registry. After waiting eight months, they received an answer not from the registry, but directly from Sutaj Estok. He argued that registering the unions as marriages would conflict with Slovak law and the constitution, which has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 2014. Among those affected are former diplomats Ivan Novotny and his husband Metod Spacek. They argue that the minister intervened in a procedure that should have been handled by the registry and are now preparing an administrative lawsuit. At the heart of the dispute is a 2025 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union involving a Polish-German same-sex couple. The court ruled that an EU country cannot refuse to recognise a same-sex marriage legally concluded in another member state if doing so interferes with rights guaranteed under EU law, particularly freedom of movement and residence. The ruling does not require member states to introduce same-sex marriage into their domestic law. The European Commission has reminded Slovakia that EU law, as interpreted by the EU’s top court, takes precedence over national law and that member states are required to implement its judgments. It told the SME daily that it would continue to monitor the situation and could use the tools at its disposal if needed. The ministry argues that EU law may require Slovakia to recognise same-sex marriages for specific purposes, but does not oblige the country to enter them in its registry as marriages with the same legal status as marriages recognised under Slovak law. Novotny, Spacek and other couples dispute that interpretation. Their planned legal challenge could now put that question before the Slovak courts.

World.title: Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law Won’t Succeed Without More Gynaecologists
World.content:
Imagine a woman called Milica. She is 29, on a fixed-term contract, and every month menstrual pain keeps her from working for several days.

Milica has not seen a gynaecologist in two years. There aren’t enough appointments where she lives and she cannot travel to the capital, Podgorica, because of work.

When she finally gets a diagnosis, she learns a law offering paid leave exists, and she must renew her medical diagnosis certificate every year.

But she wonders whether her employer will extend her contract if he learns why she has been absent.

World.title: BIRN Reality Check: What Has Albania’s AI ‘Minister’ Achieved So Far?
World.content:
According to Rama, Diella was to serve as Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, with a specific task: to eliminate corruption from public procurement tenders – a key issue for Albania as it seeks to push forward its EU accession process.

But a year later, the actual role of the bot ‘minister’ role remains unclear.

At the Public Procurement Agency, where the bot’s skills were expected to be tested, work still appears to be at the preparatory stage.

“There is a project to develop an AI-powered procurement system, but it is still in progress,” said Reida Kashta, the Agency’s director, when asked whether it had begun using AI in public procurement.

According to Kashta, the agency has “just completed the drafting of the terms of reference”. This is a document that sets out the technical criteria for launching the tender that will select the company responsible for building the system.

The public procurement system has for years been considered one of the sectors most exposed to corruption in Albania. Investigations by the Special Prosecution Office for organised crime and corruption, SPAK, have uncovered several cases involving schemes to manipulate tenders, in which winners had been predetermined before the procedures were launched. Contracts for the construction of roads, incinerators and other public investments have been subject to investigations over allegations of favouring economic operators and violating competition rules.

The government’s ambition to integrate AI into the sector has been met with scepticism by both opposition politicians and public policy experts, mainly because of the security risks it entails, its lack of human capacity and various legal uncertainties.

Opposition Democratic Party MP Klevis Balliu told BIRN that the use of AI could serve as an assisting tool for the administration, but could not replace the legal responsibility of institutions, nor guarantee the fight against corruption.

According to Balliu, without a clear constitutional and legal basis, the creation of a virtual minister raises questions about who bears responsibility for decision-making, particularly in a sensitive sector such as public procurement.

“Diella does not solve corruption. On the contrary, she raises a fundamental question: who bears responsibility for decisions influenced by a system that has no legally defined status?” Balliu said.

He argued that a virtual system could help increase efficiency and identify irregularities, but “it cannot replace transparency, oversight and human accountability.”

Public policy experts are also concerned about the use of AI in procurement without a comprehensive legal, institutional and technical framework in place.

Alba Brojka, an independent digital policy expert, said artificial intelligence should not be treated as a “magic wand solution” to complex problems such as corruption, but only as a tool to increase efficiency and automate administrative processes.

“Under [UN culture agency] UNESCO’s principles on the ethical use of AI, decision-making ultimately belongs to the expert or human, not the technology,” Brojka said. She sees this particular use of AI as “an excuse for a problem [corruption] that has existed for years”, and that what needs addressing first is the “legal gap and institutional capacity”.

For Aranita Brahaj, head of the Albanian Institute of Science (AIS) the use of AI in procurement cannot be seen as a solution to tendering problems without first consolidating the legal framework and developing a new methodology to monitor the efficiency of such systems.

“Albania still lacks a complete, secondary legal framework and, above all, this process is taking place at a time when public contracting is showing significant problems,” Brahaj said.

Multiple challenges

World.title: Lavly Perling re-elected chair of Parempoolsed
World.content:
Lavly Perling was re-elected as the chair of the non-parliamentary party Parempoolsed at the party's general assembly held in Tallinn on Saturday. She was also the only candidate.

In her speech, Perling was critical of both the governing coalition and the opposition in the Riigikogu, saying that neither the parliamentary parties are any longer capable of restoring the Estonian people's faith in a better future.

Perling said painful decisions must be made now for the sake of a better future so that Estonia does not go down the path of Greece and Latvia, which lost the right to make decisions over their own state finances during the previous financial crisis.

"We must freeze state spending at the 2026 level and say clearly that next year the state must manage with the same level of spending as this year," she said.

Perling also promised that Parempoolsed would cut taxes. "We offer Estonian people and businesses tax stability and a reduction in the tax burden, with the aim of lowering VAT back to 20 percent and income tax to 18 percent within one electoral cycle," she said.

Former Eesti 200 member to join Parempoolsed?

Kalev Stoicescu, who recently left Eesti 200, also attended the meeting. He told ERR at the beginning of last week that joining Parempoolsed was entirely possible.

On Saturday, Stoicescu did not confirm that he would join Parempoolsed.

"What I will say is that what I have heard and seen here, and I have also had private conversations with various members, and I have known quite a few people here for a long time, I have liked all of it very much," he told evening news show "Aktuaalne kaamera."

Perling said on Monday that if Stoicescu's worldview aligns with that of Parempoolsed, he is welcome to join the party.

World.title: Tallinn residents increasingly encountering rats
World.content:
Rats are increasingly being encountered on the streets of Tallinn, and the city and several districts plan to start pest control in the autumn.

Two young people told ERR they saw several rats in front of a popular restaurant in central Tallinn.

"It gave me a horrifying feeling because the rats were quite bold. So it made me think about the table where I'm eating – how sure can I be that it is completely clean?" Maia-Liis Ossip said.

"I believe they don't make it into the kitchen, but what if they've been on the same table where I've eaten, walking around and doing their thing at night?" Mihkel Kööbi said.

The rodents are increasingly being seen around the capital city, and district governments frequently receive messages from residents about sightings. Lasnamäe, Mustamäe, Haabersti and Põhja-Tallinn have already begun mapping where the rats are most often encountered.

"They are still found where there are residential buildings and where there are rubbish bins. You could say that the first step in controlling rats is to look at the places where they get food – whether the areas around our rubbish bins are clean, whether entrances to buildings are closed – if we make life as uncomfortable for them as possible, there will also be fewer rats," Põhja-Tallinn district elder Manuela Pihlap said.

Põhja-Tallinn is accepting reports of rodent sightings until Sunday, August 16. Pest control could cost up to €7,000 and will be carried out during the autumn months.

Pest control specialist Meelis Lepp said it should not be delayed.

"Right now is the last chance. If you start in November or, even worse, in February, it's already too late. By then they're in your home, or they've already chewed through the wires, or they've eaten the vegetables," Lepp said.

In apartment buildings, poison bait boxes can be placed near the building.

"A recommendation here as well is that if you start using poison, residents of several neighbouring buildings should do it at the same time, because rats are smart animals. If they realise that bad things happen to them in one place, it's easy enough for them to move to another building or woodshed," central Tallinn resident Indrek Hirs said.

Rats also reproduce quickly. Pregnancy lasts just one month, after which they are immediately capable of becoming pregnant again.

World.title: Gallery: Pärnu Literature Festival faces an uncertain future
World.content:
The Pärnu Literature Festival took place for the sixth time on Saturday in Estonia's summer capital, but organizers say it could be the last due to a lack of funding.

The festival opened with the placing of a flower wreath on the head of the statue of writer and poet Lydia Koidula (1843-1886) in Koidula Park, where the event takes place.

The 12-hour festival included lectures, meetings with authors, a book fair and a special children's and youth area.

However, festival organiser Merle Jantson said holding the event has become increasingly difficult financially with each passing year. This year's festival may be the last.

"This is a programme that runs from noon until midnight, the aim of which is to value and introduce the Estonian language, Estonian literature and Estonian writers," she said.

World.title: Tallinn mulling night-time work for Liivalaia street reconstruction
World.content:
To minimize disruption to daytime traffic, roadworks on Liivalaia tänav in Tallinn will likely be carried out at night this fall.

Tallinn Mayor Peeter Raudsepp (Isamaa) said on social media this week that roadworks must not bring traffic in Tallinn to a standstill and that he had agreed with the city's deputy mayors on steps to prevent this.

"What is happening leaves much to be desired. I have several questions myself and I am hearing them increasingly often from residents as well. One thing is clear: At the start of fall, traffic gets heavier and faster, while roadworks force people to take detours and make them late. For example, work at the Hipodroomi intersection will continue for quite some time, repairs on Sõle tänav have only just begun and work on Liivalaia tänav will start next week. And it makes no difference whether you travel by bus, car or bicycle. Changes are needed," Raudsepp wrote.

Other major streets are also undergoing repairs, with work underway on Peterburi tee and Lauteri tänav in the Kesklinn district, for example. However, the mayor's call does not mean that work planned for this fall will be postponed, Järvan said.

"There is no such plan. Naturally, the city would like to repair even more roads and streets than we are currently able to. But as for these measures [to reduce traffic disruption] — and we are not talking about street reconstruction here, but road surface repairs — the idea is for them to be carried out primarily at night and outside peak hours, so that traffic can flow without obstruction when traffic volumes are at their highest," Järvan said.

This week, Tallinn announced that road surface repairs will also begin next week on Liivalaia tänav, one of Kesklinn's main thoroughfares, and will last two months. The plan is to shift the work there to nighttime hours, Järvan said, although as of this week, the contractor had not yet been issued a permit for nighttime work.

Roadwork will begin on the section of Liivalaia tänav between Juhkentali tänav and Pärnu maantee. Source: Tallinn City Government

"It is standard practice for the Transport Department to issue nighttime work permits for such important arterial roads. Road surface repairs and other work on arterial roads are prohibited during peak hours and temporary traffic management measures cannot be in place during that time. This is one of the main measures for ensuring that traffic disruption caused by road surface repairs, at least, is kept to a minimum," Järvan said.

However, this means that noisier work, such as asphalt milling, will also take place at night and could disturb local residents. According to Järvan, the compromise is necessary.

"The people who live nearby versus the citywide continuity of infrastructure and keeping the city functioning during peak hours — these are always factors that have to be weighed. But the general practice has been to grant construction companies nighttime work permits on arterial roads with such heavy traffic volumes. As things stand today, to my knowledge, the contractor has not yet been issued a nighttime work permit, but the usual practice is for one to be issued, which means less disruption to traffic," Järvan said.

Moving some road repairs to nighttime hours, however, does not mean that roadworks will not affect traffic this fall.

"There will certainly be traffic disruptions, but at the same time, we want our streets to be in good condition. Liivalaia tänav has been waiting for repairs for years, while Pärnu maantee is due to undergo reconstruction in the coming years. It would certainly not make sense to work on a street intersecting with such a major arterial road as Liivalaia tänav at the same time. Unfortunately, the Pärnu maantee end of Liivalaia tänav is already in such a condition that even its base layers need repairs, but unfortunately, we will not be able to do that within the timeframe we are currently working with," Järvan said.

Plans for reconstructing a section of Pärnu maantee in Tallinn's city center. Autor/allikas: K-Projekt

The fact that the road surface on Liivalaia tänav between Juhkentali tänav and Pärnu maantee is now being replaced means that Liivalaia tänav will not undergo a full reconstruction in the next few years, the deputy mayor acknowledged.

"Since Pärnu maantee is due to undergo reconstruction and must be completed by 2029, Liivalaia tänav certainly cannot be reconstructed at the same time," Järvan said.

Ripping up concrete on Peterburi tee still not decided

One of the largest reconstruction projects currently underway in the capital is on the section of Peterburi tee closest to Kesklinn. According to Järvan, the section should be completed by the end of October, although it is not yet possible to say so with complete certainty. The city is currently analyzing how to proceed with the reconstruction of Peterburi tee, as the bulk of the work still lies ahead

Much of the current deliberation centers on whether to remove the concrete base, which has served road users for decades but has now turned into what Järvan described as a "roller coaster." Removing the concrete would mean significantly more work and higher costs, the deputy mayor noted.

There is not much time left to make a decision, however, as work on the next section is scheduled to begin next year.

"If our plans work out and we can go with the lighter option — removing the top layer and repairing the concrete slabs — then we would still like to start next year. But if it does require — and the analyses show that it does require — more extensive reconstruction, then that is something we still need to consider," the deputy mayor said.

According to Järvan, the city also needs to address the longstanding problem of roadworks piling up in the fall, when traffic is significantly heavier than in the summer.

Peterburi tee. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"The reason is that in the past, including last year, contracts and procurements for work to be carried out that same year were not completed in time. That means the procurement process does not begin until spring, contracts are not signed until summer and roadworks only begin after that. This year, we have arranged things so that procurements and contracts will be completed within the current year," he said.

"That means that next year, as soon as the weather permits in spring or early summer, roadworks can get underway. This will spread roadworks out more over the year, which means fewer traffic problems and allows the work to take place primarily in the summer," the deputy mayor added.

World.title: Swiping a few apples may have ended in a beating in 19th century Estonia
World.content:
Nowadays, those caught pilfering peas or apples from someone else's field or garden may justify it as a folk tradition. In the 19th century, however, getting caught meant a trip to court and a sound thrashing as punishment.

The first apple orchards began appearing on farms 150 years ago and establishing one was a very expensive undertaking at the time. That was also why farmers kept a close eye on their apples. While fences kept animals away from the valuable produce, they were no help against people.

"A very common practice was to plant apple trees near the windows so they could be watched from inside the house. There were also dogs in the yard, of course, and some farmers would stand guard themselves," gardening history researcher Anneli Banner said.

Pilfering apples could land someone in court. In 1874, for example, boys aged 13 to 14 were caught stealing apples in Piilsi village near Avinurme — some took eight, others 10 and one 17.

"This was a time when punishment was either a fine or corporal punishment, meaning a birching. The boys' fathers refused to appear in court because they were afraid they themselves might receive corporal punishment," Avinurme local historian Piret Haav said.

That left the mothers with no choice but to go to court themselves and then carry out the punishment, giving their sons 10 strokes with a birch rod. It was quite unusual for parents, rather than the court, to have to administer the punishment. An adult would not have gotten off so lightly.

"The number of strokes varied, as did the fines. They ranged from 50 kopecks to a couple of dozen rubles, or from 10 to 30 strokes with a birch rod," Haav said.

While pea growers are now the ones who mainly have trouble with people helping themselves to their crops, the Estonian term raksus käima originated in apple orchards and comes from the cracking sound made when branches break.

"The word raks is an onomatopoeic word referring to a sudden cracking sound and the expression is presumably based on that comparison. Going out to pilfer or steal is an emotionally charged activity and emotionally charged activities tend to have many synonyms. These are often based on comparisons and one way of forming them is through onomatopoeia," Estonian Language Institute vocabulary researcher Iris Metsmägi said.

But while such pilfering was considered theft in the past, how is it viewed today?

"I suppose nowadays it is, whereas in the past it wasn't really seen that way. When you were a child and took an apple from a neighbor's garden, you didn't feel like much of a thief, although maybe you did feel a little twinge of guilt inside, but..." Ülle said.

"It's like going into a pea field, secretly eating a few peas there and taking a few with you. Or going into your neighbor's garden to eat a few apples — that sort of thing," Liisa said.

World.title: Anton Aleksejev: Putin does not know the people he lives among
World.content:
By allowing Yabloko to participate in the State Duma elections and failing to anticipate its rise in popularity, Vladimir Putin's administration has confirmed that it does not understand the people it governs, writes Anton Aleksejev.

A legend says that when Yuri Andropov came to power in 1982 after Leonid Brezhnev's death, he told a Politburo meeting: "We do not know the people among whom we live."

More than forty years later, Vladimir Putin — also with a KGB background — has clearly ended up in the same situation. He prefers to believe that people who oppose the war are marginal in number and that the overwhelming majority is actually pleased about it.

In early August, Putin quoted volunteers he had previously met. They asked the president: "When the 'special military operation'"— the official term for the war in Russia — "eventually ends, what will we do then?" Putin did not say what he answered. He likely does not know himself.

Life goes on, however, and since — unlike in Ukraine — martial law has not been declared in Russia, State Duma elections will be held on September 20. "Elections" is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament.

On July 30, the Central Election Commission registered 11 parties to participate. All share unconditional loyalty to the Kremlin, but as usual only four or five will actually enter parliament. United Russia will get the majority. The Communists, Liberal Democrats, A Just Russia, and the supposedly liberal New People will divide the remaining seats the Kremlin leaves for them.

Among those who have never had access to parliamentary mandates is Yabloko, founded in 1993 and considered democratic and liberal.

"'Elections' is a conditional term, because in such cases the Kremlin has long been simply appointing the next composition of parliament."

They last entered the Duma almost 20 years ago. Since then, their chances have steadily declined — partly because the party refused cooperation with potential allies (including the then‑alive Alexei Navalny), and partly because the Kremlin decided once and for all that the Duma podium would not be given to "odd characters." Even so, Yabloko was regarded as an "old party," one Putin treated with a certain respect, and they never skipped an election.

As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!"

Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy head of the presidential administration responsible for elections, reasoned that Yabloko would again get its two to three percent, fail to enter parliament, and prove to all anti‑war citizens that they are vanishingly few.

But within a week of registration, support for the party rose from three percent to seven — with a month and a half still to go. The outsider and marginal force was becoming a poorly controllable threat right before the presidential administration's eyes.

Of course, according to Stalin's principle — "it doesn't matter how people vote, but how the votes are counted" — no level of public support would have changed anything. No one intended to let Yabloko into the Duma.

Still, the mere fact that during the fifth year of the war, the slogan "For peace and freedom!" would appear on television and in newspapers for six weeks could have unpredictable consequences.

Yabloko did not speak about who Crimea belongs to, did not oppose holding elections in occupied Ukrainian territories, and so on. Two words were enough to signal clearly: if you want the war to end as soon as possible, here are people who share your view. And voting would show how many of you there are.

The FSB's 2nd Service — responsible for protecting constitutional order — understood the problem first. Action had to be swift and decisive. On August 7, it filed a lawsuit with the Supreme Court to remove Yabloko from the elections.

As usual, the FSB chose a suitable executor. Official parties — Communists, Liberal Democrats — rushed to accuse Yabloko of extremism and near‑treason, but none dared go to court demanding a ban.

The role fit perfectly for State Duma deputy Alexei Zhuravlyov of the Rodina party. The party itself is not represented in the Duma, but Zhuravlyov was allowed in during the previous elections, presumably in hopes he might be useful.

So far, his usefulness has consisted mainly of appearances on propaganda TV shows, where he has called for killing at least two million Ukrainians and claimed that Europe has special zoophile zoos where perverts can pay to have sex with animals, even turtles.

"As befits a marginal party, Yabloko entered the elections with a slogan marginal in today's Russia: "For peace and freedom!""

Zhuravlyov did not disappoint his superiors. In his lawsuit, he accused Yabloko of extremism, foreign funding, and even copyright infringement. One Yabloko poster depicted a nuclear explosion as a symbol of war. Zhuravlyov claimed the photo showed the 1945 Hiroshima bombing and that the rights belonged to the U.S. Army.

Even the judge was surprised and asked whether Zhuravlyov could prove his claims. He was unfazed: the photo could not exist without the bombing, and since the bomb belonged to the United States, the image of its explosion must also be U.S. property.

By that logic, anyone wishing to use a photo of a nuclear explosion in the future must build a nuclear bomb, detonate it themselves, and photograph the blast — otherwise they risk being crushed by the Russian legal system.

Despite the absurdity, on August 10 the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the elections — the first time in Russian history that a party was banned just ten days after being allowed to run.

As the murdered Boris Nemtsov said, in the absence of fair elections and fair polling, the only way to understand a political force's popularity in Russia is through the authorities' reaction.

Everything happened exactly in line with Andropov's words. By allowing Yabloko to run and failing to foresee its rise, the presidential administration confirmed it does not know the people it lives among. The FSB, by removing Yabloko with Zhuravlyov and the Supreme Court, clarified: we do not know them and do not want to know them.

Meanwhile, such unwillingness to know the governed is characteristic of many governments. Volodymyr Zelenskyy likely did not expect that his July decision to dismiss former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov would bring thousands of young people into the streets in protest.

Last Monday, several hundred young Yabloko supporters gathered outside the Supreme Court in Moscow. For a city of millions, that is not many, but in a country where all unsanctioned street gatherings are effectively banned, it is a significant number.

The motivation of young Russians who do not want to go to war and fear mobilization coincides strikingly with the motivation of at least two million Ukrainians trying to avoid mobilization.

And if Yabloko's slogan "For peace!" is interpreted as a call to freeze fighting along the front line immediately and begin negotiations, then nearly 60 percent of Ukrainians today share that view.

How many Russians share it, we will not know — but judging by the authorities' reaction, enough to cast doubt on the continuation of the war. And as Vladimir Putin said: "When the war ends, what will we do then?"

World.title: Mounting public interest seeing teachers brush up on drone knowledge
World.content:
Over the next five months, 20 science and mathematics teachers will visit various companies to gain practical insights and work together to create teaching materials for the future.

The "Lae end" ("Charge Yourself") education program is aimed at middle school physics and mathematics teachers, helping them bring more practical examples and real-life connections into the teaching of science and mathematics. This year, 72 teachers applied to the program, of whom 20 were selected. Participants include both new and more experienced teachers who began the program at Metrosert's drone and defense technology testing laboratory.

"We have a whole range of laboratories here for testing subsystems. What is important about all of these laboratories is that the tests can be replicated," said Rainer Kivimäe, head of Metrosert's drone unit.

Interest in drones and artificial intelligence is also growing in schools, meaning teachers increasingly need to be able to explain these topics to students.

"Starting this academic year, as far as I know, some schools will begin talking more about drones. An educational program is also being developed in Tallinn where young people will be able to play drone soccer themselves. So young people's interest in the field is gradually beginning to grow and teachers naturally need to be knowledgeable enough to discuss it in the first place," said "Lae end" program manager Valentina Moskaljova.

For teachers, this means getting up to speed on subjects they have not encountered before.

"I knew as much about drones as I'd read in the news, basically, and as much as has recently been said about introducing a drone curriculum in schools," said Getriin Kokk, a mathematics teacher at Lodijärve School.

The program will also produce teaching materials for students in grades seven through nine.

"Young people need to understand which formulas they can use in both mathematics and physics. Right now, we're giving teachers the opportunity to work together in groups to create materials specifically designed to support that learning," Moskaljova said.

World.title: Gallery: Ukrainian children's fairytale art from Kharkiv reaches Estonia
World.content:
More than a dozen works by young artists in Kharkiv are now on display in Pärnu, blending forgotten legends and untold tales with new mythologies in large, colorful scenes.

"Lost Fairy Tales" opened at the Pärnu Museum of New Art (MONA) this week, showcasing 14 monumental original works created by about 40 children and teens ages 5–17.

Kharkiv's Aza Nizi Maza art studio continues to operate from a World War II-era bomb shelter, where kids still meet, learn and create amid ongoing drone, missile and guided-bomb strikes on the city.

The exhibition grew from the idea of a "missing museum" — a world made up of forgotten legends, untold stories and new mythologies inspired by the Baroque collections of European museums.

The young artists first drew elements found in ancient frescoes, botanical atlases, medieval maps and manuscripts before developing characters and building narratives around them.

Details like rosehips, seashells, bones, bats, lions and musical instruments meet characters ranging from beggars, saints and witches to princesses, children and those who have seen it all.

The scale of the works, which measure 2.5 x 1.5 meters, allows viewers to step into these visual worlds and become part of the unfolding narratives.

Curated by Mykola Kolomiiets and Iryna Hrytska, "Lost Fairy Tales" will remain on view in Pärnu through October 4.

World.title: Iraq Ministry of Oil inks deal with Japan’s JGC to resume FCC project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Friday, August 14, 2026, an agreement with Japan’s JGC Corporation to officially resume construction and operational work on the massive Fluid Catalytic Cracking (FCC) complex at the South Refineries Company (SRC) in Basra.

The deal follows negotiations led by a ministerial committee under directives from Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair Al-Abadi, chaired by Ministry Advisor Hamid Younis alongside SRC Director General Hussam Hussein Wali. Under the finalized agreement, JGC remobilized its technical personnel to the Basra site starting August 10 to prepare processing units for full design-capacity operations, advancing Iraq’s target of refined petroleum self-sufficiency.

Key Operational Deliverables & Production Capacity

High-Octane Gasoline: Adding 5 million liters per day to domestic fuel supplies.

Gas Oil (Diesel): Producing approximately 7 million liters per day.

Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG): Delivering 400 metric tons per day for commercial and domestic consumption.

Project Milestone: Mobilization of JGC engineering teams began on August 10, 2026, to finalize site preparations and run commissioning sequences.

Strategic Objective: Eliminating fuel import expenditures and converting heavy refining residues into high-value white petroleum products.

The FCC complex at the Shuaiba refinery in Basra is among Iraq’s most critical downstream modernization projects, designed to upgrade heavy vacuum gas oil into premium fuels.

By adding 12 million combined liters of daily gasoline and diesel alongside substantial LPG yields, the facility will significantly curtail state spending on imported refined fuels and support domestic market stability.

World.title: Iraq customs revenues hit 2.5 trillion IQD in Seven Months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s General Customs Authority collected 2.5 trillion Iraqi Dinars (approximately $1.9 billion) in revenues during the first seven months of 2026, matching total receipts recorded for the entirety of 2025, Director-General Thamer Qasim Al-Taie announced on Saturday, August 15, 2026.

Speaking to state-run Al Iraqiya News, Al-Taie stated that July alone generated 560 billion IQD, representing a 150% year-on-year surge compared to July 2025. With revenue collection accelerating across all federal border crossings, full-year receipts are projected to surpass 3.5 trillion IQD ($2.67 billion)—the highest annual total in modern Iraqi state history.

Key Revenue Indicators & Technical Upgrades

Seven-Month Total:2.5 trillion IQD (~$1.9B) collected through July 2026, equaling full-year 2025 custom receipts.

July Revenue Surge: Recorded 560 billion IQD, a 150% increase compared to July 2025.

Annual Projection: Forecasted to exceed 3.5 trillion IQD (~$2.67B) by year-end 2026, setting a national historical record.

Automation & Anti-Corruption: Revenue jumps were driven by the nationwide rollout of SCADA systems, automated customs processing, and integrated digital networks connecting border crossings with government agencies, drastically curbing tariff evasion and illicit clearances.

The sharp rise in customs collections reflects Baghdad’s wider push to modernize border controls, plug financial leakages, and reduce structural dependence on crude oil sales amid regional market volatility.

By implementing mandatory automated documentation and digital data-sharing across federal transit checkpoints, the Customs Authority has systematically reduced tariff evasion, accelerated cargo clearances, and fortified federal non-oil revenue streams.

World.title: Popular Lebanese restaurant Al Beiruti to open in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Al Beiruti, a popular Lebanese restaurant, is set to build its first Iraqi branch in Iraq Mall in Baghdad, adding another significant regional dining name to the capital’s growing restaurant scene.

The Baghdad inauguration will be the next chapter of Al Beiruti’s regional development, after previous launches in Jordan and Qatar, as well as its established presence in the UAE.

The restaurant announced that its Iraq Mall restaurant is about to open, with a local franchise arrangement handling the expansion.

Al Beiruti has become a renowned location for Lebanese food in the Middle East, providing both classic dishes and a more modern restaurant experience.

The menu includes Lebanese favorites, including manakish, fattoush, hummus, baba ghanouj, and grilled halloumi, as well as shawarma, wraps, and mixed grills. Larger meals include steak, chicken escalope, and grilled salmon.

Al Beiruti joins a growing number of international and regional food and beverage companies in Baghdad, as new malls and commercial expansions change the city’s retail and entertainment markets.

Iraq Mall has emerged as a focal point of that expansion, drawing new restaurants, boutiques, and entertainment ideas as consumer spending and private-sector investment continue to rise in the capital.

World.title: Baghdad and Erbil agree on unified digital customs system across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Baghdad and Erbil have agreed to fully adopt the digital ASYCUDA customs system across border crossings, with non-oil border earnings shared equally by the federal and Kurdistan regional governments.

The deal is a significant step toward standardizing customs processes across Iraq and addressing long-standing disagreements over border revenues and claimed import quantities.

ASYCUDA, designed by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), digitizes customs declarations, payments, and clearing processes, allowing authorities to better monitor products entering the nation and the income they earn.

Linking customs operations to Iraq’s banking and electronic payment systems may help limit the potential for underreporting, revenue leakage, and corruption at border crossings.

The deal comes as Iraq’s Finance Ministry and Central Bank work to digitize customs, payments, and government financial data in collaboration with UNCTAD.

A combined computerized customs system for Baghdad and Erbil might give more accurate revenue data while resolving one of the two governments’ ongoing financial issues.

The change is also significant for Iraq’s overall economy.

More open and uniform customs processes might facilitate cross-border commerce, boost governmental revenues, and enhance the business climate as Iraq pursues more foreign investment and closer integration with international markets.

World.title: Iraq’s Chief Justice Faiq Zidan meets Syrian President Al-Sharaa in Damascus
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zidan met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus on Thursday, marking another high-level Iraqi outreach to a neighboring Arab state as Baghdad seeks to bolster regional relations under rising security problems.

Al-Sharaa welcomed Zidan and an Iraqi delegation to the People’s Palace, which also included Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais.

According to the Syrian president, the talks focused on extending judicial and legal cooperation between Iraq and Syria, as well as resolving mutual concerns.

The visit also resulted in more practical conversations among the two nations’ judicial officials. Iraqi and Syrian authorities agreed to set up joint judicial committees to continue working on cases involving Syrian prisoners and other cross-border legal issues.

Zidan’s visit is crucial as he is one of the most prominent persons in Iraq’s state institutions, and it coincides with Baghdad’s increased diplomatic, security, and judicial interaction with its neighbors.

The Damascus meetings come after a separate Iraqi security group visited Riyadh, where senior military official Abdul Amir al-Shammari met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman.

Zidan had also just visited Ankara as part of a larger Iraqi effort to build ties with Saudi Arabia, Syria, and Turkey.

That approach has become more urgent in light of the regional escalation involving Iran-backed Iraqi forces.

In late July, the United States and Saudi Arabia conducted synchronized attacks against locations used by Iran-aligned organizations in Iraq, after Riyadh accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones against Saudi energy infrastructure.

The incident put Baghdad under strong pressure to prevent armed organizations from exploiting Iraqi territory to launch assaults on neighboring nations and also highlighted the potential that militia activity may harm Iraq’s improved ties with Arab governments.

Against this setting, Zidan’s encounter with Al-Sharaa is significant beyond regular court cooperation.

Iraq and Syria share a long border and confront shared concerns such as terrorism, organized crime, prisoners, and cross-border security. Baghdad also has a strategic interest in preserving stable ties with Damascus, as Iraq strives to boost regional connections and prevent unrest from spilling over its borders.

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s administration sees recent diplomatic efforts as part of a larger effort to strengthen Iraq’s ties with its neighbors while keeping the nation out of the developing conflict between Iran and its regional adversaries.

Baghdad has increasingly emphasized that choices on security, armament, and relations with neighboring governments must be made by Iraqi official authorities rather than armed groupings.

The travels to Damascus and Riyadh therefore convey an essential message: although Iran-aligned militias have exacerbated tensions between Iraq and certain of its neighbors, Iraqi official institutions are working directly with those nations to restore cooperation and avoid further escalation.

Strengthening judicial, diplomatic, and security ties with Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey might serve as an essential regional buffer for Iraq as it seeks to safeguard its sovereignty, control armed groups, and avoid being drawn further into the region’s crises.

World.title: Iraq’s Al-Shammari visits Riyadh to meet Saudi Defense Minister
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A top Iraqi security team has traveled to Riyadh for meetings with Saudi Arabia’s leadership, as Baghdad and the Kingdom work to improve security and military cooperation after weeks of heightened tensions in Iraq involving Iran-backed militias.

First Lieutenant General Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, met with Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman on Thursday to discuss military cooperation, regional developments, and increased coordination between the two nations.

According to reports from the visit, the conversations included cross-border drone concerns, air defense, and intelligence collaboration.

The conference is especially significant in light of the combined US-Saudi attacks on Iran-linked militia locations in Iraq on July 29.

Washington and Riyadh said the operation targeted Iran-backed terrorists’ weapons and logistical facilities in response to a series of drone assaults on Saudi oil installations that they said originated in Iraqi territory.

The strikes drastically escalated tensions between Baghdad and Riyadh, highlighting the Iraqi government’s problems in preventing armed groups from exploiting its territory to target neighboring nations.

Thursday’s visit indicates that both parties are now attempting to move beyond that conflict via direct military and intelligence collaboration.

Prince Khalid underlined Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Iraq’s security, stability, and economic growth, identifying it as an essential neighbor with whom the Kingdom has strong political and social relations.

The meetings in Riyadh follow Saudi intelligence head Khalid bin Ali al-Humaidan’s visit to Baghdad last week, during which he met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and reiterated an offer for the Iraqi leader to visit Saudi Arabia.

Baghdad’s security cooperation with Riyadh has grown more vital as the government seeks to prevent Iran-backed militias from drawing Iraq into a larger regional conflict.

Al-Zaidi has frequently said that Iraqi soil should not be used to attack other nations and has stepped up efforts for weaponry to be put solely under state control.

The most recent Iraqi trip to Riyadh symbolizes more than just normal defense diplomacy. It is part of a joint effort by Baghdad and Saudi Arabia to restore security trust after the July escalation and prevent militia activities from dragging the two neighboring nations into conflict.

World.title: Rare blind fish found in underground river in Iraq’s Anbar desert
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security and environmental teams have discovered a fascinating underground water system deep under the dry Anbar desert, where rare eyeless fish thrive in total darkness.

The location is in the Al-Khasfa region near Haditha, and crews traveled through a remote desert cave and sinkhole system to access running groundwater hundreds of meters under the surface.

The expedition’s footage shows little, pale fish moving in the subterranean water in the lack of sunshine.

The fish have evolved to live in darkness by losing their eyes and pigmentation, giving them a characteristic white-to-pink look.

The crew traveled more than 500 meters into the cave system despite challenging terrain and low oxygen levels.

The difference between above- and underground has piqued interest: underneath what seems to be an isolated and very arid stretch of western Iraqi desert, there is flowing freshwater and a specialized ecology.

Initial investigations have also suggested a link between the subterranean water system and the Euphrates basin, with the watercourse possibly running for a long distance under the desert.

However, environmental experts have highlighted that the blind fish themselves are not a novel finding.

Qais Najeh, the chairman of the Anbar Environment Directorate, stated that experts first confirmed the occurrence of eyeless fish in Al-Khasfa in 2010.

Similar fish have also been discovered in subterranean water near the Sheik Hadid mausoleum in Haditha district.

According to experts, the fish may grow to be roughly 49 millimeters long and survive in rather steady groundwater temperatures ranging from 20 to 22 degrees Celsius.

Their lack of vision and pigmentation are adaptations to generations of living in perpetually dark subterranean habitats.

The recent mission is nonetheless noteworthy because it has refocused attention on one of Iraq’s least-known natural ecosystems, perhaps allowing scientists to better research the subterranean water network, its geology, and the creatures that rely on it.

The fish’s severely limited environment renders it vulnerable.

Changes in groundwater levels, pollution, or human intervention might endanger a population that has acclimated to highly particular subsurface circumstances.

The Al-Khasfa location offers a unique dimension to Anbar, a region best known for its wide western desert and the Euphrates.

Hidden under that terrain lies an environment few Iraqis have ever seen: flowing subterranean water that feeds fish who have evolved to survive their entire lives without sunshine.

World.title: Israel reopens once-closed West Bank settlement
World.content:
GANIM – Israel officially reopened the West Bank settlement of Ganim on Thursday, more than 20 years after it withdrew from the community, in a move emblematic of the current government’s policy of rapid settlement expansion.

The smell of freshly-poured asphalt hung in the air above Ganim’s new and only street, where future residents and their families — who had come to help with the move — smiled at the sight of their pre-fabricated homes.

“A month ago there was nothing here. A rocky mountain, barely any trees, barely any shade. We’re arriving now,” new resident Reut Baran, 35, told AFP in front of her new home.

In a nearby truck, dozens of brand new air conditioning units still in their boxes were waiting to be installed.

Matan Berkovitch, a 25-year-old who moved into the new settlement with his wife and child, said he was satisfied with the government’s policy towards settlements as he looked around a brand new home just connected to the electric grid.

“I’m happy to be part of a time like this where there are ministers in the government who support and guide us in the right direction and know how to get things done properly,” he said.

Berkovitch’s mother Carmit, who came from Jerusalem to move him in, said another one of her sons would soon study at the religious school in the settlement, and expressed pride at their active part in the settler movement.

“Here, this is the Land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said at the ceremony, after arriving by helicopter.

Ganim is one of four Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank that Israel evacuated under former prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan in 2005.

The move came partly because of their isolated location in the north of the territory among many Palestinian cities and villages.

Under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, settlement construction and expansion have soared, including with the official re-establishment of three of the four evacuated communities — Ganim, Sa-Nur and Homesh.

In Ganim, about two dozen pre-fabricated homes have already been installed, while steamrollers and other construction machinery busily created new space for future houses on the hillside on Thursday.

About a hundred people from Israel and other West Bank settlements attended the ceremony, including Katz and Yossi Dagan, head of the Israeli authority in charge of settlements in the northern West Bank.

“The era of evacuation is over — from here, we only build,” Dagan said.

In the valley below, Palestinians who spoke to AFP feared Ganim’s construction would make their lives harder, or even mean eventual displacement.

On both sides of the road leading to the settlement from Israel, the army has demolished stores in recent days and blocked several dirt roads to Palestinian communities with piles of rubble.

Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the territory, which are illegal under international law, among some three million Palestinians.

Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.

World.title: Air India Express passenger fires during weapon check at Varanasi airport, 2 injured
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A passenger travelling with his wife on an Air India Express flight to Mumbai fired a round during a weapon check at Varanasi airport on Sunday, injuring two security screeners.

The incident took place around 9.30 am when the passenger, travelling on flight IX-1810, declared that he was carrying weapons on board.

During the weapons check, the passenger fired a round, injuring two AAICLAS screeners. Both were taken to New Laxmi Trauma Centre for treatment.

Local police have been informed and an investigation into the incident is under way, Varanasi Airport Director said.

World.title: E. coli bacteria found in drinking water samples across railway stations: CAG report
World.content:
NEW DELHI: E. coli bacteria, some strains of which can cause food poisoning, diarrhoea and kidney failure, has been detected in drinking samples collected from water coolers at several railway stations, according to a report by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India.

The CAG study assessed passenger services at 512 non-suburban grade railway stations across all Indian Railway zones.

It found that water samples from coolers tested positive for E. coli at eight railway stations across four zones.

"Water sample from water cooler was positive for E.coli at two stations (Coimbatore and Palakkad Junctions) in SR (Southern Railway), one station (Hyderabad) in SCR (South Central Railway), four stations (Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, Bhiwandi Road, Kalyan and Lonavala) in CR (Central Railway) and one station (Madhupur) in ER (Eastern Railway)," the report said, according to PTI.

The audit also found that 458 of the 512 selected stationsâmore than 89%âwere deficient in providing Minimum Essential Amenities (MEA). At these stations, MEAs were either not provided or were available below the prescribed norms.

"In April 2018, RB (Railway Board) issued comprehensive instructions prescribing Minimum Essential Amenities (MEA), Recommended Amenities (RA) and Desirable Amenities (DA) for stations categorised as NSG 1 to NSG 6.





RB stipulated that MEAs were to be ensured at all stations by 31 August 2018," the report stated.

"RB's instructions (April 2018) mandated that MEAs be provided first at all stations, irrespective of category. These include drinking water, waiting halls, seating arrangements, platform shelters, urinals, latrines, high-level platforms, fans, Foot Over Bridges (FOBs), dustbins, clocks and public address systems," it added.

According to the CAG, Indian Railways has 5,908 stations under the Non-Suburban Group (NSG), while it operated more than 7,424 non-suburban passenger trains daily and carried 292.4 crore non-suburban passengers in 2023-24.

Deficiencies were found even at NSG-1 stations such as CSMT and Mumbai Central (both in Mumbai), Howrah and Sealdah (both West Bengal) and New Delhi, including in seating arrangements, sanitary facilities such as urinals and latrines, dustbins and electronic train indicator boards.

Explaining the rationale for the detailed inspection, the CAG noted that the Railway Board had issued various guidelines for providing passenger amenities at stations. The audit assessed whether the Railways' efforts to provide passenger amenities and sanitation facilities were delivering the intended benefits.

An analysis of the Passenger Amenities Management System also revealed shortfalls against MEA norms, including inadequate latrines at 201 stations, urinals at 403 stations and water taps at 2,035 stations, among other deficiencies.

Among its key recommendations, the CAG urged the Railways to "ensure compliance with prescribed protocols for inspection of water supply systems and comprehensive testing of drinking water quality, including all parameters under the Uniform Drinking Water Quality Protocol."

World.title: Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn, Tiger Shroff get FDA notice over Vimal ad
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued show-cause notices to actors

,

and

over their  for Vimal Elaichi.

The FDA said the  may amount to âindirect or surrogateâ promotion of prohibited pan masala and tobacco-related products.

According to the notice issued by the FDAâs Greater Mumbai division on August 11, the use of the name âVIMAL Elaichiâ in the  appears to create an association with the Vimal Pan Masala brand. The department said this could mislead consumers and indirectly promote a prohibited product.

The FDA described the notice as a âfinal warningâ and said the  appeared to be misleading and contrary to provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and related regulations.

Actors asked to stop promoting ad

The FDA has directed the three leading film-stars to immediately stop participating in or endorsing the Vimal Pan Masala/Elaichi .

They have also been asked to remove the promotional content from their official social media accounts, websites and other digital platforms under their control.

The actors have been told not to provide any further assistance in broadcasting, publishing or promoting the  in any form.





The FDA has also sought details of the checks carried out by the actors or their agencies before they agreed to the campaign.

FDA seeks details of Vimal Elaichi

The action followed the departmentâs examination of the Vimal Elaichi , which was being shown on television, digital platforms, social media and other promotional media.

The FDA said the Vimal brand is strongly associated with pan masala in Maharashtra, where pan masala containing prohibited substances is banned.

The actors have been asked to provide documents showing whether Vimal Elaichi is an independent product actually available in the market or whether it is being used as a surrogate or brand-extension  for Vimal pan masala or tobacco-related products.

They have also been asked to submit details of their endorsement agreements, campaign briefs, product information, payments and other arrangements, along with details of the advertising agency and brand owner involved.

The notice also seeks details of the television channels, digital platforms, social media accounts and other media where the  was published or broadcast, as well as the period during which it was shown.

15 days to respond

The actors have 15 days from the date they receive the notice to submit written explanations and supporting documents. They can also request a personal hearing, either themselves or through an authorised representative.

The FDA warned that if no response is received within the deadline, or if the explanation is found unsatisfactory, further action could be taken without another notice.

The action follows a prohibition order issued by the Maharashtra Food Safety Commissioner on July 13 under the Food Safety and Standards Act. The order is valid for one year and covers specified tobacco, nicotine and areca-nut-based prohibited food products.

World.title: ‘Proud to be a dimagi naxal’: P Chidambaram hits back at PM Modi
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former Union minister and senior Congress leader

on Sunday hit back at Prime Minister

over his âdimagi naxalâ remarks, saying he was âproudâ to be described by the term.

âI am proud to be a dimagi naxal!â Chidambaram said in a post on X, a day after PM Modi, in his 80th Independence Day address from the Red Fort, warned that although armed Naxalism was nearing its end, people with an ideological Naxal mindset continued to pose a threat.

PM Modi had urged people to âidentify and isolateâ such individuals, saying they were looking for opportunities to promote violence and unrest and âdrag the country on the wrong pathâ.

The Prime Minister said his government had made ending Naxalism a priority after coming to power in 2014. He said decades of Maoist violence had destroyed the lives and aspirations of young people and claimed that more than 3,500 security personnel had been killed in the conflict.

âNaxalism, Maoism destroyed the dreams of lakhs of youth. It stole the sons of numerous mothers, crushed the dreams of numerous mothers,â PM Modi said in his Independence Day address.





He also alleged that people with a Maoist mindset had earlier occupied positions of influence in government committees and policymaking.

âFor years, people with Maoist thinking were there in public life, even in government committees this thinking had affected various institutions and initiatives,â PM Modi said, before calling for the âdimagi naxalâ to be identified and isolated.

Congress attacks PM Modiâs âdimagi naxalâ remark

Chidambaram's response came a day after Congress had already attacked PM Modi over the remarks.

Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh accused the Prime Minister of reviving the âurban naxalâ label to target political opponents. He argued that the government had previously used the term despite Union home minister Amit Shah clarifying in Parliament that there was no official definition of âurban Naxalâ.

Ramesh also alleged that the government eventually adopted some of the issues raised by people it had labelled âurban Naxalsâ.

He cited the caste census as an example, saying the idea had earlier been dismissed as reflecting âurban Naxalâ thinking before the government announced a caste-based census.

âFirst, you make derogatory remarks--calling them 'Urban Naxals' or 'Mental Naxals'--but later, you accept the very demands your political opponents were making,â Ramesh said, according to news agency ANI.

The Congress leader had also earlier called PM Modi a âmaster abuserâ in âEntire Political Scienceâ while reacting to his use of the âurban naxalâ and âdimagi naxalâ labels.

The broader Opposition has also criticised PM Modi's remarks. CPI(M) general secretary M A Baby said his party opposed Naxalism but accused the government of using the âNaxal mentalityâ label to target political opponents.

CPI general secretary D Raja described âdimagi naxalâ as an attempt to stigmatise dissent.

TMC leader Saket Gokhale similarly accused PM Modi of using the Independence Day platform to take âcheap shotsâ at his critics.

PM Modi says armed Naxalism âbreathing its lastâ

PM Modi's remarks came as he declared that the government had made substantial progress in tackling armed Naxalism.

He said Naxalism had kept large parts of the country and its population âhostageâ for decades and had resulted in the deaths of thousands of security personnel.

World.title: Can reputation of a celebrity be inherited, asks HC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The

, which has recently become the preferred place to secure "personality rights", has raised concerns over the expanding nature of such rights.

While hearing a suit filed in 2023 over "misleading" YouTube content about the health and private life of Aradhya Bachchan, the minor daughter of actors Abhishek Bachchan and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan, the HC questioned whether a family's reputation flows down generations, how far personality rights extend and whether even "egregiously despicable" fake news can violate intellectual property rights.

"A certain last name has a reputation because of its eminence in a certain field of work. So, does that reputation, that you are couching as virtually as a trademark, flow down generationally? If so, up to what point?" Justice Anup J Bhambhani asked, flagging points that need to be examined in such cases.

In 2023, a single-judge bench had restrained several YouTube channels from publishing misleading content on Aaradhya's health, calling such misinformation about a child "morbid perversity" and "completely intolerable in law", and saying every child is entitled to respect.

- Abhinav Garg
