World.title: Experts: As Inflation Falls, Kazakhstan Faces New Monetary Policy Trade-Off
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s annual inflation slowed to 10.2% in July, extending its decline for a tenth consecutive month, while lending is increasingly shifting from consumer borrowing toward business financing, according to National Bank (NBK) Governor Timur Suleimenov’s report to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Aug. 13.

The figures point to a changing balance in Kazakhstan’s economy. Inflation is moving lower, and the NBK has already begun cautiously easing monetary policy, cutting the base rate to 16.75% in July. At the same time, stronger investment activity and continued quasi-fiscal stimulus are supporting faster economic growth, creating a potential limit on how quickly borrowing costs can decline further.

The National Bank’s next policy decision is scheduled for Sept. 4, when markets will be watching to see whether the regulator finds sufficient evidence that the slowdown in inflation is sustainable.

Inflation slows, creating room for cautious easing

According to Suleimenov, annual inflation declined to 10.2% in July. The slowdown follows a series of policy decisions that have gradually reduced the National Bank’s base rate. The regulator kept the rate at 18% in April, lowered it to 17% in June and then reduced it by another 25 basis points to 16.75% on July 24.

The latest reduction was significant because it marked a shift from maintaining restrictive conditions toward a cautious normalization of monetary policy. However, the National Bank has stressed that the decline in inflation does not mean the inflation problem has been resolved. In its July decision, the regulator noted that some underlying components of price growth remained elevated and inflation expectations continued to pose risks. The NBK therefore said that further decisions would depend on evidence that disinflation is sustainable, rather than on a predetermined path of rate cuts.

The central bank expects inflation to remain between 9% and 11% in 2026, then slow to 5.5%-7.5% in 2027 and approach its 5% target in 2028.

The key contradiction: growth is helping the economy but complicating inflation policy

One of the most important factors shaping the National Bank’s next steps is the strength of economic activity. According to the report, GDP growth reached 3% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, supported by stronger-than-expected investment activity.

Investment demand is expected to remain a major driver of growth, including through quasi-fiscal financing, subsidized loans, development institutions and guarantees supporting large projects. This creates a more complicated environment for monetary policy.

Normally, lower inflation would provide a stronger argument for cutting interest rates. But faster economic growth and continued investment stimulus can increase demand and liquidity, potentially adding new pressure to prices.

The National Bank has repeatedly identified the scale and parameters of quasi-fiscal stimulus as one of the major risks to the inflation outlook. In its monetary policy assessment, it warned that active quasi-fiscal financing can partly offset the effects of tighter monetary conditions and weaken the transmission of the base rate through the economy.

In other words, Kazakhstan is entering a phase in which monetary and quasi-fiscal policies will need to be more closely coordinated. The faster the government and quasi-public sector stimulate investment and demand, the more cautious the National Bank may need to be about reducing interest rates.

Credit growth shifts toward business

Suleimenov also reported a notable change in the structure of bank lending. As of July 1, business lending had increased 17.1% year-on-year, while lending to small and medium-sized enterprises accelerated to 29.6%. Meanwhile, consumer lending growth slowed from 21% at the beginning of the year to 13%, reflecting prudential measures and a gradual normalization of retail credit growth.

The shift is important for the broader economic strategy. Kazakhstan has long faced concerns about rapid growth in household borrowing and its potential contribution to consumption-driven demand. A slowdown in consumer lending combined with faster business financing could help redirect credit toward investment and production. Earlier National Bank data showed that SMEs were already the primary source of growth in corporate lending, while mortgage lending continued to expand, supported by preferential housing programs.

Whether this shift becomes sustainable will matter. Business lending can support productivity and supply capacity over the longer term, potentially reducing inflationary pressures if financing results in higher output. But in the short term, large-scale investment spending can also increase demand for imports, labor and construction materials.

A stronger tenge offers additional support

The strengthening of the tenge has also become an important part of the recent disinflation story. According to economist Ruslan Sultanov’s analysis of July currency market data, the rate on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange fell from 480.72 to 473.59 tenge per dollar during the month, while the weighted average rate on the over-the-counter market strengthened from approximately 486.2 to 471.4 tenge per dollar.

According to Sultanov, the strengthening occurred despite continued substantial demand for foreign currency. The Unified Accumulative Pension Fund purchased $375 million on the market in July, while the mandatory sale of part of quasi-public-sector foreign-currency revenues was suspended as of July 15.

At the same time, the National Bank did not conduct foreign exchange interventions, while sales from the National Fund totaled $200 million, and quasi-public-sector entities sold around $195 million.

“This is an interesting signal: even with significant counter‑demand from the fund and a reduction in one of the sources of the mandatory currency supply, the market still ended the month with a stronger tenge,” Sultanov wrote in his Telegram channel.

A stronger tenge can help slow inflation by reducing the cost of imported goods and limiting the pass-through of exchange-rate movements into consumer prices. The National Bank has identified the stronger currency as one of the factors supporting disinflation.

Markets expect another cut, but not a rapid easing cycle

Professional market participants surveyed by the Association of Financiers of Kazakhstan in August have become more optimistic about both inflation and the tenge. Their 12-month inflation forecast declined to 10.1%, while 60% of respondents expected the National Bank to lower the base rate to 16.5% at its Sept. 4 meeting. Another 28% expected the rate to remain unchanged at 16.75%, while 12% allowed for a rate increase.

Over a 12-month horizon, respondents expect the base rate to fall to 14.75%. Yet even this forecast points to gradual rather than aggressive easing. According to the AFK’s analytical center, the projected real interest rate would remain positive at around 4.65%, reflecting expectations that inflation risks will continue to constrain the speed of rate cuts.

That cautious outlook broadly corresponds with the National Bank’s position. The regulator has emphasized that the return to its 5% inflation target depends not only on interest rate policy, but also on fiscal consolidation, a narrowing of quasi-fiscal stimulus, stable inflation expectations and predictable tariff policies.

The Sept. 4 rate decision will therefore be about more than whether the base rate is reduced by another 25 basis points. It will provide a clearer indication of how the regulator views this trade-off: whether the recent decline in inflation is sufficient to justify a broader easing cycle, or whether Kazakhstan’s accelerating investment-driven economy will require monetary policy to remain restrictive for longer.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, people leave” – from a march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video blog
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Judges vs ordinary pensioners in Azerbaijan: what the law and figures show
World.content:
Judges and pensions in Azerbaijan

The pension of Azerbaijani judge Jahangir Yusifov was increased from 4,700 manat (around $2,765) to 7,500 manat (around $4,412) after he took the matter to court. Thanks to special pension rules, judges’ pensions can be dozens of times higher than the country’s average pension.

For comparison: the minimum labour pension in Azerbaijan is 320 manat (around $188).

When Baku Court of Appeal judge Jahangir Yusifov retired in 2025 at the age of 65, the State Social Protection Fund awarded him a monthly pension of 4,700 manat. That amount was equivalent to around 58% of his average monthly salary while serving as a judge.

Yusifov demanded that his pension be increased to 8,200 manat (around $4,824), arguing that he had worked all his life under difficult conditions, possessed special professional qualifications, and had been subject to a high level of responsibility.

The Baku Administrative Court upheld most of his claim, increasing his pension to around 7,500 manat. His request for additional financial assistance equal to 10% of his pension was rejected.

This is not the first such case. Other retired judges have filed similar claims, including Azad Majidov, Anvar Seyidov, Ulvi Mayilov and others. The courts have upheld all of the claims filed.

These cases clearly demonstrate how the special social protection mechanism provided for judges under Azerbaijani law is applied in practice.

Judges’ pension provisions

Under Article 109 of the Law “On Courts and Judges,” judges’ pensions are calculated according to special rules and depend on their length of service as a judge.

For those who have served as a judge for at least five years, the pension may be set at 45% of their average salary.

For between 5 and 10 years of service, an additional 2% is added to the 45% for each additional year.

For between 10 and 15 years of service, the pension is set at 55% of the average salary, plus 5% for each additional year, but cannot exceed 80% of the average salary.

Pension calculations also take into account pension capital and other allowances предусмотренные by law.

These higher percentage rates and additional benefits based on length of service provide judges with special pension conditions compared with other groups of the population.

Is it possible to live on a pension?

A judge’s pension of 7,500 manat (around $4,412) is 23 times higher than the minimum pension and 12–13 times higher than the average pension.

For comparison, the official subsistence minimum for a pensioner, regardless of profession, is 245 manat (around $145).

The average pension is significantly higher than this threshold. Nevertheless, it can be difficult for a single pensioner to maintain a stable standard of living solely on an average pension. Older people often need additional sources of income, such as employment, family support or targeted social assistance.

According to official statistics, as of April 1, 2026, more than 105,000 old-age pension recipients were still working.

But state officials, prosecutors and judges are provided with a fundamentally different level of social protection. Many people in Azerbaijan view this approach as a “double standard” enshrined in law. And when it comes to lawsuits filed by judges seeking higher pensions, public discussions often include comments along the lines of: “Apparently, even that wasn’t enough for the judges.”

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Heavy rain floods streets, basements and metro stations in Tbilisi – video
World.content:
Heavy rain in Tbilisi

Following heavy rainfall overnight on 14 August, the Georgian capital was once again flooded. Tbilisi City Hall issued a statement on the situation, saying the intense rainfall had “caused certain problems”.

According to the city authorities, central districts were the worst affected. Private homes and basements were flooded, while a retaining wall at one residential property collapsed. Streets across the city and areas around several metro stations were also inundated.

Throughout the night, residents posted videos from different parts of the capital showing flooded streets and squares. Residents of one street in the city centre also blocked the road, calling for help in dealing with the damage.

Videos published by city residents:

“The heavy rainfall in the capital caused problems in all ten districts. Gravel and stones were washed onto roads. Our staff are carrying out clean-up work around the clock. The rain was particularly heavy in the Vake, Mtatsminda and Krtsanisi districts.

“More than 500 personnel and 30 pieces of equipment have been mobilised across all affected areas and are involved in the clean-up operation. The work will continue until all the problems have been fully resolved,” said Giorgi Papava, head of Tbilisi’s main municipal services operator, Tbilservice Group.

World.title: More than 32,000 applications for Armenian citizenship in a year: who is applying and why
World.content:
Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

“There has been a sharp increase in the number of applications for Armenian citizenship. In 2025, the number exceeded 32,000, a historic high for the entire history of the Republic of Armenia,” said Armen Kazaryan, acting deputy interior minister.

According to him, the number of citizenship applications exceeded 20,000 in each of the previous two years, compared with 7,000-8,000 in earlier years.

Kazaryan believes the main goal of applicants is to obtain a document that allows them to travel:

“We have seen certain developments, in particular the outbreak of hostilities in Ukraine and restrictions on travel for Russian citizens. After that, we saw an increase in applications for Armenian citizenship. By the way, most Russian citizens applying for Armenian citizenship are ethnic Armenians.”

He rejected claims that obtaining Armenian citizenship is a complicated process:

“The requirements for ethnic Armenians are ‘zero’. People may face administrative difficulties. For example, some may lack the necessary documents proving their ethnicity, or their records may contain errors. In such cases, we need to compare the information with other records and verify it. Essentially, Armenia imposes no requirements on ethnic Armenians.”

Kazaryan himself considers the lack of requirements for ethnic Armenians problematic. In his view, this devalues the institution of citizenship itself.

“We will soon present a draft of the relevant legislative amendments addressing these issues,” he said, without specifying what changes the amendments would introduce.

Border crossings: more people entered than left

Nelli Davtyan, acting head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, also spoke to journalists. She recalled that last year Armenia recorded a “significant positive figure” in the difference between the number of citizens entering and leaving the country. The figure stood at 8,660.

In the first half of this year, the difference between entries and exits stood at 1,347.

“There were 871,409 entries and 870,062 exits. If we compare this with figures for the first half of previous years, last year’s figure was -20,065, while in 2024 it was -22,893,” Davtyan noted.

She stressed that the figure usually rises in the second half of the year. This happens because seasonal migrant workers return home after leaving the country for temporary work. They usually leave in early spring and return in autumn. Davtyan therefore described a positive figure already in the first half of the year as “exceptional”.

More than 6,000 people granted temporary residence permits

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia had transformed from a country that “sends” migrants abroad into a country that receives migrants. “The second major trend is the growing interest in Armenia among foreign nationals,” he noted.

Nelli Davtyan said the Migration and Citizenship Service had received 9,534 applications for one-year temporary residence permits: “Of these, 6,059 were approved. Compared with previous years, the number of applications has almost tripled. The proportion of approved applications has also nearly tripled.”

According to Davtyan, the number of applications for three-year residence permits has also increased, although more modestly: “In previous years, the figure stood at 1,500-1,700, while in the first half of this year it had already reached 2,085.”

Armenia implementing 53 EU recommendations on visa liberalisation

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia was actively cooperating with the European Union on visa liberalisation. He recalled that Armenia received its first report on the implementation of the action plan in May 2026. The report gave a fairly positive assessment of the steps taken by the Armenian government.

“The EU presented us with 53 recommendations. To complete our work, we divided them into specific actions. We broke down the recommendations so that we could clearly identify the steps we need to take to implement them,” Kazaryan explained.

Based on the 53 recommendations, an Armenian working group drew up a list of 117 actions. More than half of them have already been completed.

The recommendations form part of the first stage of the visa liberalisation action plan. This stage covers legislation and policy development only. The authorities expect to assess how effectively Armenia has implemented the first stage by early 2027 or during the first half of the year. If the results prove positive, work on the second stage will begin.

World.title: Myth Detector: 230 fake social media accounts created to create illusion of support for Georgian PM’s statements
World.content:
Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

1On 2 August, marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 August War, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze held a briefing. He focused in particular on what he described as the spread of “Russophobia” in Georgia and the role of the so-called “deep state” in this process.

After the briefing, pro-government messages began circulating widely on social media. Various media outlets also published visual materials promoting these messages.

According to a study by Myth Detector, 230 fake accounts took part in the campaign. The organisation analysed likes on social media posts, as well as the photos and activity of the profiles that shared them. It identified signs of coordinated and suspicious behaviour that, according to the study, aimed to increase support for specific government narratives.

The study also says the profiles were designed to appear as if they belonged to different socio-demographic groups. Some accounts used photographs depicting idyllic family life to make themselves appear more trustworthy.

Profile photos were generated using artificial intelligence (AI)

According to Hive Moderation, a tool for detecting AI-generated images, there was more than a 90% probability that all 230 profile photos had been generated using AI. In some cases, the probability reached 100%. A visual inspection also identified features typical of AI-generated images, including unnatural shapes of hands and fingers, as well as certain distortions.

The photos repeat the same settings and compositions

Some accounts use identical or very similar photos, including the same images with minor changes. The visual design of different accounts also repeats similar photography styles and details. These include photos with a consistent aesthetic, featuring Tbilisi in the background, a glass of wine or a cup of coffee, a hand touching the head, or similar compositional choices. The accounts also use images showing people having fun, relaxing or taking part in sports to create an impression of authenticity. In some cases, different accounts use the same first and last names.

An illusion of broad support is created through artificially diverse social and demographic profiles

The campaign creates the impression that it brings together people of different ages, appearances and interests. The profiles include young and older people, supporters of conservative and alternative views, as well as religious people, family-oriented users, sports enthusiasts and people who enjoy outdoor activities.

AI-generated accounts use real workplaces and educational institutions to make their profiles appear more credible

Most profiles list places of education and employment, including the Tbilisi Transport Company, various Georgian insurance companies, commercial banks, microfinance organisations, government agencies and municipal services.

Different accounts show identical behaviour

Most profiles list a date between 20 and 24 July 2026 as the date they began living in Georgian cities, although some accounts appear to have been created earlier.

Profile activity focuses on the same messages

The activity of the suspicious accounts, particularly their likes, is concentrated on posts featuring conspiracy claims by the ruling party’s chairman about the “party of global war”, the “deep state’s plan” and the “opening of a second front”. They also engage with the narrative about “Russophobia”, suggesting an artificial increase in the level of support.

Fake accounts created to support Georgia’s prime minister

World.title: Russia no longer attracts Armenian migrant workers as they look for new opportunities in Europe
World.content:
Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

The geography of labour migration from Armenia is changing. Russia, which until recently remained the main destination, has become less attractive. The main reasons are Russia’s economic downturn, driven by the war in Ukraine, and the depreciation of the rouble.

Many migrants are now returning from Russia to Armenia. Some are trying to find work in their home villages or in the capital, while others are looking for new opportunities, particularly in Europe. The direction of labour migration is changing, with European countries becoming increasingly popular.

Work visa for Poland

After two years working at a meat-processing plant in Poland, 40-year-old Serob (name changed) returned to Armenia for a month. He came to prepare all the necessary documents and take his wife and children with him to Warsaw.

“I received a three-year residence permit and the right to work. Living away from my family is difficult. I decided that we should be together. I should also say that Poland has become one of the first steps towards the European labour market for many people. Many of my friends work in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands and other countries on legal work visas. I was also offered a job in the Netherlands, but I decided to stay in Poland,” he says.

Serob is a butcher. He was also in demand in Armenia. However, he says his salary there was not enough to support his family:

“I had friends who worked as butchers in Europe. They told me that the profession was in demand there and well paid. Gradually, I started thinking: why not try going to Europe and working there? I also had a lot of debts and loans. I went to Poland on a work visa. The process moved slowly. The Polish embassy invited me for an interview a year after I submitted my application.”

A recruitment agency then sent his details to a meat-processing company. Representatives of the company interviewed Serob online. During the video call, he demonstrated his professional skills to the employer, including how he deboned meat.

“The employer liked my work and sent me a contract and the necessary documents. The embassy then approved my work visa. At first, I lived in a house in Poland with people of different nationalities. They all worked for the same company and lived in separate rooms. Later, when my financial situation improved, I moved into a separate flat with a friend from Armenia. I sent most of my earnings to my family to help resolve our financial problems. I did not work in a shop or at a market. I worked at a specialised meat-processing plant with refrigerated storage facilities. It is physically demanding work,” the butcher says.

He notes a shortage of butchers in the European labour market, which creates demand for migrants with the necessary skills. Meat-processing plants employ workers from Ukraine, Argentina, Azerbaijan and Armenia.

“Many Armenians are now going to European countries for work. And not only to meat-processing plants. When I flew to Poland, I met some women who worked as pastry chefs on the plane. They were also travelling to Poland under legal employment contracts. Many Armenians also work in shops. These are people who speak foreign languages. In any case, I am happy. I will return to work in a month, this time with my family,” Serob says.

Working at a German medical clinic with an Armenian degree

Doctors, teachers and highly skilled professionals in various fields are also in demand on the European labour market. Dentist Edgar Mirzoyan has been living and working in Germany for nine months.

Edgar Mirzoyan

“One day, my nurse told me that her friend worked in Germany and that they might need a dentist. I simply gave her my contact details and forgot about it. Some time later, they contacted me. At the same time, I started learning German. The whole process took two years: learning the language, preparing documents and taking exams. Finally, I moved to Germany. By the way, getting my Armenian degree recognised in Germany seemed more realistic and achievable than in other European countries,” Edgar says.

At the same time, the 30-year-old dentist studied not only the professional requirements but also the overall situation in the country, including its economy, level of safety and even happiness index.

“Geography also influenced my final decision. It was important for me to stay connected to Armenia. You can get from Germany to Armenia in just a few hours. In this sense, Europe was a much more convenient destination for me than, for example, Canada. Before moving to Germany, I had a completely different idea of what it would be like. Of course, everyone’s experience is different. Some doctors who arrived at the same time as me had a much harder journey. A lot depends on which city you move to, who your employer is and who you interact with. Everyone has their own experience,” he says.

Edgar started working two days after arriving in Germany. Some time later, his wife also joined him.

“Before moving to Germany, I registered in advance to take a language exam. They tested my knowledge of medical German. I passed the exam successfully. After that, I received a temporary licence valid for two years. I can work during this period, but I must work under the supervision of an experienced doctor.

However, the process of having my degree fully recognised is still under way. The authorities compare my entire university curriculum, the number of hours I completed and the subjects I studied with the German curriculum. I applied for this process while I was still in Armenia. They only started reviewing my documents after two years of waiting. If they find differences between the curricula, I will have to make up the gaps. It is not yet clear how significant those differences will be,” the doctor says.

According to Edgar, working in Germany has its own particularities. Berlin is a multicultural city, and his patients include not only Germans. About 30 per cent are Armenians and Yazidis, while another 30 per cent are Russians and Ukrainians.

Edgar continues to practise in Armenia as well:

“I can take leave twice a year. I come to Armenia, mainly perform implant procedures and surgeries, and then return to Germany. I have many patients who wait for me to come back. They book appointments in advance, I come and perform the surgery, and the next stage of treatment takes place three to six months later, when I can return again.”

When labour migration is a family choice

For many people who move to Europe, leaving is a decision about their family’s future, improving their living conditions and trying to build a new life in a different environment.

Vergine (name changed) chose this path. She has lived in the Czech Republic with her husband for seven years and now has two children.

“First, my husband moved to Prague on a work visa. He started working in the security department of a shopping centre. Two years later, I joined him. We made the decision consciously, after carefully considering everything. We wanted to settle down and continue our lives in a European country. In this sense, the Czech Republic seemed like a suitable option, and we are very happy with our choice,” Vergine says.

Before moving to the Czech Republic, the couple worked at Zvartnots Airport.

“At first, I worked at a language centre as an English teacher. Then my second child was born here. Of course, there were many difficulties. We lived in a foreign country without support from relatives and with a small child, but we managed. I now work as an English teacher at a school,” she says.

The young family does not plan to return to Armenia for now, but they regularly visit their relatives.

“We have the right to live and work here, but I am sure that one day we will definitely return,” Vergine says.

Changing migration patterns

According to Tatevik Bezhanian, an expert with the migration programme of the charitable organisation Armenian Caritas, Armenia currently has no statistics showing how many people leave for European countries to work.

One reason is that Armenia has no intergovernmental labour migration agreements with EU countries. Bulgaria is the only exception. In addition, most people who leave for Europe find jobs through private recruitment agencies, and the state does not register this process.

“You will not find this data in official statistics. On the other hand, we also do not have a migration card system under which people have to state when entering or leaving the country that they are going abroad to work. They may not indicate the purpose of their departure at all,” Bezhanian says.

She says this problem is not unique to Armenia. Internationally, governments mainly register migrant workers arriving in their countries because they can manage these migration flows. Countries that pursue targeted labour migration policies, sign bilateral agreements and organise the recruitment of their citizens abroad usually have comprehensive data on those who leave. The Philippines and Uzbekistan are among them, for example.

Tatevik Bezhanian notes that even when Armenian authorities want information about labour migrants leaving for Russia, they have to rely on official Russian statistics:

“If the geography of labour migration expands, we will have to approach the relevant authorities in countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. We will need to obtain data and determine how many Armenian citizens work there.”

Armenian workers turn to Europe instead of Russia

World.title: Opinion on Georgian petrol in Abkhazia: ‘If needed, it’s possible’
World.content:
The indirect consequence of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries has been a fuel crisis in Abkhazia, which in recent years has been buying petrol from Russia.

After struggling with shortages for two weeks, Abkhazia decided to buy petrol from Georgia. Given the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, this was a rather “unorthodox” move, but at the same time the only viable way out of the situation.

In a blog post, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz outlet Chegemskaya Pravda, discusses whether Abkhazia can trade with Georgia.

Inal Khashig: “Abkhazia has been grappling with a petrol shortage for the past two weeks. There is virtually no fuel left in the country. Government assurances that the situation is under control and that a new shipment of petrol is about to arrive have done little to reassure people — if anything, they have only deepened the pessimism. Queues at petrol stations stretch as far as the eye can see.

And then petrol arrived from an unexpected source — Georgia.

Tbilisi says the government has nothing to do with it and that it is entirely a private business matter. Sukhumi, for its part, says that when the country is facing a fuel shortage, it will not prevent petrol tankers from entering from Georgia. After all, there is precedent for this kind of economic contact: during the difficult 1990s, we supplied Georgians with relatively cheap fuel.

This particular fuel crisis has once again brought an enduring Abkhaz question to the fore: should we trade with an enemy state or not?”

To me, it is quite straightforward: if this kind of cooperation is vital for the country as a whole, its economy and the well-being of its people, then it is justified. Sukhumi has, after all, cooperated with Tbilisi in the energy sector throughout the post-war years, and no one objects because there is no alternative. This cooperation is vital to both Abkhazia and Georgia.

And now, when the whole of Abkhazia — and with it the country’s economy — has ground to a halt because of the lack of petrol, refusing to buy fuel from the Georgians looks like outright posturing.

Incidentally, I think the government’s argument that Abkhazia actively sold petrol to Georgia in the 1990s is a very good one. At the time, war-ravaged Abkhazia was under a severe blockade: Russia under Boris Yeltsin had effectively sealed us off on all sides. Nothing could be brought in or taken out. About the only thing permitted was taking mandarins across the border in handcarts, with Abkhaz women effectively serving as beasts of burden.

Abkhazia’s tiny budget was funded by selling timber and scrap metal to Turkey, as well as by smuggling fuel into Georgia.

The latter involved considerable risk and loss of life, as fuel tankers had to travel towards the Georgian border through the Gali district, which was unstable at the time. But there was effectively no other way of bringing even a little money into the state coffers. Whatever anyone may say, those modest revenues helped Abkhazia survive at the time.

And yes, we traded with Georgia then because we had to.

And we need to do so now to protect the country from a fuel crisis.

And in future, we need to take similarly responsible steps, even if they run counter to established dogmas. Rigid dogma is not the best guide to action in crises like the one we are facing now.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Analysts say Ukraine is preparing a large-scale offensive
World.content:
Ukraine Launches Large-Scale Offensive

Based on reporting by Novosti Donbassa

Ukrainian defense forces have liberated 19 settlements across several sectors of the front, according to DeepState, a Ukrainian battlefield monitoring project, which reported the advances after updating its combat map.

According to the analysts, Ukrainian forces have regained control of Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Hrushevske, Tolstoi, Zirka, Yalta, Piddubne, Myrne, Voskresenka, Sichneve, Vorone, Ternove, Berezove, Stepne, Kalynovske, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Rybne and Krasnohorske.

In addition, Ukrainian troops pushed Russian forces back in six other settlements: Novopavlivka, Novoheorhiivka, Novomykolaivka, Novohryhorivka, Zaporizke and Pryvilne.

The Ukrainian military also released video footage from settlements it said had been liberated in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.

World.title: Death in Tasmanian prison after reports man 'unresponsive' in cell
World.content:
A 23-year-old man has died while being held in custody at the Hobart Reception Centre, Tasmania Police said.

Police said prison staff alerted them to the man's death after they found him unresponsive in his cell just before 11am on Sunday.

Tasmania Police Assistant Commissioner Doug Oosterloo said the deceased man was from New Norfolk, north of Hobart.

He had been arrested on Saturday in relation to a wounding incident in Claremont the day before, and was transferred to the Hobart Reception Centre around 5:30pm, police said.

The New Norfolk man had been in custody for one night before being found unresponsive. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"Ambulance Tasmania crews were called, Hobart uniform police attended and Hobart reception prison staff all attempted to revive the man," Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said.

" But tragically those attempts were unsuccessful. "

Assistant Commissioner Oosterloo said forensic specialists, detectives from Tasmania Police's professional standards' unit and the coroner had attended the scene.

"The professional standards investigation includes examining CCTV footage at Hobart Reception, records and interviewing all witnesses, and that is information that will come out in the investigation," he said.

Acting Director of Prisons Tristan Bell said the Tasmania Prison Service would not comment further, with the matter being referred to the coroner.

"On behalf ot the Tasmania Prison Service, I extend my sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased man at this difficult time," Mr Bell said.

Claremont incident 'targeted', police say

On Friday around 5am, police responded to reports of an assault at a home on Curlew Parade, Claremont — which they believe to be a targeted incident.

Police said they were told two people had entered the residence and assaulted two occupants.

A man his 20s was shot in the hip and is now in hospital in a serious condition.

The other occupant, a woman in her 20s, was reportedly struck multiple times with the side of an axe.

She received medical treatment but was not hospitalised, police said.

Police did not confirm what role the deceased man was alleged to have played — if any — in the incident.

World.title: Shock defeat to Bangladesh reveals bigger picture hiding in plain sight
World.content:
You could pick a handful of moments during the first Test at Marrara Oval in Darwin where it was clear not everything was as it seemed on surface level.

On day two, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted off with his usual exuberance from the infield to chase down a shot that trickled towards the boundary.

The immaculately manicured outfield, offering a playing surface that was nigh on pristine, had already been praised for its lawn-like quality.

Mark Waugh on Fox Sports noted you could probably play bowls or tennis on it.

Yet as soon as Labuschagne slid for the ball, the ugly truth was revealed, as a huge clump of turf was ripped up in a heaped mass of mud and grass and injury potential.

This was a pattern repeated throughout the match: The outfield's undoubted beauty was only surface deep.

Australia's standing at the top of the Test match rankings may only be surface deep, as deep fissures have been revealed in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

An analogy to what transpired over the next four days, as the number nine-ranked Test team that were missing two of their best bowlers, thumped the world number one side at full strength on their own turf, could not have been clearer.

Bangladesh's stunning victory in Darwin has delivered Australian cricket the shock that it undoubtedly needed.

A team that arrived without fanfare or pedigree has slapped down the world's number one Test playing nation by playing simple, sensible Test cricket.

The bowling was slow but accurate. The batting, unspectacular but patient and disciplined.

The Tigers' attitude was exceptional.

As the growth of the big three has accelerated inequalities between the haves and have-nots of Test cricket, Bangladesh are one of those teams that have been left firmly on the outer, yet proved in Darwin that the paucity of opportunities that have come their way has in no way blunted their potency or hunger for success within the format.

They were here to play Test cricket and play it well.

Najmul Hossain Shanto led his team with skill and composure throughout. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Given it had been 23 years since they last played a Test on Australian soil, their commitment to playing such an impressive style against a country that has snubbed them for so long was more than admirable.

Credit for that has to go to coach Phil Simmons and unflappable skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto.

Shanto made correct decision after correct decision on the pitch, Bangladesh never succumbing to the pressure or enormity of what was transpiring around them right up until Mominul Haque crushed Beau Webster through the covers to seal victory, a simple hug between the two not out batters sufficing as the bench finally exploded in joy on the boundary.

Bangladesh's historic win deserves all the praise that will undoubtedly be heaped upon it, the context of which will forever be extraordinary.

Bangladesh held their nerve throughout a tense contest. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Legendary English cricket writer Neville Cardus once wrote that to properly consider Test cricket, you need to see the big picture.

"I wish to present the Test matches in their setting," he wrote in the introduction to his book chronicling the 1936/37 Ashes series.

"To me cricket must be put against a background."

So what is the background here for Australia?

Australia is about to embark on as busy a Test match year as they have ever had, playing as many as 20 Tests in the next 12 months.

From the Top End, the men's Test team will head to South Africa, play New Zealand and England at home, then face overseas tours to India and England for the Ashes in 2027.

It is a demanding schedule both as physically gruelling and mentally taxing as they come.

Steve Smith and Australia have a lot of thinking to do ahead of the next Test. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Starting off with a two-Test series against Bangladesh, a country Australia has only deigned to host once before for a Test series and only played against in red ball cricket six times in total before this week was considered by most to be a friendly warm up, a competitive practice during a winter sojourn in the Top End sun.

It is, of course, incredibly admirable Cricket Australia is taking Test matches to regions that cannot ever hope to host an Ashes contest.

For financial reasons as much as from a societal responsibility, playing these sorts of Tests in this continent's more remote, northern reaches is undoubtedly the right thing to do.

But maybe there is a sense that this is considered a form of benevolence to the lesser-populated areas of the nation.

Perhaps, for some, even playing Bangladesh is a form of charity to a nation that simply does not have the financial pull of the major nations, little more than an obligation to the World Test Championship.

Maybe, despite protestations to the contrary, that attitude sneaks into the minds of the players, so subliminally that they themselves do not even notice it.

Pat Cummins defended the team's preparation, but perhaps they didn't even realise they were underdone. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

For how can playing in front of about 5,000 spectators in a venue where only half the oval is bordered by a grandstand compare with the cathedral-like cavernous majesty of the MCG, or the lack of pressure contrast with the parochial furnace of a packed Gabba?

Marrara Oval offers neither the stately splendour of the Adelaide Oval or SCG, nor the admittedly under-populated grandiosity of the new Perth Stadium.

Darwin is definitively off-Broadway.

And although Australia's defeat didn't seem to be for lack of effort, the application and necessary quality was lacking throughout the match.

Horror drops from Steve Smith and Nathan Lyon were surely aberrations, but the lazy stroke play and jittery, muddled thinking of the batters was very not.

Steve Smith was not his usual best in the field. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

This shock to a team that has been creaking under the weight of their own success for a number of years now is one that has probably arrived eight months too late.

It was due last summer against England before those Bazballers tripped up over their own hubris.

A papering of the cracks was the result of that emphatic 4-1 Ashes victory, the foundations of sand upon which the top order was built were never tested, the supposedly seismic impact of a fired up England bowling attack never coming to bare, self-sabotaging itself amidst a storm of recriminations in the boozy sand of Noosa.

So on we continued. Australia's brittle batters went off to earn their coin in meaningly limited overs matches and failed to address the issues that have plagued them in red ball cricket, perhaps even accentuating the problems by promoting angled bats and rash shots.

Now the show moves to Mackay and presents Australia with an ever-bigger list of questions and problems to face.

Jake Weatherald's status as opener has to be looked at. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia were rusty and not up to speed in Darwin.

Even if Mackay's Harrup Park, the newest venue to host a men's Test in Australia, provides a suitably refreshed outlook and attitude from Australia next Saturday, will victory there do anything else other than to plaster even more paper over gaps that are swiftly turning into chasms?

It's been eight years since a rambunctious tour almost boiled over, a sorry spectacle that was quickly overshadowed by a sandpaper-scraping that was barely as coarse as the friction generated by two teams flirting on the edge of respectability throughout.

Any weakness in Australia's psyche will be ripe for exploitation in southern Africa, and the venom is unlikely to be as hidden as it was in the far north of Australia.

World.title: 'Eleventh hour' expert submission delays former Sydney nurses' trial
World.content:
The criminal trial of two former Sydney nurses accused of making menacing comments towards Israeli patients is expected to be delayed until next year, after a dispute over expert testimony on the Israel-Palestine conflict.

Bankstown Hospital nurses Sarah Abu Lebdeh and Ahmad Rashad Nadir were due to stand trial on August 31, but the date will now likely be pushed back after an "eleventh hour" submission of expert evidence.

A report from Dr Rodger Shanahan has been submitted at the last minute. (ABC News)

Mr Nadir's lawyer, Zemarai Khatiz, said the trial was vacated on Thursday after the Crown served an expert report compiled by Middle East analyst Dr Rodger Shanahan at the last minute.

"The additional brief material was dated May 31 and provided to us on August 5," Mr Khatiz said.

He said the defence had not had enough time to properly assess the report before it would be used as evidence and would need time to secure its own expert.

"We have to obtain our expert in order to address the matters in the report," he said.

" It will probably take between two and three months for us to obtain our own expert. "

Dr Shanahan is also expected to be called as a witness at the trial.

Mr Khatiz (right) says they received the additional material on August 5. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

New trial date to be set

Ms Abu Lebdeh and Mr Nadir were charged after Israeli content creator Max Ilinsky, who goes by Max Veifer online, filmed the pair allegedly making threats against Israeli patients at Bankstown Hospital.

The footage was filmed on the cam-chat app Chatroulette, and drew international attention when it emerged in February 2025.

Both nurses have pleaded not guilty and were sacked following the incident.

The video was ruled admissible last month after previously being excluded on the grounds it was improperly obtained and breached privacy laws.

The matter will next be heard in Parramatta District Court on August 21, when a new trial date is expected to be set.

"It is anticipated that new trial will take place sometime in 2027," Mr Khatiz said.

World.title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
World.content:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.

1. Das's day four redemption

Das made amends after missing a chance early on day four. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.

So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.

It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.

Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.

But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.

This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.

It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.

Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.

2. Webster falls to a beauty

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.

On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.

Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.

Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.

Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.

With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.

A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.

3. Starc's desperate review

Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.

So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.

There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.

Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.

He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.

There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.

4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down

Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.

But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.

Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.

But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.

Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.

It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.

5. Green's drought-breaking ton

Cameron Green scored his first Test century since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.

A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.

But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.

There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.

But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.

It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.

World.title: She designed jumpers worn by Princess Diana and Olivia Newton-John, then lost everything
World.content:
Eighties knitwear designer Liz Newman walks into a gallery space hung with the quirky, colourful jumpers made from patterns she created decades ago.

She thought these designs were lost forever.

"I'm absolutely amazed, a bit overwhelmed, and just awe-struck," Ms Newman said, looking around at dozens of newly knitted jumpers sporting the Australiana themes she developed in her early 20s, and some well-kept originals.

Liz Newman at her surprise Knitwear: Back to the Future exhibition at the 2026 South Australian Living Artists Festival. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

At just 20, Liz Newman started a knitwear label that became globally renowned.

She said it really took off in the mid-80s when Hey Hey It's Saturday star Jacki MacDonald started wearing her jumpers.

"Every time Jacki wore one of the designs on Hey Hey, the Channel Nine switchboard would jam with people wanting to know where they could get the knitwear," Ms Newman said.

Liz Newman was a national and global success. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

From a boutique in Twin Street in the Adelaide CBD, she was selling jumpers to stars like ice-skating duo Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean, Olivia Newton-John, and even Princess Diana.

Stars align in the US

She ventured into the US at the time the Australian international hit Crocodile Dundee arrived in cinemas, with designs like "Australian pizza with the lot", a jumper covered with Aussie tourism icons.

"Australiana was very, very popular and Americans couldn't seem to get enough of anything Aussie," Ms Newman said.

"All the stars seemed to align, and it just took off."

Liz Newman's exhibition is being held in the Adelaide Hills until the end of August. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

At the height of her success, she was supplying 150 stores in the US, two Liz Newman boutiques in Sydney, one in Melbourne, another in Surfers Paradise and the original Adelaide store.

She was employing more than 500 hand knitters, many based in country locations around Australia, to make the jumpers using intarsia, a style of knitting complex patterns using multiple colours.

"It was a huge part of my life and an amazing time of my life, and then it all ended very quickly," Ms Newman said.

Hard times ahead

A culmination of unfortunate events, including the collapse of the SA Bank, led to the label's demise in the mid-1990s.

"The state bank was going under, and they took me with them," Ms Newman said.

Jayne Torvill, Christopher Dean, Olivia Newton-John, and Princess Diana are some celebrities who have worn Liz Newman's designs. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

"It was probably one of the worst periods of my life because I had worked so hard."

But there were more hard times to come.

In 2011 she was diagnosed with a brain tumour that she said was the size of an orange by the time it was eventually identified in an MRI scan.

She said the doctors likened it to dismantling a time bomb.

"They said, 'Liz you don't have that much time, there's been so much wear and tear on it, that it's likely to burst'.

"If I'd continued, I'd have three months left to live."

Rock bottom

After she recovered from the operation, she had to spend 14 months in brain injury rehab, learning how to do everything again.

"Even making a cup of coffee was a challenge," she said.

"I knew you needed a kettle, I knew you needed coffee and sugar and milk, but I couldn't remember what to do first."

Ms Newman said confronting her mortality led her to make some big life decisions.

"I made a promise to myself that I'd make big changes and leave a very unhappy relationship," she said.

It was not an easy journey.

At rock bottom, she was living in housing trust accommodation and surviving on the disability pension.

"It's been really hard. I don't have any superannuation, I don't have anything to fall back on, and surviving on a pension is really hard," she said.

Meanwhile, her now vintage jumpers were selling for huge sums of money, but Ms Newman had kept only six of them, and lamented the loss of the patterns, which had been sold off with the business while she was unwell.

"My cousin rang me, he works in South Korea, and he said there was a shop with one of my jumpers in the window and it was $1,000," she said.

Another turn of fate

A social media post and a chance encounter with vintage clothing collector and media personality Amanda Blair led to another turn of fate in Ms Newman’s life journey.

Ms Blair, an avid collector of 80s jumpers, had recently gifted a mohair Liz Newman featuring bears doing Aerobics Oz Style to friend and popular podcaster Monique Bowley, who posted it to Instagram.

Amanda Blair at the Liz Newman Knitwear: Back to the Future exhibition.

When Ms Newman introduced herself as the designer of the jumper, the story of the missing patterns intrigued Ms Blair, who already had a sizeable Liz Newman collection.

"I used to get on eBay and search for ugly Australian jumpers," Ms Blair said.

"That's not to say that Liz Newman jumpers are ugly, but I wanted to preserve some South Australian fashion history.

"I think I've watched CSI far too many times, and watched too many crime shows, and I'm like, 'I am going to find those patterns for her'.

"And I did. I found the patterns."

Amanda Blair gifted a Liz Newman jumper featuring bears doing aerobics to popular podcaster Monique Bowley, who posted it to Instagram. (Supplied: Instagram)

Facebook Marketplace led Ms Blair to a seller, who was helping an elderly couple who had bought the Liz Newman business after the state bank fiasco.

It turned out they still had the 300 patterns stored in the cellar of their home in Birdsville in the northern Adelaide Hills.

"Liz was huge nationally, and internationally, from Twin Street in Adelaide," Ms Blair said.

"These jumpers were worn in New York; they were worn on the catwalks of Paris.

"She really spearheaded the whole kind of fashion movement of Australiana jumpers.

" To be able to preserve that, and then say to this woman, 'Hey, guess what, I found your patterns, and they're coming back to you', it's just awesome. "

Twelve years after promising Ms Newman she would find her patterns, Amanda Blair not only returned the treasure trove of designs, but with the help of volunteers from the Hand Knitters Guild of South Australia, recreated 34 of her designs for a surprise exhibition.

Liz Newman's designs have been spotted in international vintage stores, still selling for large amounts of money. (Supplied: Tricia Watkinson)

Ms Newman only learned about the project two months ago.

She says she didn't dream it would be so big.

"To meet Amanda and for all this to happen, and for her to know that she had found the patterns, and that secretly she was organising this incredible surprise, the amount of work that she did was just amazing.

"This has given me something to look forward to, the possibility of doing something else.

"I think the jumpers were fun, and now I'm starting to get that sense of fun back in my life."

World.title: 'Staggering' increase in number of lockdown incidents at WA schools
World.content:
Violent threats have triggered more than 1,100 lockdowns at public schools in Western Australia last year, education department figures show, with the the numbers of students forced to shelter in their classrooms more than doubling since 2017.

The figures were tabled in Parliament this week and show that out of the 1,327 lock down incidents reported at schools, the majority were due to threats including including physical assault, intimidating behaviour and verbal, written or cyber threats.

A lockdown can apply to the whole school, a block or a classroom.

State opposition spokesperson for education Liam Staltari said the increase was "staggering".

The government must put an end to school violence, opposition education spokesperson Liam Staltari said. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Students and teachers deserve to be safe in school and parents should have every confidence that's going to be the case and the buck stops with our government when it comes to that safety in public schools," Mr Staltari said.

" Simply brushing this away is not going to cut it with parents or teachers or students. "

During the emergency, classroom doors and windows are locked, blinds are pulled down and students ordered to keep a low profile until the "all clear" is given, which can mean hiding under their desks.

Whole school evacuations were not included in the report tabled in Parliament this week.

School lockdowns have soared in Western Australia since 2017, according to education department figures. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

School violence 'unacceptable'

Education Minister Sabine Winton acknowledged there had been an increase in schools reporting lockdowns since the government introduced an Incident Management Manual in 2020 to safeguard schools.

She also said the government empowered school principals to automatically suspend, or move to exclude, students who instigate violence.

Education Minister Sabine Winton said the government takes a strong stand against school violence (ABC News: Kenith Png)

"Threats of violence at school, or anywhere in the community, are unacceptable," Ms Winton told the ABC in a statement.

"The Department of Education's Incident Support Unit has strengthened face-to-face training to help schools identify when a lockdown is required and ensure staff are equipped to respond appropriately."

Last year, a teenage boy was taken to hospital after being stabbed in the arm in a "targeted" knife attack that put Ellenbrook Secondary School in Perth into lockdown.

At least 10 teenagers have been charged over the assault, in which knives and an axe were used.

World.title: Pallister makes history by beating Ledecky as Short breaks Hackett’s 1500m record
World.content:
Breaking SportSwimmingSwimming Pallister makes history by beating Ledecky as Short breaks Hackett’s 1500m record Tom Decent Updated August 16, 2026 — 6:20pm ,first published 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irvine: Death, taxes and US great Katie Ledecky winning 800-metre freestyle finals on the international stage. Australia’s Lani Pallister showed on an extraordinary Saturday evening in Irvine, California, that only two of life’s three perceived certainties remain. Loading On one of Australian cricket’s worst days, swimming enjoyed one of its finest nights on the final evening of the Pan Pacific Championships 12,500 kilometres away from the carnage inflicted by Bangladesh in Darwin. Pallister’s 800m freestyle win for the ages handed Ledecky, a four-time Olympic champion in the event, her first defeat over the distance in international competition. She has been near impossible to beat and this undoubtedly was one of Australian swimming’s most magnificent feats.



Since she was a 13-year-old in 2010, Ledecky did not lose a 800m freestyle final in more than 13 years. That was until Summer McIntosh knocked her off in a domestic meet in the USA, but doing so on the international stage is a more impressive feat. Lani Pallister celebrates her 800m freestyle win over Katie Ledecky. Getty Images This was simply dessert for a dominant Dolphins team after Sam Short’s victory in the men’s 1500m freestyle in a time of 14 minutes, 33.97 seconds, which lowered Grant Hackett’s 25-year-old Australian record. From Boy Charlton’s world record in 1924, through the eras of John Konrads, Murray Rose and Kieren Perkins, to Hackett’s then-world record at the 2001 world championships in Fukuoka, Short wrote his name into Australian swimming folklore in an event that holds a special place in the nation’s sporting history. “This is the best moment,” said an ecstatic Short. “I will remember this for the rest of my life.”



It came after golden entrées from Jamie Jack in the 50m freestyle – one-upping sister Shayna by snaring an individual Pan Pacs gold medal – and stalwart Zac Stubblety-Cook snatching victory from the jaws of defeat in the 200m breaststroke with a last-gasp win that shocked even him. “That’s the best I could ask for,” Jack said of his personal best of 21.35 seconds. Loading Australia fell four gold medals shy of the USA’s tally of 19, but there was a palpable sense in Irvine that this Dolphins team will be a formidable force at the LA Olympics in two years when stars Cam McEvoy, Mollie O’Callaghan, Kaylee McKeown, Kyle Chalmers and Flynn Southam return. If all were in Irvine, Australia would have beaten the USA on the medal tally. The magnitude of Pallister and Short’s victories cannot be overstated. Both will leave California with three individual gold medals and considerably enhanced reputations.



This was the most nervous Pallister had been in her entire life. In the stands were Australian swimming royalty Ian Thorpe, swanning about the VIP section, her Olympian mother Janelle Elford, former coach Michael Bohl, and rock star and former training partner Cody Simpson, who had driven down from LA. And, of course, there was her coach, Dean Boxall, initially hiding at the back of the stand, barely able to watch as his prodigy tried to down not only the greatest female swimmer of all time in an event she has become synonymous with, but the athlete Pallister grew up idolising. View post on X Armed with supreme confidence from her 200m and 400m freestyle victories, Pallister attacked the race with an audacity and fearlessness that cannot be taught. Under world record pace at the 550-metre mark, Pallister began to tire but drew on countless hours of training to summon enough energy to hold on for a 1.16 second victory. “I was so locked in,” Pallister said. “I saw her coming on the last 50 and thought, ‘holy shit’.”



Pallister’s time of 8:06.10 was a Pan Pacs record, but outside Ledecky’s world record of 8:04.12. That mattered little. This was a line-in-the-sand moment, proof that on July 30, 2028, in front of 38,000 spectators at SoFi Stadium, Pallister could silence the home crowd. Pallister raced out of the water towards an elated Boxall, who rushed down from the stands and cradled her head in a warm embrace. Lani Pallister is hugged by her coach Dean Boxall after brilliant 800m freestyle victory at Pan Pacs. Getty Images Ledecky looked back at the pool, perhaps processing a feeling almost completely foreign to her after an 800m freestyle race: defeat. “It’s the race I care about most,” Pallister said.



It was quite the day for international swimming. American Kate Douglass lowered Gretchen Walsh’s women’s 50m freestyle world record from 23.55s to 23.49s in the heats, before slicing a whopping three-tenths of a second off it again in the evening to win gold, with Australia’s Meg Harris clocking a personal best of 23.89s to settle for bronze. “Hopefully one day I’ll be able to put something incredible up there, too,” Harris said. Meanwhile, in Paris, German teenager Johannes Liebmann shaved almost four seconds off Bobby Finke’s 1500m freestyle world record to clock 14:26.79. “It was the best swim I’ve ever seen,” Short said after he and Pallister pored over Liebmann’s live splits in the hotel lift together. Before the Pan Pacs, Short said he wanted to “smash those yanks” and “destroy them”. Brimming with confidence and an unquenchable thirst for dominance, Short took an early lead and blitzed the field, winning by 8.63 seconds and snaring one of his hero’s Australian records.



A big thumbs up from coach Damien Jones was a subtle acknowledgment of the magnitude of the swim, as Thorpe applauded a few metres away. “I talked the talk and, hopefully, I walked the walk,” Short said. “That then was straight guts. I’m proud of that. Sam Short is overjoyed after winning the men’s 1500m freestyle at Pan Pacs. Getty Images “I was glad I got to perform with one of my childhood heroes in the stands. Hopefully I impressed him. I heard 14:33 and was like, ‘holy moley’.” It has been more than two decades since Thorpe graced a media mixed zone, but he was coaxed downstairs to join Short and reflect on the performance of a swimmer who now owns the Australian records in the 800m and 1500m freestyle.



Short, however, is still 0.44 seconds shy of Thorpe’s Australian 400m freestyle record. Related Article Swimming Ledecky told a 14-year-old Lani Pallister to ‘dream big’. She just beat her for the first time “It’s been a great meet for Sam,” Thorpe said. “His consistency has been impressive. He broke my Pan Pac record, which I didn’t know I had any more.” Short laughed, adding: “He couldn’t drive when he set that record.” The 1998 world championships were a pivotal meet for Thorpe on the road to Sydney 2000. Two years out from the LA Olympics, Australia now has two genuine superstars making similar statements. There is work to do, but Thorpe’s words carry weight when he surveys what he says is a golden generation Australian swimming.



“It’s exciting. We have a team that is producing the best result we’ve ever seen in the pool,” Thorpe said. “It was also amazing for Lani. She’s had a great meet. She is making her own mark. “But I know what Katie Ledecky is like. She has a four-year plan. She will be wanting to be the first person to win five golds in a row [in the same event]. It’s a great result for now but a great motivator ahead of LA.”

World.title: Dragons down Tigers in battle of cellar dwellers; Knights keep top four dream alive
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Dragons down Tigers in battle of cellar dwellers; Knights keep top four dream alive Dan Walsh Updated August 16, 2026 — 6:14pm ,first published 4:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

St George Illawarra have held out a fast-finishing Wests Tigers – just – in the battle of the joint-venture rebuilds, securing a nail-biting 24-22 victory at Commbank Stadium. A sparse Sunday afternoon crowd of just 9773 said plenty as to the stakes in this 17th v 14th affair. Loading So too did the Dragons’ two-point triumph though, securing their first back-to-back wins since August last year and consigning the Tigers to an eighth-straight loss. The Tigers ran last in this two-horse race for all-but the final 10 minutes, but threatened one hell of a jailbreak when rookie centre Solomone Saukuru bagged two tries and put a grandstand finish in play.



With just two wins from their past 15 games, the Tigers have slid from second on the ladder to the bottom four, reinforcing their cellar-dwelling status with seemingly never-ending drama around Jarome Luai, Adam Doueihi, professional standards and players vaping along the way. St George Illawarra’s late-season revival, meanwhile, continues to impress. It may yet eventually shove them up the ladder too. The Dragons celebrate a Hamish Stewart try against the Tigers. Getty Images With three games remaining, they are now only two wins adrift of Brisbane as the premiers endure one of the most stunning post-premiership slides in rugby league history. Stranger things have happened in this game than the Dragons dodging the wooden spoon. They’re certainly playing well beyond that dishonour. Daniel Atkinson’s move to fullback to cover for injured captain Clint Gutherson showed promise – especially welcome promise at that, given his struggles in the halves as a marquee recruit.



A bench utility role, or perhaps a start at centre, looms for Atkinson given Scott Drinkwater, Luke Metcalf and Kodi Nikorima all arrive next season. Related Article NRL 2026 Brisbane’s title defence is the worst in 118 years. Things just got even worse It was Atkinson who threw the last pass for Tyrell Sloan to score the Dragons’ first of the afternoon after an early Valentine Holmes HIA played into the Tigers opening the scoring. Sunia Turuva had his first try since April when Hamish Stewart was caught defending at centre in St George Illawarra’s hasty backline reshuffle. But when first Doueihi and then Luai were exposed with lackadaisical defensive efforts, the Tigers were in all sorts and trailing 18-6 at half-time.



Doueihi would be disappointed with his jumper-grabbing effort on his tryline as Stewart roared past him in the 31st minute. Luai was just as culpable a few minutes before the break when Moses Suli broke through and ran 45 metres to score. Suli, who is contracted for 2027 but has also been told he is free to find a new club, doubled down with a fine defensive effort to start the second half when he chopped down a tryline-bound Jahream Bula. Loading Doueihi kept the Tigers in the game by setting up Samuela Fainu’s try, while Holmes did the same as his last pass for Sloan floated forward to deny what should have been a simple four-pointer. It mattered little though when the Super League-bound flyer broke into the backfield and put Lyhkan King-Togia’s try on a platter with a wonderful chip kick.



The Tigers did eventually find their voice and some attacking flair, finished off twice by Saukuru, but ultimately, deservedly, fell short. So it goes when you’re at the wrong end of the ladder and rebuilding. Though right now, in the short-term at least, the two joint-ventures are travelling in opposite directions. Knights keep top-four hopes alive with win over Titans Jack Brady Dane Gagai, Greg Marzhew and Fletcher Sharpe all scored try doubles as Newcastle kept their slim hopes of a top-four finish alive with a 36-26 home win over the Gold Coast.



With a final-round bye in hand and fifth-placed Cronulla staring down consecutive losses, the Knights sit just two competition points adrift of the fourth-placed Dolphins. Loading An unlikely top-four berth would complete a remarkable 12-month turnaround for the Knights following their 2025 wooden spoon finish. Sunday’s 10-point win wasn’t without its issues for Newcastle with Dane Gagai failing to return after half-time with a reported hamstring injury. The absence of the veteran centre led to an unexpected first grade debut for Toby Winter, who three months ago was playing in the SG Ball under-19s grand final.



A crucial try-saving tackle by the 19-year-old on back-rower Beau Fermor proved the highlight of his maiden game. The Knights celebrate a try on Sunday. Getty Images Gagai’s double and winger Marzhew’s first try all came within 18 minutes, and held Newcastle in good stead at 16-0. But the Titans overcame a hefty penalty deficit to keep in touch with the Knights through tries for Fermor and Jayden Campbell. A critical intervention from the bunker minutes into the second half prevented the Titans from hitting the lead, when it ruled that centre Jojo Fifita’s elbow had hit the ball in the lead-up to him scoring.



Ill-discipline was the story of the day for the Titans and soon led to Newcastle centre Fletcher Hunt, who had been denied by the bunker twice in the game, capping off a long-range effort to extend his side’s lead. Kurtis Morrin’s try in the 57th minute was countered by the Knights within four minutes through a darting 55-metre dummy-half try-scoring run from five-eighth Sharpe. Further tries to Marzhew and Sharpe rounded out the win for the Knights, despite the best efforts of Fermor and halfback Lachlan Ilias at the death. AAP
