World.title: Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalResolve Political Monitor Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches James Massola August 16, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Voters have condemned the Albanese government’s handling of immigration policy, with 54 per cent agreeing the government is running the portfolio in an “unplanned and unmanaged way” even as Labor prepares to unveil tougher rules on visa overstayers and dodgy asylum claims. But the government will be buoyed by 60 per cent of voters supporting lower house prices, while nearly twice as many people back Labor’s changes to the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing as oppose them, according to the latest Resolve Political Monitor. The majority of Australians think Labor’s management of immigration isn’t carefully planned. Aresna Villanueva Concern about the cost of living has fallen significantly, by 9 points to 36 per cent, the lowest level since February 2023, though the issue still remains voters’ No.1 concern by a considerable margin. But after a week in which the prime minister was subjected to heavy criticism for seemingly joking about the Japanese prime minister’s personal appearance, there was little change to the major parties’ or leaders’ standing.



Core support for Labor, the Coalition and One Nation remained unchanged over the last month, with the government recording a primary vote of 28 per cent, the opposition steady on 23 per cent and Pauline Hanson’s party on 26 per cent. The findings are contained in the Resolve Political Monitor conducted for this masthead from August 9 to 15. More than 2200 voters were surveyed, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.1 per cent. While 54 per cent of people marked Labor down for its handling of immigration, 26 per cent said the government was handling Australia’s immigration program in a carefully planned and managed way. Twenty per cent were undecided. Strong majorities of Coalition, One Nation and even Greens voters marked down Labor’s performance in the portfolio. At the same time, 35 per cent of voters said Hanson’s party was best placed to manage immigration and refugees, while 23 per cent backed Labor and just 17 per cent backed the Coalition.



The findings come after Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke delayed an appearance at the National Press Club in which he was expected to unveil an immigration crackdown, amid concerns from cabinet colleagues that his proposal needed more work and had unanswered questions about costs. Asked on Sunday when he would outline changes to immigration policy following the delay to his speech, Burke said “we’re talking about a cabinet process” and declined to comment further. The speech and policy shift are expected in the next fortnight. The most recent May budget forecast suggested net overseas migration would fall to 225,000 by 2027-28, while Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg suggested a future Coalition government would cut the figure to 180,000 – a suggestion that led to his being counselled by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. One Nation wants to cut the rate to 130,000 a year. The findings also underscore Australians’ broader discomfort with immigration, with 57 per cent of voters saying immigration was too high, 28 per cent saying it was about right and just 4 per cent saying current rates are too low. That is a rise of 8 per cent in people saying immigration is too high since September 2025.



On the government’s changes to the tax system, which constitute a broken promise from Albanese, 35 per cent backed Labor’s policy of stopping the current 50 per cent discount on capital gains tax payable when investments are sold, while 21 per cent of people opposed it and 44 per cent said they were undecided or neutral. It was a similar story on restricting negative gearing to new properties only, with 35 per cent backing the move, 20 per cent opposing it and 45 per cent undecided. Sixty per cent of voters said they supported lower house prices, 10 per cent opposed lower prices and almost a third were undecided or neutral. Resolve pollster Jim Reed said Labor “simply aren’t getting credit for falling home values because they’ve refused to own that outcome, and drops in bowser prices are seen as at the whim of international events. “It seems strange that the government would not take a bow for taking some of the investor heat out of the housing market, and only take the pain of the broken promise, but who knows where this goes.”



The decision to end the halved fuel excise discount does not appear to have damaged the government electorally, with petrol prices remaining below the peaks reached earlier this year and a number of cost-of-living relief measures starting on July 1. When asked about their No.1 policy priority, 36 per cent nominated the cost of living, down from 45 per cent last month. While it is too early to say if voters’ diminishing concern about the cost of living is a trend, the big movement down in concern over one month – well outside the margin of error – will be welcomed by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his government. The findings come after a warning from ANZ economists that house prices could fall by 15 per cent over this year and next, and after RBA governor Michele Bullock warned last week that the bank was willing to keep raising interest rates to curb inflation.



In the preferred prime minister ratings, Albanese leads with 32 per cent of the vote, down 1 point on last month, while Hanson moved up 1 point and remains in second place on 26 per cent. Twenty-three per cent of voters said they were undecided, while Taylor was down 2 points and languishing on just 19 per cent. Related Article Updated

Property prices Rate rises still on table: Bullock says even 20% house price slump wouldn’t spark crisis But Taylor outperformed Albanese when voters were asked to rate his performance, with a net score of plus 8 percentage points. In contrast, Albanese’s ratings suggest the prime minister has become an increasingly polarising, love-or-hate figure. Just 37 per cent of voters said the prime minister was doing a good or very good job, 53 per cent said his performance was poor or very poor – for a net score of minus 16 percentage points – with 10 per cent of people undecided.



Hanson’s ratings were similarly polarising. A solid 46 per cent of those surveyed said the One Nation leader was doing a good or very good job, 41 per cent said she was doing a poor or very poor job – a net score of plus 5 percentage points – while just 14 per cent were undecided. Reed said people either loved or hated Albanese and Hanson, but for very different reasons. “Taylor remains less of a known quantity. He’s not hated by any means, but many voters are yet to make up their minds. Hanson is being rewarded for raising issues in plain terms, but whether you agree with her take on those issues is another thing,” he said. “The biggest problem for the prime minister is now a trust deficit, rather than inaction. It may be naive, but we still expect our leaders to stick to their word come what may.” On the likeability ratings, Albanese’s remains solidly in negative territory – where it has been since January 2026 – on minus 14 per cent, a 1 point improvement on last month. Taylor’s rating is plus 7 per cent, down 1 point on last month but still the highest score of any politician, while Hanson’s is plus 4 per cent, having fallen 10 percentage points since June.



Taylor is comfortably ahead as preferred Liberal leader, with 30 per cent of voters nominating him, 10 per cent choosing leadership aspirant Andrew Hastie and 5 per cent choosing shadow treasurer Tim Wilson. A whopping 56 per cent of people were undecided. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh Daniel Brettig Updated August 16, 2026 — 5:56pm ,first published 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Pat Cummins conceded Australia’s malfunctioning batting order may need to be overturned after the Test team’s bubble was comprehensively burst by Bangladesh in the tourists’ first-ever red ball victory on these shores. Having presaged this game with innings defeats by Zimbabwe and then a modest Cricket Australia XI, the tourists turned Darwin into Tiger land by thoroughly outplaying Australia in every session, for a result that will force urgent conversations about the makeup of an ageing team. Cameron Green is bowled by Hasan Mahmud on day 4 at Marrara Stadium in Darwin. Getty Cameron Green (104) was the lone source of substantial resistance for the Australians, who briefly glimpsed the possibility of an innings defeat before they were bowled out for 284. Bangladesh lost the sole wicket of first innings century-maker Tanzid Hasan before skating home. Cummins did not deny his side had played poorly in a game they had been widely expected to dominate, and his comments about the trends in the batting lineup will leave the likes of Jake Weatherald and Marnus Labuschagne wondering about their places.



Former opener Matt Renshaw trained with the Test squad in Brisbane and is available to come in, as are Campbell Kellaway and Sam Konstas, who played in the CA XI. Josh Inglis is the spare batter in the current 13-man squad. “I think it’s a balance of it’s one Test, but it’s also a bit of a trend as well, so trying to work out do you need to intervene now, or let it play out, and you think it’s the way forward,” Cummins said. “That’s the question over the next couple of days, we’ll sit down and have a think, selectors will have a think, is there something there that’s going to take us forward, or is it starting to become a trend that we think needs to be changed. “It’s pretty clear it’s not quite functioning as well as we’d like as a group, so I’m sure the batters will get together and talk. Review some footage, review methods, their approaches to how they were this week. If we need to make some changes to our style, we’ve got a week or so and we better do it pretty quickly.” Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto hailed his side’s best victory in any format in their history, and also stated he would have bowled first on a fresh pitch had he won the toss. Cummins said he would make the same decision again, a posture that places more pressure on the batters who failed to get through the first morning.



“It’s not the desired result by any means, and I think the standard we hold is a bit higher than what we played this week,” Cummins said. “I thought our preparation was really excellent. “It just felt like we didn’t get off to a great start and once you’re behind on a pretty good wicket against a pretty good side, it’s hard to wrestle momentum back. Hard to put your finger on one thing but it felt like we were a bit off the pace. “I’d probably do the same thing, you get through that first hour, even the seam numbers weren’t very high after that first hour, so you’d hope as a team we could bat longer than the overs we batted for the Test.” All-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz (5-66) bowled magnificently for Bangladesh, getting some deliveries to turn sharply out of the footmarks and others to skid through straight. With the benefit of scoreboard pressure, he comfortably out-bowled Nathan Lyon. Loading



First innings hero Hasan Mahmud (3-56) was also a vital contributor, finishing the match with nine wickets, including the final hammer blow to remove Green. Former skipper Ricky Ponting has already called for significant change to the Test side. “I’m the last one to want to make change,” Ponting said on Seven when the match was in its death throes. “As a captain or as a player, I wanted to keep a group together, so it has to get to a bad point before I start saying you’ve got to leave somebody out. View post on X “But there’s been enough evidence for me coming here to suggest they weren’t going to lose anything, or much at all, by starting that regeneration, bringing in another opener, bringing in someone at three ... I think that has to happen.” Alex Carey never looked to be in command, and twice edged Mahmud through the slips before Mehidy dismissed him with a classical off-break that took an edge behind.



Green was more solid, and played one nicely down the ground to raise his first Test match 50 since the tour of the West Indies over a year ago. Beau Webster was then befuddled by another beauty from Mehidy, a slightly quicker off-break that drifted then skidded through to beat the outside edge and flick the off stump. Green unfurled a superb pull shot for six to move into the 90s. A pair of twos, the second of them tight, then took Green to his first Test hundred in Australia, an excellent innings that showcased why he is the future of the batting line-up. Mehidy Hasan Miraz celebrates the wicket of Beau Webster. Getty Images He marked the moment with a clenched fist before acknowledging a strong ovation from the Darwin faithful, who totalled 18,352 spectators over four days.



Green alluded to criticism of his recent lack of runs when interviewed by Adam Gilchrist after his century, and also indicated he had returned to his former batting methods after struggling lately to balance the competing demands of three formats. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Smith and lesson: Batters in the gun as Australia face horror loss to Bangladesh “I feel like there’s always wolves when you play Test cricket,” Green said on Fox Cricket. “Especially when you play for Australia, you’ve always had to perform, so yeah it’s nice to get a performance. “I think I just went back to what I used to do back in the day. I think I’ve just been chopping and changing a little bit recently, so yeah it’s nice just to go back to what worked.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Five arrests over threats to Scots College accused
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWPolice Five arrests over threats to Scots College accused Nigel Gladstone and Christopher Harris Updated August 16, 2026 — 5:10pm ,first published 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW Police have arrested five boys for allegedly throwing eggs at the home of a Scots College student accused of sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl in Bondi last month. Police were called to Dover Heights on Saturday after reports of a group of boys throwing eggs at a home and arrested five boys aged between 13 and 17 nearby. Four of the boys were later released without charge. A 17-year-old boy was charged with breach of bail and custody of a knife in a public place and will appear before a children’s court on Monday. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert emailed parents on Sunday saying police had made arrests and warning other students against making online threats.



Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert has written to parents about the alleged assault. None of the people charged were students or employees at the college. “Police have advised that a number of young people – none of them Scots students – have been arrested in relation to recent activity directed towards those involved in the matter currently under investigation,” Dr Lambert said in a newsletter to parents. “Police are also aware of concerning online commentary within the wider community and have asked that young people do not post threats, organise action or otherwise involve themselves.” Police said further action will be taken if the behaviour continues, the email said.



An email to parents about the police action and warning to others about threats. Scots College A member of the Scots community, not authorised to speak publicly, said staff had been emailed over the weekend and advised by the school they will be required to speak to students about the alleged incident. Scots staff told the Herald they were emailed over the weekend to be prepared to speak to students about the alleged incident and “raise a discussion”, to determine if any of the boys have been emotionally affected by it. “If they have, they will be invited to have a one-on-one discussion with their tutor to talk more about it,” the person said. A 13-year-old and a 14-year-old were charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others, and two counts of aggravated sexual touching of another person. Another 14-year-old was charged with a single count each of the same offences.



Pressed on Thursday afternoon about the allegations, the school refused to answer questions about the students’ enrolment status, or when it became aware of the alleged incident, citing the ongoing criminal investigation. The school confirmed the alleged attack occurred outside school hours. The boys, who cannot legally be identified, were granted conditional police bail on Thursday and will appear in a children’s court on August 25. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Pallister makes history by beating Ledecky as Short breaks Hackett’s 1500m record
World.content:
Breaking SportSwimmingSwimming Pallister makes history by beating Ledecky as Short breaks Hackett’s 1500m record Tom Decent Updated August 16, 2026 — 6:20pm ,first published 2:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irvine: Death, taxes and US great Katie Ledecky winning 800-metre freestyle finals on the international stage. Australia’s Lani Pallister showed on an extraordinary Saturday evening in Irvine, California, that only two of life’s three perceived certainties remain. Loading On one of Australian cricket’s worst days, swimming enjoyed one of its finest nights on the final evening of the Pan Pacific Championships 12,500 kilometres away from the carnage inflicted by Bangladesh in Darwin. Pallister’s 800m freestyle win for the ages handed Ledecky, a four-time Olympic champion in the event, her first defeat over the distance in international competition. She has been near impossible to beat and this undoubtedly was one of Australian swimming’s most magnificent feats.



Since she was a 13-year-old in 2010, Ledecky did not lose a 800m freestyle final in more than 13 years. That was until Summer McIntosh knocked her off in a domestic meet in the USA, but doing so on the international stage is a more impressive feat. Lani Pallister celebrates her 800m freestyle win over Katie Ledecky. Getty Images This was simply dessert for a dominant Dolphins team after Sam Short’s victory in the men’s 1500m freestyle in a time of 14 minutes, 33.97 seconds, which lowered Grant Hackett’s 25-year-old Australian record. From Boy Charlton’s world record in 1924, through the eras of John Konrads, Murray Rose and Kieren Perkins, to Hackett’s then-world record at the 2001 world championships in Fukuoka, Short wrote his name into Australian swimming folklore in an event that holds a special place in the nation’s sporting history. “This is the best moment,” said an ecstatic Short. “I will remember this for the rest of my life.”



It came after golden entrées from Jamie Jack in the 50m freestyle – one-upping sister Shayna by snaring an individual Pan Pacs gold medal – and stalwart Zac Stubblety-Cook snatching victory from the jaws of defeat in the 200m breaststroke with a last-gasp win that shocked even him. “That’s the best I could ask for,” Jack said of his personal best of 21.35 seconds. Loading Australia fell four gold medals shy of the USA’s tally of 19, but there was a palpable sense in Irvine that this Dolphins team will be a formidable force at the LA Olympics in two years when stars Cam McEvoy, Mollie O’Callaghan, Kaylee McKeown, Kyle Chalmers and Flynn Southam return. If all were in Irvine, Australia would have beaten the USA on the medal tally. The magnitude of Pallister and Short’s victories cannot be overstated. Both will leave California with three individual gold medals and considerably enhanced reputations.



This was the most nervous Pallister had been in her entire life. In the stands were Australian swimming royalty Ian Thorpe, swanning about the VIP section, her Olympian mother Janelle Elford, former coach Michael Bohl, and rock star and former training partner Cody Simpson, who had driven down from LA. And, of course, there was her coach, Dean Boxall, initially hiding at the back of the stand, barely able to watch as his prodigy tried to down not only the greatest female swimmer of all time in an event she has become synonymous with, but the athlete Pallister grew up idolising. View post on X Armed with supreme confidence from her 200m and 400m freestyle victories, Pallister attacked the race with an audacity and fearlessness that cannot be taught. Under world record pace at the 550-metre mark, Pallister began to tire but drew on countless hours of training to summon enough energy to hold on for a 1.16 second victory. “I was so locked in,” Pallister said. “I saw her coming on the last 50 and thought, ‘holy shit’.”



Pallister’s time of 8:06.10 was a Pan Pacs record, but outside Ledecky’s world record of 8:04.12. That mattered little. This was a line-in-the-sand moment, proof that on July 30, 2028, in front of 38,000 spectators at SoFi Stadium, Pallister could silence the home crowd. Pallister raced out of the water towards an elated Boxall, who rushed down from the stands and cradled her head in a warm embrace. Lani Pallister is hugged by her coach Dean Boxall after brilliant 800m freestyle victory at Pan Pacs. Getty Images Ledecky looked back at the pool, perhaps processing a feeling almost completely foreign to her after an 800m freestyle race: defeat. “It’s the race I care about most,” Pallister said.



It was quite the day for international swimming. American Kate Douglass lowered Gretchen Walsh’s women’s 50m freestyle world record from 23.55s to 23.49s in the heats, before slicing a whopping three-tenths of a second off it again in the evening to win gold, with Australia’s Meg Harris clocking a personal best of 23.89s to settle for bronze. “Hopefully one day I’ll be able to put something incredible up there, too,” Harris said. Meanwhile, in Paris, German teenager Johannes Liebmann shaved almost four seconds off Bobby Finke’s 1500m freestyle world record to clock 14:26.79. “It was the best swim I’ve ever seen,” Short said after he and Pallister pored over Liebmann’s live splits in the hotel lift together. Before the Pan Pacs, Short said he wanted to “smash those yanks” and “destroy them”. Brimming with confidence and an unquenchable thirst for dominance, Short took an early lead and blitzed the field, winning by 8.63 seconds and snaring one of his hero’s Australian records.



A big thumbs up from coach Damien Jones was a subtle acknowledgment of the magnitude of the swim, as Thorpe applauded a few metres away. “I talked the talk and, hopefully, I walked the walk,” Short said. “That then was straight guts. I’m proud of that. Sam Short is overjoyed after winning the men’s 1500m freestyle at Pan Pacs. Getty Images “I was glad I got to perform with one of my childhood heroes in the stands. Hopefully I impressed him. I heard 14:33 and was like, ‘holy moley’.” It has been more than two decades since Thorpe graced a media mixed zone, but he was coaxed downstairs to join Short and reflect on the performance of a swimmer who now owns the Australian records in the 800m and 1500m freestyle.



Short, however, is still 0.44 seconds shy of Thorpe’s Australian 400m freestyle record. Related Article Swimming Ledecky told a 14-year-old Lani Pallister to ‘dream big’. She just beat her for the first time “It’s been a great meet for Sam,” Thorpe said. “His consistency has been impressive. He broke my Pan Pac record, which I didn’t know I had any more.” Short laughed, adding: “He couldn’t drive when he set that record.” The 1998 world championships were a pivotal meet for Thorpe on the road to Sydney 2000. Two years out from the LA Olympics, Australia now has two genuine superstars making similar statements. There is work to do, but Thorpe’s words carry weight when he surveys what he says is a golden generation Australian swimming.



“It’s exciting. We have a team that is producing the best result we’ve ever seen in the pool,” Thorpe said. “It was also amazing for Lani. She’s had a great meet. She is making her own mark. “But I know what Katie Ledecky is like. She has a four-year plan. She will be wanting to be the first person to win five golds in a row [in the same event]. It’s a great result for now but a great motivator ahead of LA.”

World.title: Dragons down Tigers in battle of cellar dwellers; Knights keep top four dream alive
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Dragons down Tigers in battle of cellar dwellers; Knights keep top four dream alive Dan Walsh Updated August 16, 2026 — 6:14pm ,first published 4:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

St George Illawarra have held out a fast-finishing Wests Tigers – just – in the battle of the joint-venture rebuilds, securing a nail-biting 24-22 victory at Commbank Stadium. A sparse Sunday afternoon crowd of just 9773 said plenty as to the stakes in this 17th v 14th affair. Loading So too did the Dragons’ two-point triumph though, securing their first back-to-back wins since August last year and consigning the Tigers to an eighth-straight loss. The Tigers ran last in this two-horse race for all-but the final 10 minutes, but threatened one hell of a jailbreak when rookie centre Solomone Saukuru bagged two tries and put a grandstand finish in play.



With just two wins from their past 15 games, the Tigers have slid from second on the ladder to the bottom four, reinforcing their cellar-dwelling status with seemingly never-ending drama around Jarome Luai, Adam Doueihi, professional standards and players vaping along the way. St George Illawarra’s late-season revival, meanwhile, continues to impress. It may yet eventually shove them up the ladder too. The Dragons celebrate a Hamish Stewart try against the Tigers. Getty Images With three games remaining, they are now only two wins adrift of Brisbane as the premiers endure one of the most stunning post-premiership slides in rugby league history. Stranger things have happened in this game than the Dragons dodging the wooden spoon. They’re certainly playing well beyond that dishonour. Daniel Atkinson’s move to fullback to cover for injured captain Clint Gutherson showed promise – especially welcome promise at that, given his struggles in the halves as a marquee recruit.



A bench utility role, or perhaps a start at centre, looms for Atkinson given Scott Drinkwater, Luke Metcalf and Kodi Nikorima all arrive next season. Related Article NRL 2026 Brisbane’s title defence is the worst in 118 years. Things just got even worse It was Atkinson who threw the last pass for Tyrell Sloan to score the Dragons’ first of the afternoon after an early Valentine Holmes HIA played into the Tigers opening the scoring. Sunia Turuva had his first try since April when Hamish Stewart was caught defending at centre in St George Illawarra’s hasty backline reshuffle. But when first Doueihi and then Luai were exposed with lackadaisical defensive efforts, the Tigers were in all sorts and trailing 18-6 at half-time.



Doueihi would be disappointed with his jumper-grabbing effort on his tryline as Stewart roared past him in the 31st minute. Luai was just as culpable a few minutes before the break when Moses Suli broke through and ran 45 metres to score. Suli, who is contracted for 2027 but has also been told he is free to find a new club, doubled down with a fine defensive effort to start the second half when he chopped down a tryline-bound Jahream Bula. Loading Doueihi kept the Tigers in the game by setting up Samuela Fainu’s try, while Holmes did the same as his last pass for Sloan floated forward to deny what should have been a simple four-pointer. It mattered little though when the Super League-bound flyer broke into the backfield and put Lyhkan King-Togia’s try on a platter with a wonderful chip kick.



The Tigers did eventually find their voice and some attacking flair, finished off twice by Saukuru, but ultimately, deservedly, fell short. So it goes when you’re at the wrong end of the ladder and rebuilding. Though right now, in the short-term at least, the two joint-ventures are travelling in opposite directions. Knights keep top-four hopes alive with win over Titans Jack Brady Dane Gagai, Greg Marzhew and Fletcher Sharpe all scored try doubles as Newcastle kept their slim hopes of a top-four finish alive with a 36-26 home win over the Gold Coast.



With a final-round bye in hand and fifth-placed Cronulla staring down consecutive losses, the Knights sit just two competition points adrift of the fourth-placed Dolphins. Loading An unlikely top-four berth would complete a remarkable 12-month turnaround for the Knights following their 2025 wooden spoon finish. Sunday’s 10-point win wasn’t without its issues for Newcastle with Dane Gagai failing to return after half-time with a reported hamstring injury. The absence of the veteran centre led to an unexpected first grade debut for Toby Winter, who three months ago was playing in the SG Ball under-19s grand final.



A crucial try-saving tackle by the 19-year-old on back-rower Beau Fermor proved the highlight of his maiden game. The Knights celebrate a try on Sunday. Getty Images Gagai’s double and winger Marzhew’s first try all came within 18 minutes, and held Newcastle in good stead at 16-0. But the Titans overcame a hefty penalty deficit to keep in touch with the Knights through tries for Fermor and Jayden Campbell. A critical intervention from the bunker minutes into the second half prevented the Titans from hitting the lead, when it ruled that centre Jojo Fifita’s elbow had hit the ball in the lead-up to him scoring.



Ill-discipline was the story of the day for the Titans and soon led to Newcastle centre Fletcher Hunt, who had been denied by the bunker twice in the game, capping off a long-range effort to extend his side’s lead. Kurtis Morrin’s try in the 57th minute was countered by the Knights within four minutes through a darting 55-metre dummy-half try-scoring run from five-eighth Sharpe. Further tries to Marzhew and Sharpe rounded out the win for the Knights, despite the best efforts of Fermor and halfback Lachlan Ilias at the death. AAP

World.title: Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalResolve Political Monitor Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches James Massola August 16, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Voters have condemned the Albanese government’s handling of immigration policy, with 54 per cent agreeing the government is running the portfolio in an “unplanned and unmanaged way” even as Labor prepares to unveil tougher rules on visa overstayers and dodgy asylum claims. But the government will be buoyed by 60 per cent of voters supporting lower house prices, while nearly twice as many people back Labor’s changes to the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing as oppose them, according to the latest Resolve Political Monitor. The majority of Australians think Labor’s management of immigration isn’t carefully planned. Aresna Villanueva Concern about the cost of living has fallen significantly, by 9 points to 36 per cent, the lowest level since February 2023, though the issue still remains voters’ No.1 concern by a considerable margin. But after a week in which the prime minister was subjected to heavy criticism for seemingly joking about the Japanese prime minister’s personal appearance, there was little change to the major parties’ or leaders’ standing.



Core support for Labor, the Coalition and One Nation remained unchanged over the last month, with the government recording a primary vote of 28 per cent, the opposition steady on 23 per cent and Pauline Hanson’s party on 26 per cent. The findings are contained in the Resolve Political Monitor conducted for this masthead from August 9 to 15. More than 2200 voters were surveyed, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.1 per cent. While 54 per cent of people marked Labor down for its handling of immigration, 26 per cent said the government was handling Australia’s immigration program in a carefully planned and managed way. Twenty per cent were undecided. Strong majorities of Coalition, One Nation and even Greens voters marked down Labor’s performance in the portfolio. At the same time, 35 per cent of voters said Hanson’s party was best placed to manage immigration and refugees, while 23 per cent backed Labor and just 17 per cent backed the Coalition.



The findings come after Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke delayed an appearance at the National Press Club in which he was expected to unveil an immigration crackdown, amid concerns from cabinet colleagues that his proposal needed more work and had unanswered questions about costs. Asked on Sunday when he would outline changes to immigration policy following the delay to his speech, Burke said “we’re talking about a cabinet process” and declined to comment further. The speech and policy shift are expected in the next fortnight. The most recent May budget forecast suggested net overseas migration would fall to 225,000 by 2027-28, while Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg suggested a future Coalition government would cut the figure to 180,000 – a suggestion that led to his being counselled by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. One Nation wants to cut the rate to 130,000 a year. The findings also underscore Australians’ broader discomfort with immigration, with 57 per cent of voters saying immigration was too high, 28 per cent saying it was about right and just 4 per cent saying current rates are too low. That is a rise of 8 per cent in people saying immigration is too high since September 2025.



On the government’s changes to the tax system, which constitute a broken promise from Albanese, 35 per cent backed Labor’s policy of stopping the current 50 per cent discount on capital gains tax payable when investments are sold, while 21 per cent of people opposed it and 44 per cent said they were undecided or neutral. It was a similar story on restricting negative gearing to new properties only, with 35 per cent backing the move, 20 per cent opposing it and 45 per cent undecided. Sixty per cent of voters said they supported lower house prices, 10 per cent opposed lower prices and almost a third were undecided or neutral. Resolve pollster Jim Reed said Labor “simply aren’t getting credit for falling home values because they’ve refused to own that outcome, and drops in bowser prices are seen as at the whim of international events. “It seems strange that the government would not take a bow for taking some of the investor heat out of the housing market, and only take the pain of the broken promise, but who knows where this goes.”



The decision to end the halved fuel excise discount does not appear to have damaged the government electorally, with petrol prices remaining below the peaks reached earlier this year and a number of cost-of-living relief measures starting on July 1. When asked about their No.1 policy priority, 36 per cent nominated the cost of living, down from 45 per cent last month. While it is too early to say if voters’ diminishing concern about the cost of living is a trend, the big movement down in concern over one month – well outside the margin of error – will be welcomed by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his government. The findings come after a warning from ANZ economists that house prices could fall by 15 per cent over this year and next, and after RBA governor Michele Bullock warned last week that the bank was willing to keep raising interest rates to curb inflation.



In the preferred prime minister ratings, Albanese leads with 32 per cent of the vote, down 1 point on last month, while Hanson moved up 1 point and remains in second place on 26 per cent. Twenty-three per cent of voters said they were undecided, while Taylor was down 2 points and languishing on just 19 per cent. Related Article Updated

Property prices Rate rises still on table: Bullock says even 20% house price slump wouldn’t spark crisis But Taylor outperformed Albanese when voters were asked to rate his performance, with a net score of plus 8 percentage points. In contrast, Albanese’s ratings suggest the prime minister has become an increasingly polarising, love-or-hate figure. Just 37 per cent of voters said the prime minister was doing a good or very good job, 53 per cent said his performance was poor or very poor – for a net score of minus 16 percentage points – with 10 per cent of people undecided.



Hanson’s ratings were similarly polarising. A solid 46 per cent of those surveyed said the One Nation leader was doing a good or very good job, 41 per cent said she was doing a poor or very poor job – a net score of plus 5 percentage points – while just 14 per cent were undecided. Reed said people either loved or hated Albanese and Hanson, but for very different reasons. “Taylor remains less of a known quantity. He’s not hated by any means, but many voters are yet to make up their minds. Hanson is being rewarded for raising issues in plain terms, but whether you agree with her take on those issues is another thing,” he said. “The biggest problem for the prime minister is now a trust deficit, rather than inaction. It may be naive, but we still expect our leaders to stick to their word come what may.” On the likeability ratings, Albanese’s remains solidly in negative territory – where it has been since January 2026 – on minus 14 per cent, a 1 point improvement on last month. Taylor’s rating is plus 7 per cent, down 1 point on last month but still the highest score of any politician, while Hanson’s is plus 4 per cent, having fallen 10 percentage points since June.



Taylor is comfortably ahead as preferred Liberal leader, with 30 per cent of voters nominating him, 10 per cent choosing leadership aspirant Andrew Hastie and 5 per cent choosing shadow treasurer Tim Wilson. A whopping 56 per cent of people were undecided. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket Cummins flags batting changes after Australia’s bubble burst by Bangladesh Daniel Brettig Updated August 16, 2026 — 5:56pm ,first published 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Pat Cummins conceded Australia’s malfunctioning batting order may need to be overturned after the Test team’s bubble was comprehensively burst by Bangladesh in the tourists’ first-ever red ball victory on these shores. Having presaged this game with innings defeats by Zimbabwe and then a modest Cricket Australia XI, the tourists turned Darwin into Tiger land by thoroughly outplaying Australia in every session, for a result that will force urgent conversations about the makeup of an ageing team. Cameron Green is bowled by Hasan Mahmud on day 4 at Marrara Stadium in Darwin. Getty Cameron Green (104) was the lone source of substantial resistance for the Australians, who briefly glimpsed the possibility of an innings defeat before they were bowled out for 284. Bangladesh lost the sole wicket of first innings century-maker Tanzid Hasan before skating home. Cummins did not deny his side had played poorly in a game they had been widely expected to dominate, and his comments about the trends in the batting lineup will leave the likes of Jake Weatherald and Marnus Labuschagne wondering about their places.



Former opener Matt Renshaw trained with the Test squad in Brisbane and is available to come in, as are Campbell Kellaway and Sam Konstas, who played in the CA XI. Josh Inglis is the spare batter in the current 13-man squad. “I think it’s a balance of it’s one Test, but it’s also a bit of a trend as well, so trying to work out do you need to intervene now, or let it play out, and you think it’s the way forward,” Cummins said. “That’s the question over the next couple of days, we’ll sit down and have a think, selectors will have a think, is there something there that’s going to take us forward, or is it starting to become a trend that we think needs to be changed. “It’s pretty clear it’s not quite functioning as well as we’d like as a group, so I’m sure the batters will get together and talk. Review some footage, review methods, their approaches to how they were this week. If we need to make some changes to our style, we’ve got a week or so and we better do it pretty quickly.” Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto hailed his side’s best victory in any format in their history, and also stated he would have bowled first on a fresh pitch had he won the toss. Cummins said he would make the same decision again, a posture that places more pressure on the batters who failed to get through the first morning.



“It’s not the desired result by any means, and I think the standard we hold is a bit higher than what we played this week,” Cummins said. “I thought our preparation was really excellent. “It just felt like we didn’t get off to a great start and once you’re behind on a pretty good wicket against a pretty good side, it’s hard to wrestle momentum back. Hard to put your finger on one thing but it felt like we were a bit off the pace. “I’d probably do the same thing, you get through that first hour, even the seam numbers weren’t very high after that first hour, so you’d hope as a team we could bat longer than the overs we batted for the Test.” All-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz (5-66) bowled magnificently for Bangladesh, getting some deliveries to turn sharply out of the footmarks and others to skid through straight. With the benefit of scoreboard pressure, he comfortably out-bowled Nathan Lyon. Loading



First innings hero Hasan Mahmud (3-56) was also a vital contributor, finishing the match with nine wickets, including the final hammer blow to remove Green. Former skipper Ricky Ponting has already called for significant change to the Test side. “I’m the last one to want to make change,” Ponting said on Seven when the match was in its death throes. “As a captain or as a player, I wanted to keep a group together, so it has to get to a bad point before I start saying you’ve got to leave somebody out. View post on X “But there’s been enough evidence for me coming here to suggest they weren’t going to lose anything, or much at all, by starting that regeneration, bringing in another opener, bringing in someone at three ... I think that has to happen.” Alex Carey never looked to be in command, and twice edged Mahmud through the slips before Mehidy dismissed him with a classical off-break that took an edge behind.



Green was more solid, and played one nicely down the ground to raise his first Test match 50 since the tour of the West Indies over a year ago. Beau Webster was then befuddled by another beauty from Mehidy, a slightly quicker off-break that drifted then skidded through to beat the outside edge and flick the off stump. Green unfurled a superb pull shot for six to move into the 90s. A pair of twos, the second of them tight, then took Green to his first Test hundred in Australia, an excellent innings that showcased why he is the future of the batting line-up. Mehidy Hasan Miraz celebrates the wicket of Beau Webster. Getty Images He marked the moment with a clenched fist before acknowledging a strong ovation from the Darwin faithful, who totalled 18,352 spectators over four days.



Green alluded to criticism of his recent lack of runs when interviewed by Adam Gilchrist after his century, and also indicated he had returned to his former batting methods after struggling lately to balance the competing demands of three formats. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Smith and lesson: Batters in the gun as Australia face horror loss to Bangladesh “I feel like there’s always wolves when you play Test cricket,” Green said on Fox Cricket. “Especially when you play for Australia, you’ve always had to perform, so yeah it’s nice to get a performance. “I think I just went back to what I used to do back in the day. I think I’ve just been chopping and changing a little bit recently, so yeah it’s nice just to go back to what worked.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Five arrests over threats to Scots College accused
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWPolice Five arrests over threats to Scots College accused Nigel Gladstone and Christopher Harris Updated August 16, 2026 — 5:10pm ,first published 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW Police have arrested five boys for allegedly throwing eggs at the home of a Scots College student accused of sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl in Bondi last month. Police were called to Dover Heights on Saturday after reports of a group of boys throwing eggs at a home and arrested five boys aged between 13 and 17 nearby. Four of the boys were later released without charge. A 17-year-old boy was charged with breach of bail and custody of a knife in a public place and will appear before a children’s court on Monday. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert emailed parents on Sunday saying police had made arrests and warning other students against making online threats.



Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert has written to parents about the alleged assault. None of the people charged were students or employees at the college. “Police have advised that a number of young people – none of them Scots students – have been arrested in relation to recent activity directed towards those involved in the matter currently under investigation,” Dr Lambert said in a newsletter to parents. “Police are also aware of concerning online commentary within the wider community and have asked that young people do not post threats, organise action or otherwise involve themselves.” Police said further action will be taken if the behaviour continues, the email said.



An email to parents about the police action and warning to others about threats. Scots College A member of the Scots community, not authorised to speak publicly, said staff had been emailed over the weekend and advised by the school they will be required to speak to students about the alleged incident. Scots staff told the Herald they were emailed over the weekend to be prepared to speak to students about the alleged incident and “raise a discussion”, to determine if any of the boys have been emotionally affected by it. “If they have, they will be invited to have a one-on-one discussion with their tutor to talk more about it,” the person said. A 13-year-old and a 14-year-old were charged with aggravated sexual assault in the company of others, and two counts of aggravated sexual touching of another person. Another 14-year-old was charged with a single count each of the same offences.



Pressed on Thursday afternoon about the allegations, the school refused to answer questions about the students’ enrolment status, or when it became aware of the alleged incident, citing the ongoing criminal investigation. The school confirmed the alleged attack occurred outside school hours. The boys, who cannot legally be identified, were granted conditional police bail on Thursday and will appear in a children’s court on August 25. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Twelve killed and at least 10 injured in Polish bus crash in Hungary
World.content:
A dozen people were killed and at least 10 have been injured injured after a Polish bus overturned at night on a motorway in eastern Hungary, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar says.

The bus ran into a ditch and tipped over early on Sunday near the town of Mezokeresztes in eastern Hungary, police said, adding that the bus was heading towards the city of Nyiregyhaza on the motorway when the accident happened.

State news agency MTI said there were 57 passengers and two drivers on the bus. Pictures from the scene showed a badly damaged red bus lying on one side in a ditch by the motorway with windows smashed and belongings and suitcases scattered around.

"A Polish-registered bus travelling on the M3 motorway towards Nyiregyhaza ... veered off the straight stretch of road into a ditch and overturned. Preliminary information suggests the driver likely fell asleep," police said on their website.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki said on X: "It is with deep sorrow that I received the tragic news of the Polish bus accident in Hungary, in which so many of our compatriots died."

Twelve people lost their lives and several others were injured in the accident, police said, adding that they were taking the bus driver into custody.

The injured have been taken to hospital.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on X that a "tragic accident" involving a bus carrying Polish tourists happened in Hungary.

World.title: Less than a quarter of schools using $34m system for sharing student information
World.content:
Less than a quarter of schools are using a $34-million Education Ministry system for sharing student information.

The ministry said 551 of the 2536 schools in New Zealand were using the cloud-based system called Te Rito, but a further 503 were signed up and waiting to be connected.

The programme began in 2019, but was paused in 2021 because of security weaknesses in the various student management systems (SMS) schools used to record student details.

Roll-out resumed in January 2023 but this year's Budget trimmed $6m from the programme's original $40m budget to spend elsewhere.

The ministry said Te Rito connected with schools' student management systems (SMS) only if they passed Safer Technologies for Schools (ST4S) accreditation, which checked that their security and privacy settings were appropriate.

"Te Rito will only share data with an SMS that has met a minimum-security standard of ST4S," it said.

"We are proactively ensuring new security vulnerabilities are mitigated as an ongoing process that all SMS vendors need to manage."

The ministry's Te Rito website said the four main SMS systems used by schools could connect to Te Rito.

It said the system allowed schools to share learners' records including NCEA achievement, health and language information, and any ministry-funded support for which they might be eligible.

However, the ministry said it would not be used for a new learning support case management system for children with disabilities and extra learning needs.

"Te Rito was not designed as a learning support case management system. Te Rito is a data exchange platform designed to securely move data between schools and from schools to the Ministry and vice versa. It does not have case management functions," it said.

The ministry said it would develop the register itself using technology belonging to Salesforce, a platform the ministry used for functions including emergency management notifications, curriculum support services and school transport assistance.

"The ministry is developing a Learning Support Case Management system using existing Salesforce technology and an in-house project team. While the Ministry may draw on specialist Salesforce technical expertise as needed, Salesforce is not responsible for developing or delivering the system," it said.

The ministry would not say how much it spent on Salesforce licences for schools.

"The spend is commercially sensitive. Because Salesforce is used for a range of Ministry services it wouldn't be accurate to provide a figure for the number of schools covered by these licences," it said.

World.title: Time to rein in power of big tech, Auckland professor says
World.content:
An academic is calling for regulation to rein in the power of big tech corporations, likening them to Frankenstein's monster.

A paper by the University of Auckland's professor Susan Watson, Reining in Big Tech Corporations: Why Platform Governance Requires Structural Regulation, argues companies such as Amazon, Meta and Google no longer competed within markets.

"Today's tech titans represent a new version of this concentration of corporate power, but on digital rather than physical territory," the paper stated.

"Instead, they own essential digital infrastructure, control platforms on which people and businesses depend, and set many of the rules for operating within them.

"Their influence can also extend to governments. They lobby against laws that could restrict their activities and increasingly position governments as customers or partners for their technology."

The Second Gilded Age

Watson's paper was expected to form part of a Cambridge University Press collection edited by Professor Alexandra Andhov, which draws parallels with earlier periods when a few businesses became extraordinarily powerful.

The Auckland professor's paper argues history is repeating itself when it came to powerful global businesses.

Notably, England's East India Company was granted powers normally associated with governments, including the ability to make laws in territories where it held monopoly trading rights and, later, the right to collect taxes in India.

Watson said the Gilded Age of the late 19th century also produced unbridled corporate power that ended with regulation.

"The Rockefellers and the oil barons and railroad barons that controlled much of industry and transport in the US ... the state was forced to regulate," she said.

"And in the case of the railroad companies, they essentially invented competition law to deal with them."

The 1890 Sherman Act was the first US competition law, which saw the breakup of the powerful corporations in control of key infrastructure.

Watson said what the world is experiencing now was little changed from the first period of extreme wealth and inequality.

AI 'far from human'

Watson's paper also discussed AI tools. She said they should be called out for what they are - the assets of a small group of tech titans.

"I think calling it artificial intelligence ... makes it seem human when it's not human. It's far from human."

Watson said understanding how big tech became so powerful began with understanding corporations themselves.

She said corporations were essentially legal entities created and empowered by government.

Is AI contributing to NZ’s high unemployment rate? Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"Capitalism is both one of humanity's greatest inventions, the greatest source of prosperity the world has ever seen, and a menace on the verge of destroying our planet and destabilising society," she said.

"Big Tech corporations are the latest and most potent manifestation."

She said an incorporated business can own property, enter contracts, make its own internal rules and continue to exist even as the people behind it change.

It can also hold onto invested money and use it to generate more wealth over time.

"Corporations have been likened to Frankenstein's monster. They are artificial persons created by man. Just as we make them, we can unmake them, or reform and re-form them in a way that serves us all rather than just the gilded few."

A proposed fix

The paper suggests regulation that would ban surveillance-based business models, limit big tech companies' claims over data, and require major platforms to be licensed, with conditions attached to their continued operation.

Another possibility was giving people affected by these companies a greater say in how they are governed.

Watson points to New Zealand's Whanganui River, which was given legal personhood as part of a system allowing different groups to share responsibility for its governance.

She suggested a similar idea could be applied to major technology platforms, with governance rights given to people affected by them and public regulators and the State providing oversight.

The Whanganui River was given legal personhood to help allow different groups to govern it. Pixabay

Watson said people who interact closely with these companies, particularly their employees and users, could reasonably expect their interests to be considered.

Issues raised by Watson's paper also formed part of the conversation at a recent New Zealand Centre for Leadership and Governance panel discussion about big tech's power.

"The challenge is that mostly regulation is reactive. So something goes wrong, and we regulate to deal with the harm that's already occurred, and that famously happens in securities law," she said.

World.title: Wintry blast to bring snow, frost and rain
World.content:
Temperatures in some areas will get as cold as -9 overnight, says MetService.

The Twizel and Mount Cook area will be almost double digits in the negative.

Showers are expected in the east of the South Island, with snow to 400 metres in the Kaikoura ranges.

The North Island will see widespread showers, and snow to 600 metres.

Waiouru is forecast to be the coldest spot in the North Island, at -2.

Showers are expected to come down hard in Taranaki and Taumarunui in the morning.

The Desert Road also has a snowfall warning in place, along with State Highway Five between Napier and Taupo until 3am Monday morning.

MetService weather warnings on 16 August. MetService/Screenshot

Road snow fall warnings were in place for Napier-Taupo Road (SH5), Desert Road (SH1), Lewis Pass (SH7), Arthur's Pass (SH73) and Porters Pass (SH73) from Sunday morning into the the evening and Monday morning.

All state highways in the South Island are open this morning, despite snow sweeping through overnight.

World.title: Around-the-clock coalition watch over simulated space attack a 'milestone'
World.content:
New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) space operators have helped test how to detect an attack on a commercial satellite in a US military-led exercise.

The US Space Force called Exercise Salitre in Chile last month a "milestone".

Operators from South America, NATO, Korea and New Zealand tracked a simulated attack on a real satellite which maneuvred to get away.

The joined-up "around-the-clock coalition watch" was a first for the Space Force's southern command, its website said.

The watchers passed the "picture" on to each other across three continents as overhead a pretend aggressor spacecraft went after the real satellite.

"This milestone demonstrates that security in the space domain is a team sport," said commander of Space Forces Southern Colonel Brandon Alford.

Air forces were also involved. Their integration with the space side multinationally was "exactly how we prepare for the future of combat", said another officer.

The watching was done by Joint Commercial Operations (JCO) hubs.

New Zealand hosted one of three JCO hubs globally set up and largely funded by the US, that pulled in space-monitoring data from 20 countries with a focus on commercial rather than military activity worldwide. Chile has just joined.

The Space Systems Command, located in Los Angeles Air Force Base, California, oversees the military’s major space procurement programmes. Space Systems Command

The website said the space support ranged from weather reports to providing satellite images of exercise target areas.

The JCOs share a lot of space-watching information with hundreds of civilian organisations and industry in many countries, though lately the Pentagon has been expanding the military side of what they do. The NZDF said last year it was not involved in that expansion.

As the hubs expand geographically not just to Chile but also to Brazil, Argentina and Colombia, the US has been training their space operators on the basics of spacecraft maneuvering, how to intercept satellites and defence measures.

The Pentagon has been on a big and growing push to integrate other countries and commercial space operators into its satellite and other space efforts, some of them centred on missile detection, tracking or targeting.

World.title: 'Super clinics' cut Taranaki wait limes for ear, nose and throat patients
World.content:
A specialist surgeon has been going the extra mile quite literally to help cut wait times for patients in Taranaki.

Ear, nose and throat specialist surgeon Sahr Kortequee has been travelling from Rotorua to New Plymouth to help run "super clinics" at Taranaki Base Hospital.

"One time I came through and the Awakino Gorge had been closed following the significant slip, so I had to take the Forgotten World Highway in the middle of the night," Kortequee said.

"I came through and there had just been a rock fall on that highway too. So I had to get out of the car and push enough rocks to one side so I could get through!"

Kortequee now usually flew from Rotorua via Auckland to ensure he could continue supporting the weekend clinics.

More than 2000 patients waiting for their first specialist assessment have now been seen through a series of weekend super clinics, helping to halve wait times for both Orthopaedic and Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) patients from 18 to nine months.

Since January 2026, clinicians have completed 544 long-waiting ENT first specialist assessments and 1511 orthopaedic assessment, significantly reducing backlogs and improving access to specialist care.

Behind the scenes, the Surgical Booking Administrators team had also played a critical role in making the clinics possible. For last weekend's super outpatient clinics alone, the team made more than 200 patient contacts to schedule 120 appointments.

Planned care manager Dani Cowley said running from 8am to 6pm across Friday, Saturday and Sunday, the clinics were continuing to reduce waiting times for patients.

"At the start of the year there was still an 18-month wait for patients to have a first specialist assessment with an ENT specialist.

"With Lakes ENT specialist Sahr Kortequee travelling down from Rotorua for super clinic weekends this year, we have been able to reduce that wait time to nine months."

World.title: Kiwi Ferns halve masterminds win over Warriors in NRL-W clash
World.content:
The Warriors have come up short in a topsy-turvy NRL-W match against the West Tigers in Sydney on Sunday afternoon.

A try to interchange player Fathye Manera and two goals from impressive Kiwi Ferns halfback Raecene McGregor, inside the last five minutes, sealed the victory for the Tigers 30-22.

The loss sees the Warriors drop to sixth on the ladder with a four-win, three-loss record.

McGregor's game management and goal kicking were a key feature in the game, and it did not take her long to impose herself, as she set up the first try for the Tigers after just 12 minutes, when fullback Caitlin Turnbull gathered a well-measured kick on the last tackle from McGregor, to jump out to a 6-0 lead.

They doubled that lead six minutes later, after winger Lily Rogan finished off a well executed shift to the left edge. The try was also converted by McGregor.

The Tigers continued their early dominance when Rogan went in for a double just a couple of minutes later, after finishing off another sweeping move.

But rather than dropping their heads, despite being down 16-0, the Warriors showed some heart and courage, after winning back-to-back penalties with eight minutes left in the first half.

Winger Tysha Ikenasio dotted down in the corner to get the Warriors on the board, and they followed it up with two more tries inside the final two minutes of the first half.

Centre Stacey Waaka scored the first of them hitting an inside pass from Emma Paki with perfect timing, to surge over to score.

A sensational third try came right on the halftime hooter, when Paki finished off an 80 metre effort, set up by fullback Apii Nicholls and lock Kaiyah Atai.

That saw the Warriors narrow the gap to 16-12 at the break.

But the Tigers hit the reset button nicely during halftime, and began the second half in fine style, with a try to centre Namoe Gesa.

The try was again converted by McGregor, whose goalkicking was now becoming a crucial factor in the scoreline, with three successes from four attempts, while the Warriors' Patricia Maliepo had missed all three of hers.

But just like in the first half, the Warriors fought back.

Down 22-12, they scored back-to-back tries through Ikenasio, who went in her for second, and Atai who powered over.

Maliepo finally found her kicking boots to convert Atai's try, and suddenly the score was 22-22.

World.title: Young adult dies of meningococcal disease in Waikato
World.content:
People are being urged to get vaccinated against meningococcal disease following a death in Waikato.

Meningococcal disease can cause an infection around the brain and blood poisoning.

Health NZ Waikato medical officer of health Dr Kate Meerkerk said it was more common in children, teenagers and young adults.

She confirmed the latest death was a young adult in the region.

"Our thoughts are with the person's whānau and loved ones during this difficult time."

She said the meningococcal B vaccine was free for babies and children under five years old.

It was also free for those between the age of 13 and 25 in their first year of certain close-living situations - such as boarding school hostels, halls of residence, military barracks, youth justice facilities and prisons.

"It is important that people know the symptoms and seek medical attention early if they are concerned," said Dr Meerkerk.

World.title: Dragons give hope to wooden spoon battle after downing Tigers
World.content:
St George Illawarra can dream of avoiding the wooden spoon after several players with uncertain futures stood up to consign Wests Tigers to an eighth straight loss.

After they led by 12 with four minutes to play, the Dragons had to hold on for a nervous final three minutes before claiming a 24-22 victory at Parramatta Stadium on Sunday.

Fresh off their first back-to-back wins this year, the last-placed Dragons now finish the round only four points behind Brisbane and the Gold Coast.

The Tigers could also still be caught while six points ahead, with the Dragons to face Canterbury, Manly and Parramatta to finish their season.

Much has been made of the potential of the Dragons' younger forwards this year, and what is building at St George Illawarra ahead of next year's big-name arrivals.

But this was a Sunday afternoon for those whose futures at the club appear clouded.

Daniel Atkinson proved he can offer utility value for the Dragons next year, after going from first-choice halfback at the start of the year to filling in at fullback.

Playing No.1 for the first time in his NRL career, Atkinson was solid at the back, put on a cut-out ball for a Tyrell Sloan try and had a couple of big kick returns.

It remains unclear what role he will have next year, given Luke Metcalf and Kodi Nikorima are arriving to play in the halves and Scott Drinkwater will be fullback.

The same could be said of Lykhan King-Togia, who on Sunday had one of his best games of the year.

The Dragons five-eighth caught out Adam Doueihi in defence and sent Hamish Stewart over for the Saints' first try.

And he had one of his own in the second half, digging into the line to create space for a Sloan linebreak before backing up to take a kick back inside from his Super League-bound winger.

Moses Suli, who has pledged to fight for his spot after being told by the Dragons he could leave, also had a strong afternoon.

The Tigers came up short despite a big finish. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings )

The 28-year-old burst his way through two defenders to go 50 metres and score once in the first half, before pulling off a try-saver on Jahream Bula in the second.

For the Tigers, a season that started so well can't end soon enough.

They led 6-0 early through Sunia Turuva, and briefly fought back into the game at 18-12 after halftime when Samuela Fainu finished off an Alex Seyfarth break.

The one bright spot was a late double to centre Solomone Saukuru, who reduced the margin to two with three minutes to play.

But the fact just 9773 fans turned up for a Sunday afternoon match against another Sydney team is telling of how badly this season has spiralled.

Earlier, Newcastle captain Kalyn Ponga credited the performance of Fletcher Sharpe for keeping the Knights' NRL top-four hopes alive in their 36-26 home win over the Gold Coast.

With Sunday's game in the balance heading into the final 20 minutes, five-eighth Sharpe took charge with a darting 55-metre dummy-half try-scoring run to extend Newcastle's lead.

Sharpe followed up in the final six minutes with a second try, when he scooped up a wayward Titans ball to race 60 metres downfield to seal victory.

"Sharpie doing what he does today was pretty special. I'm very appreciative of him after that," Ponga said.

"Without him, I don't know if we play the way we did, to be honest. He broke open the game for us in the second half and when he's streaking away it is a nice feeling."

With a final round bye in hand and Cronulla staring down consecutive losses, the Knights sit just two competition points adrift of the fourth-placed Dolphins.

An unlikely top-four berth would complete a remarkable 12-month turnaround for the Knights following their 2025 wooden spoon finish.

AAP
